title: Penalties were a big factor in Buffalo vs. Houston
summary: For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. This week will be a bit shortened just like the game week. Standard and Advanced […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills looks to pass the ball during the first quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images For those of you new to the site (and I hope there are many of you), here’s the gist; every week I review the penalties from the Bills game. We talk the rules, what was a big deal. What wasn’t. This week will be a bit shortened just like the game week. Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts This is where most traditional penalty analysis lives and breathes. For us it’s just the journey. The league averages are likely a good deal higher now than they will be at the end of the season, but this is where things stand right now. Buffalo was significantly higher than average while Houston was right around it. The easy conclusion is that the Bills had the rougher day, but that’s not necessarily true. Let’s keep going. For yards called on the field, both teams had a very rough go of it. And here the script is flipped. At least on the assessed yards. Here’s where we diverge from traditional analysis. On the right side are “true yards” which count yards impacted/negated by flags as well. And when they’re added in, it’s a dead heat. Penalty harm Buffalo Bills I apologize as I have a time crunch this week so I won’t go through all the flags or have GIFs but look for those next week. The short version for any new readers is that “Harm” factors in not just the assessed yards of a flag, but those negated by penalty as well. It also counts lost downs, points negated, etc. For an example of the calculation, Christian Benford’s defensive pass interference call was assessed for 21 yards which is 2.1 harm (yards x 0.1) but also gave up a free down from second. That adds in 1.0 harm for the total of 3.1. Davison Igbinosun has a “negative” harm on his defensive holding as the Texans had gained seven yards on the play but gave that up for the free five to retain the down. It’s a rare quirk in the formula. It happens, but not enough to drastically revise the whole thing. Overall I felt the penalties were warranted on Buffalo. The too many men on the field which negated what should have been an easy conversion was in my opinion the most egregious one. I know this is brief, so let me know if you have any questions/thoughts/concerns in the comments. The Bills had 13.2 harm for this game total. 10.0 is a good enough divider between a good day and bad, so it’s safe to say the yellow laundry had an impact on Buffalo. Houston Texans The Texans by count looked much better off than Buffalo, but a closer look at impact says otherwise. The Texans had two flags over 4.0 Harm. Kamari Lassiter was called for defensive pass interference and that is all assessed yards. This occurred in the end zone, putting the ball on the one-yard line and was a true field flipper. David Montgomery was called for a chop block and this was more complex. The flag itself was 15 yards. It also wiped out a six-yard gain on 3rd & 5. That negated a first down or, put differently, impacted two downs for another 2.0 Harm. The Texans had 14.2 total harm. While not by much, despite the lower counts compared to the Bills, the Texans had the worse day.

title: 5 Detroit Lions to watch at the Buffalo Bills
summary: The Buffalo Bills are set to take on the Detroit Lions on Thursday night, and they’ll look to open play at the new Highmark Stadium with a win. After slaying their demons down south by beating the Houston Texans in Houston for the first time since 2006, Buffalo is riding high to open the 2026 […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions runs onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are set to take on the Detroit Lions on Thursday night, and they’ll look to open play at the new Highmark Stadium with a win. After slaying their demons down south by beating the Houston Texans in Houston for the first time since 2006, Buffalo is riding high to open the 2026 NFL season. The Lions also won their first game, though they took a slightly different route to do so. Detroit needed overtime to dispatch the New Orleans Saints, holding on to win 31-30 in a back-and-forth contest. Neither the Bills nor the Lions were able to pull away from their respective opponents, and it’s likely that we’re set for an entertaining game between two of the more exciting offensive clubs in the league this season. If the Bills are going to start this season 2-0, they’ll need to slow some of Detroit’s top players, and they have plenty of weapons to highlight. Here are five Lions to watch against the Bills this week. _____________________________________________________________________________ RB Jahmyr Gibbs Detroit’s top running back might wear number zero, but he’s arguably the best running back in the NFL right now. Equally dangerous as a runner and a receiver, Gibbs can hurt teams in a variety of ways. against New Orleans on Sunday, he totaled 156 rushing yards on a league-leading 29 carries. Nearly half of his rushing attempts resulted in a first down, as he achieved that mark a league-leading 14 times in Week One. As if averaging 5.4 yards per rush wasn’t impressive enough, Gibbs also totaled five receptions for 30 yards on five targets. That was actually a lower-end day for him as a receiver, as he has caught 186 passes for 1,479 yards and ten scores over the course of his career. Now in his fourth year, Gibbs is the bellcow back for the first time, as his former running mate David Montgomery is now playing for Buffalo’s Week One opponent in Houston. Montgomery scored three times in the opener against the Bills, and while Buffalo limited his efficiency by holding him to three yards per carry, he doesn’t have nearly the same burst that Gibbs does. Buffalo needs to be disciplined in its run fits, and the defense needs to be much better overall when it comes to tackling. Otherwise, Gibbs will make them pay. WR Amon-Ra St. Brown The Saints kept St. Brown relatively quiet last week, and he still caught ten passes for 67 yards and two touchdowns on 14 targets in the game. He currently leads the league in targets, receptions, and receiving touchdowns. After Buffalo allowed Nico Collins to catch seven passes for 75 yards and a score last week on ten targets, they’ll face yet another challenge this week in trying to contain St. Brown. He can operate from multiple places on the field, and whether he’s inside or outside, he’s extremely dangerous. Will defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard have top corner Christian Benford travel with him like Benford did with Collins on Sunday? Or, will Leonhard try a different strategy this week? With speedster Jameson Williams on the other side, it’s difficult to commit too many resources to one offensive target, and that’s without even discussing tight end Sam LaPorta. The Benford vs. St. Brown matchup is going to be tremendous on Thursday night. G Ben Bartch After starter Christian Mahogany suffered an injury, which looks likely to keep him out of action this week, Bartch filled in admirably against the Saints. However, with a backup center in Juice Scruggs already starting, the difficulty for Detroit’s offensive line is cranked up a notch this week. Second-year man Deone Walker was a tremendous problem for Houston on Sunday, as was veteran Ed Oliver. Not only is the talent of Buffalo’s interior defensive line something to contend with, but the crowd noise is certainly to be amped up this week. Buffalo’s home crowd is always lively, but with Thursday night being the home opener in a brand-new stadium, I expect the twelfth man to make communication difficult for Detroit. Starting a few backup offensive linemen on the road isn’t ideal, and if Buffalo’s top-line unit can take advantage of some backups up front for the Lions, they can have a huge impact on the game. DE Aiden Hutchinson This guy is a monster. Just four days after having to deal with the combination of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, Buffalo will have to find a way to deal with Hutchinson, a former No. 2 overall pick. On Sunday against New Orleans, Hutchinson had two sacks, four quarterback hits, and two tackles for loss. That’s how you impact the game up front. Buffalo had a great protection scheme in that they used double-teams, slides, and chips to keep Houston’s edge rushers off balance. They varied who was staying in to chip, and they kept switching who they double teamed, as well. The Bills will have to be just as disciplined in their plan to limit Hutchinson, as he is the kind of player who can single-handedly ruin a game plan. Left tackle Dion Dawkins and right tackle spencer Brown have to bring their A-game. CB Rock Ya-Sin A banged-up Detroit secondary is an area that Buffalo’s explosive passing offense should look to exploit this week. They’re already missing starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, who are on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Reserve safeties Thomas Harper and Christian Izien are also dealing with injuries, so players like Avonte Maddox and Chuck Clark have stepped into larger roles. That kind of unrest at the safety level puts stress on the corners, and Saints quarterback Tyler Shough picked on Ya-Sin last week. On ten targets, Ya-Sin allowed seven catches for 52 yards and a touchdown for a passer rating against of 115.2. Buffalo looked like a completely different team passing the football last week thanks in large part to the addition of DJ Moore on the outside. He opens things up for everyone, as does tight end Dalton Kincaid. If Ya-Sin is one-on-one against anyone on Thursday, I assume that quarterback Josh Allen will take his shots.

title: Exploring Detroit Lions tendencies ahead of Week 2’s game against Buffalo Bills
summary: The Lions have a clear identity. On both sides of the ball. That’s been the case for the entirety of the Dan Campbell era, the most successful era in Lions football since the Barry Sanders era in the mid-to-late 1990s. Let’s dive into those clear tendencies before the Buffalo Bills host the Lions on Thursday […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on during warm-ups before a preseason game against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Lions have a clear identity. On both sides of the ball. That’s been the case for the entirety of the Dan Campbell era, the most successful era in Lions football since the Barry Sanders era in the mid-to-late 1990s. Let’s dive into those clear tendencies before the Buffalo Bills host the Lions on Thursday Night Football in Week 2. You know, the home-opening prime time game you’ve had circled on the calendar for months now. It’s finally right around the corner. Lions offense Jared Goff vs. pressure Every quarterback experiences a dip in efficiency while under pressure. It’s only natural. BUT, no one has a larger discrepancy in performance from a clean pocket compared to when pressured over the past three seasons. Check this from Fantasy Points’ Scott Barrett, posted right before the season: Jared Goff is literally the worst most pressure-sensitive QB in football @FantasyPtsData https://t.co/g8Vm0sf90n pic.twitter.com/eMa02boPe0 — Scott Barrett (@ScottBarrettDFB) September 3, 2026 So while technically every week “pressure the quarterback” could be key to the game for a defense, it’s really important in this game for the Bills against Goff. He might be the last true drop back quarterback in today’s NFL. Not only does he have the largest EPA per drop back difference in his clean pocket vs. pressured drop backs, his clean pockets amounted to the No. 1 EPA per drop in all of football from 2023 to 2025. Bananas! He was only pressured on 22% of his drop backs against the Saints in Week 1 — a very low number — and went 3-of-7 for 49 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions. But the larger-sample based point remains. Getting to Goff is absolutely paramount. Under center The surge in under center plays across the NFL was one of the fascinating storylines from Week 1, and a reminder of the league’s cyclical nature. NFL league wide under center usage jumped dramatically in Week 1. On normal situation 1st & 10 plays, NFL offenses were under center 66.5% of the time, up from 45.9% in Week 1 of 2025, a 20.6 percentage point jump. That’s higher than every full season rate since 2012. — Ryan Paganetti (@RyanPaganetti) September 14, 2026 The Lions want to live under center. And their narrow victory over the Saints was an indicator of the point of emphasis for Detroit’s offense. Per Football Insights on Twitter , via Fantasy Points Data, the Lions were under center on 75% of their offensive plays in Week 1, second only to the Raiders (75.5%). The third place team in under-center snaps (Ravens) came in at 66.7%. The Bills were under center on 64.3% of their offensive plays in Houston. Jahmyr Gibbs, workhouse In his first two seasons in with the Lions, Gibbs was indisputably in a running back committee with David Montgomery. ‘Tis not the case anymore, especially with Isaiah Pacheco on IR. Gibbs toted the rock 29 times — for 156 yards — against the Saints. Backup Sione Vaki had two carries for seven yards. Gibbs also caught five passes for another 30 yards. His 29 carries were five attempts more than anyone else in the NFL in Week 1. Make no mistake about it — Gibbs is a distinct workhorse in this Lions offense. They want him to touch the ball as frequently as realistically possible, and he’s super explosive, all of which is why he likely went No. 1 overall in your fantasy draft. Play Action I’ll be brief here, because this is straight-forward. Due to their ground-game affinity, the Lions like to first sell the run before passing as much as any club in football. In 2024, Goff led qualifying quarterbacks with 35.7% of his drop backs coming on play action. A season ago his percentage dipped to 28.1% but still ranked in the Top 10 of the NFL. On Sunday against the Saints, Goff utilized play action on 34.1% of his drop backs. This has long been a staple of Detroit’s aerial attack. Lions Defense Blitz happy Detroit defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard — yes, that Kelvin Sheppard — had his unit blitz at the 13th-highest rate in 2025 at 26.6%. In Week 1, he ignited the blitz, sending an extra rusher on 43% of the Saints drop backs, which amounted to the fifth-highest rate among all teams. For the record, Jim Leonhard blitzed C.J. Stroud 24.7% of the time, the 17th-highest in Week 1. Given the Lions don’t have their starting safeties, Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, who, when healthy, might be the best safety tandem in the NFL, if Week 1 is any indication of Sheppard’s philosophy, he simply wants to regularly send the house in hopes of getting the football out of the hands of the opposing quarterback as quickly as possible to limit long-developing routes being targeted downfield. Aidan Hutchinson, workhorse For as much as Gibbs is a one-man show — and a damn good one at that — in the backfield for the Lions, Hutchinson is a one-man wrecking crew on the edge getting after the passer on this Detroit defense. In Week 1, he registered a whopping 10 pressures. The next-highest pressure total came from nose tackle Alim McNeill, who had three. Last season, counting the playoffs, Hutchinson accumulated 100 pressures. Second on the team was Al-Quadin Muhammad, with 53, and he signed with the Buccaneers in free agency. In April, the Lions drafted Derrick Moore in the second round, a rusher I liked quite a bit before the draft, but expectations shouldn’t be astronomically high for him. D.J. Wonnum was the free-agent signee to bookend Hutchinson on the edge. He did muster three pressures against New Orleans yet has only eclipsed the 40-pressure plateau once in his NFL career, and that came back in 2021, his second professional season. The Lions lean on Hutchinson to generate consistent pressure probably more than any other club relies on its No. 1 pass rusher.

title: Bills at Texans Week 1 snap counts: Tight ends take over,  defense logs 79 snaps
summary: The Buffalo Bills opened the 2026 season with a thrilling 36-31 win over the Houston Texans, but the final score only tells part of the story. Buffalo’s offense produced 36 points and 409 total yards on just 58 snaps. The defense, meanwhile, was forced to play 79 snaps as Houston sustained drives and repeatedly tested […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 13: Tight end Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills screams after a first down reception during the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Buffalo Bills on September 13, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX.(Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Buffalo Bills opened the 2026 season with a thrilling 36-31 win over the Houston Texans, but the final score only tells part of the story. Buffalo’s offense produced 36 points and 409 total yards on just 58 snaps. The defense, meanwhile, was forced to play 79 snaps as Houston sustained drives and repeatedly tested Buffalo’s secondary. The Week 1 snap counts give us our first meaningful look at how head coach Joe Brady and his staff plan to divide Buffalo’s roles this season. They also reveal several immediate storylines, including an offense built around multiple tight ends, a surprisingly straightforward running-back rotation and a defensive front that relied heavily on its top four players. Bills offensive snap counts: 58 snaps Offensive line starts with perfect attendance There was no rotation or interruption along Buffalo’s offensive line. Alec Anderson, Dion Dawkins, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence and Spencer Brown played all 58 offensive snaps. That continuity helped Buffalo avoid a repeat of last season’s nightmare in Houston, when Allen was sacked eight times and took several additional hits. The Texans still created pressure, but Buffalo’s starting five remained intact and gave Allen enough time to throw for 334 yards and lead the game-winning 96-yard drive. Tackle Tylan Grable was the only reserve offensive lineman to appear, joining the offense for one snap as an extra blocker. The tight ends were everywhere Buffalo’s tight-end usage may be the most revealing number from the entire offensive table. Joe Brady did not simply keep four tight ends on the roster for decoration. Dalton Kincaid played 42 snaps, or 72%, while Dawson Knox was on the field for 39 snaps, or 67%. Jackson Hawes added another 25 snaps, reaching 43%. Even Keleki Latu saw action, playing four offensive snaps. Altogether, Buffalo’s four tight ends accounted for 110 player-snaps across 58 offensive plays. That works out to nearly 2 tight ends per play. Buffalo used 13 personnel, featuring one running back and three tight ends, on 37% of its offensive snaps which strongly suggests that multiple-tight-end formations will serve as a foundation of this offense. James Cook leads a clean running-back rotation Unsurprisingly, James Cook had 42 snaps, 72% of the offensive counts. The more interesting backfield number came behind him. Frank Gore Jr., elevated from the practice squad with Ty Johnson unavailable, played 11 offensive snaps. Ray Davis received only five. Neither had much rushing production, with one carry for three yards apiece. Still, Gore receiving more than twice as many offensive snaps as Davis is something worth following. DJ Moore immediately took over a major role DJ Moore led every Bills skill-position player with 44 offensive snaps, good for a 76% share. He also delivered five receptions for 100 yards and a touchdown in his Buffalo debut. There should be no question about Moore’s place in this offense after one week. He was Buffalo’s most-used wide receiver. Khalil Shakir played 31 snaps, followed closely by Keon Coleman with 29. Joshua Palmer received only 18 offensive snaps below that of Coleman, but one of them produced the biggest play of the afternoon: his 34-yard game-winning touchdown reception. That is an important reminder that snap counts explain opportunity, but they do not always measure impact. Bills defensive snap counts: 79 snaps Buffalo’s defense had a much heavier workload than its offense, playing 21 additional snaps. That helps place some of the individual percentages in context. Several members of the defense were asked to handle enormous workloads in the first game of the season. Three defenders never left the field The Bills had three defenders play all 79 snaps: linebacker Terrel Bernard, cornerback Christian Benford and safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson. Cole Bishop played 72 snaps. Maxwell Hairston played 66 snaps, giving the second year cornerback an 84% share in his first start of the season. Dee Alford handled 48 snaps in the slot. The secondary rotation will be worth monitoring, but the larger concern is how frequently Houston found favorable matchups against it. The defensive front carried a heavy load Ed Oliver led Buffalo’s defensive linemen with 65 snaps, an 82% share. That is a substantial workload for an interior defender. Deone Walker followed with 51 snaps, while Dorian Williams played 53. The snap counts show that Buffalo did not treat Deone Walker as a rotational project. He was one of the defense’s primary players in the opener. The interior rotation existed, but Oliver and Walker carried the overwhelming majority of the workload. Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb each played 63 snaps, or 80% from the EDGE. Like Oliver and Walker inside, Rousseau and Chubb were clearly established as Buffalo’s preferred edge combination. With the defense playing so many snaps, however, managing those workloads on a four-day turnaround will be worth watching. Bernard and Williams form the primary linebacker pairing Terrell Bernard never left the field, while Dorian Williams played 53 snaps, or 67%. Buffalo’s linebacker distribution was fairly straightforward. Bernard handled every-down communication duties, while Williams served as the primary linebacker next to him when the defensive package required it. Bills special-teams snap counts Sam Franklin Jr. led Buffalo with 25 special-teams snaps, or 81%, without appearing on defense. Jordan Hancock was directly behind him with 23 snaps, or 74%. Joe Andreessen and Keleki Latu each played 20, or 65%. Latu’s usage is particularly informative. He played only four offensive snaps but was one of Buffalo’s busiest special-teams players. That role helps explain his value on a tight-end depth chart that already includes Kincaid, Knox and Hawes. What do these numbers tell us? Buffalo’s Week 1 snap counts reveal an offense that wants to use size and versatility. The Bills kept multiple tight ends involved, made Moore their leading receiver by playing time and trusted Kincaid with a much broader role. They also received steady work from an offensive line that did not miss a snap. Defensively, the story was different. Buffalo’s starters were asked to play far too much football. Bernard, Benford and Gardner-Johnson never left the field, while Oliver, Rousseau and Chubb all handled heavy workloads. The Bills have little time to recover or make corrections. Detroit arrives Thursday night for the first regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium, giving Buffalo only four days between games to determine how the Bills will get their defense off the field.
author: Sara Larson

title: Detroit Lions at Buffalo Bills Week 3 injury tracker
summary: The Buffalo Bills returned from their little field trip to Houston fairly healthy, but now as they prepare to face the Detroit Lions on Thursday Night Football’s Week 2 airing, they aren’t going to have much time to heal up what things bumps and bruises they are dealing with.  The first report of Week 2 is a little […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: DJ Moore #2 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Houston Texans during the second quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills returned from their little field trip to Houston fairly healthy , but now as they prepare to face the Detroit Lions on Thursday Night Football’s Week 2 airing, they aren’t going to have much time to heal up what things bumps and bruises they are dealing with. The first report of Week 2 is a little longer than last week’s, but it’s still not scary. NOTE: This tracker will be updated following each injury report leading up to kickoff. _____________________________________________________________________________ Buffalo Bills injury report Monday It’s important to remember that the Bills did not actually practice on Monday. This list just represents what they estimate participation would have been had they actually done anything much more than film work and rest and recovery exercises. Monday injury report pic.twitter.com/vvOoRtQuKf — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 14, 2026 Limited Practice LB Terrel Bernard – Calf RB Ty Johnson – Hamstring DL T.J. Sanders – Knee Full Practice S Cole Bishop – Knee/Groin OLB Bradley Chubb – Thumb DB Jordan Hancock – Quad What we’re watching The good news is that DJ Moore’s quick trip to the medical tent Sunday afternoon, along with Josh Allen’s temporary hand discomfort, didn’t amount to anything. I would expect Ty Johnson to return this week, but if he does, what does that mean for Frank Gore, Jr.? The second-year running back was called up from the practice squad Sunday and out snapped Ray Davis on offense. In fact, the Bills’ fourth running back doubled Davis’s snaps: Gore, Jr. 10, Davis 5. Offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael, Jr. — or Joe Brady depending on how we want to look at the Buffalo offense – seemed very content using Gore, Jr. in a blocking role. It’s unlikely that Bernard will be unavailable, but if he can’t we could see Shaq Thompson called up from the practice squad. Tuesda y Tuesday injury report pic.twitter.com/FteY4KZ9jd — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) September 15, 2026 No Practice DT T.J. Sanders Limited Practice LB Terrel Bernard S Cole Bishop RB Ty Johnson Full Practice OLB Bradley Chubb DB Jordan Hancock What we’re watching Bishop was technically “downgraded” to limited after an estimated full practice on Monday. There’s no serious indication he could miss this game, however. Apparently Sanders was sick, which led to his absence. He did not play in Week 1 against the Texans, remember. I’m mostly zeroing in on Johnson. Despite getting in a practice on Friday before Week 1’s game in Houston, Buffalo decided to keep the veteran on the sidelines as he nurses his hamstring injury back to full health. For as much as it might seem like he should be close to 100% by now — after suffering the injury in the Blue & Red Scrimmage in early August — the Bills could be staring at the 10-day layoff after this game and decide to keep him on the shelf for one more (game) week. He’s appeared in 64 games with 38 starts in his six seasons to date. As for Scruggs, who, at this point, seems more likely to play than Miller, if he’s unavailable for Thursday night’s game, the Lions would have to do some positional shuffling, as they don’t have a dedicated backup center on the 53-man roster right now. summary: Let’s start my season of analysis with an apology. First off, the Buffalo Bills are on a short week and everything is very compressed. I’m also on-call for my full time position and they needed my Monday night too. Even worse, I was wholly prepared to highlight D.J. Moore and how awesome he was, but then Dalton Kincaid also had an amazing game. And Khalil Shakir had a steady game too. So what’s a Skare to do with very little time and so many things to cover? Easy, rip through a few highlights and pretend it’s some kind of deep analysis. What the heck, I think we’re all in a celebratory mood anyway. Highlights masquerading as analysis Dalton Kincaid pic.twitter.com/14haAAmiTs — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 15, 2026 If you look at the yardage of 130, it’s hard to believe that Dalton Kincaid only had five receptions on six targets. That’s a preposterous 26-yards per reception. A huge part of that is the route tree with Kincaid being asked to run more like a wide receiver. In just the three clips above, Kincaid is lined up in three different spots with some pretty deep routes. Kincaid delivered on the trust given to him by Joe Brady and Josh Allen. In the first play, expert use of hands leaves Kincaid with space to high point the ball for an incredible catch. On the second one, Kincaid compresses himself to slip by a defender (finesse) then drags some dudes for extra yards like you’d want a tight end to do. On the final play, there’s more of the wiggle to avoid the first tackle, shifts lanes quickly to avoid a second tackle, and is only stopped by the sideline. This is the tight end Bills fans have been dreaming of for quite some time. Fingers crossed this is the new normal. D.J. Moore pic.twitter.com/zRNO9vXHwm — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 15, 2026 It’s pretty amazing that D.J. Moore’s stat line of five catches (eight targets) and 100 yards would be in second place for yards per reception after hitting 20 yards per. It’s arguable he had the better day thanks to a long touchdown, but it’s a true argument hence the dual “analysis.” For D.J. Moore, I’d like to emphasize his capability to protect himself when contact is unavoidable, but also the timing he’s already shown with Josh Allen. Both of the first catches shown have Allen winding up before Moore is even looking and hitting the receiver on his break. Moore also did an incredible job snatching a frozen rope pass from Allen. I’d add that there was a bit of luck on the touchdown. The defender went for the pass breakup rather than the tackle and it cost them big. I would also add that Moore plays the sideline perfectly and manages to maneuver and make the score. Week 1 lies in the NFL, but there’s some hope this is the new look offense for the Bills. It was hard to improve on offense but after a single contest it’s looking quite possible.

The Patriots played the Dolphins at Gillette Stadium on January 4, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers have waived their primary returner and second-year wide receiver Jimmy Horn Jr just a couple days after an abysmal performance in their season opener against the Chicago Bears. They have signed linebacker Tyrel Dodson off the practice squad in a corresponded roster move. This is a two-for-one response to failures from both the special teams unit and the defense from Sunday’s surrender of 59 points. Horn routinely struggled to field punts and kicks and has not provided positive value in a crowded receiver room to date. Meanwhile, on defense, the Panthers gave up 291 rushing yards on 39 attempts (7.5 yards per attempt) and four rushing touchdowns to the Bears. Clearly they need some additional help. Enter Tyrel Dodson. He had 129 tackles, ten for loss, and five sacks last season in 16 starts for the Miami Dolphins. The 28-year old linebacker has long been seen as more of a run defender than a true coverage linebacker, but that seems to fit the Panthers weakness right now. In the return game, look for Chuba Hubbard and Xavier Legette to take the majority of punts and kicks.

title: Will the Vikings’ Dallas Turner stop the Bears in their tracks?
summary: The chatter around the Chicago Bears’ offense has hit a new zenith. The laughter around Ben Johnson’s assertion of being the “highest-scoring offense of all time” has quieted significantly after hanging 59 points on a defense with legitimate talent. Still, the Bears offense faces a daunting challenge in Week 2 as they face off against […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - SEPTEMBER 13: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Dallas Turner (15) celebrates his strip sack of Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) during the fourth quarter of a NFL game between the Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers on September 13, 2026, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis MN. (Photo by Nick Wosika/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The chatter around the Chicago Bears’ offense has hit a new zenith. The laughter around Ben Johnson’s assertion of being the “highest-scoring offense of all time” has quieted significantly after hanging 59 points on a defense with legitimate talent. Still, the Bears offense faces a daunting challenge in Week 2 as they face off against the Minnesota Vikings and Brian Flores. Flores, as many of you already know, has developed quite the reputation for causing chaos for other teams’ offenses, mixing up exotic blitz packages that frequently confuse quarterbacks. I expect no different from Flores this Sunday as he aims to stymie the Caleb Williams-led attack. In fact, Brian Flores blitzed Jordan Love on 78.3% of dropbacks, per Next Gen Stats, resulting in a pressure rate above 50% and 4 sacks. An absolute manic. Still, Flores has an emerging weapon who may let him drop more into coverage — Dallas Turner. Turner, in his third season, had nine pressures, seven QB hits, one sack, and one forced fumble in the first game of the season. For those keeping track at home, seven is a lot of QB hits to have in one game. This would suggest that Turner is continuing to build on the improvements he made last season, jumping from three sacks as a rookie in 2024 to eight, and with the departure of Jonathan Greenard, Turner is now the feature EDGE on a defense that relies on having good DEs. Turner primarily lines up on the right side of the line, across from the LT, which means that he will likely lock horns with Braxton Jones. This matchup will be crucial for both sides. It is well documented that Jones relies primarily on his athleticism to stay with quicker DEs, while he struggles to anchor against bigger/stronger DEs. Turner is a smaller EDGE at 6’-3” and 247 lbs who relies on his speed and bend to beat opposing OLs. This is a strength-against-strength matchup, as the Bears will rely heavily on Jones’ quick feet to neutralize Turner. While struggling on a handful of pass sets against Trevis Gipson, Jones looked relatively sharp against a deep DL in Carolina, only surrendering 2 pressures on the day. While Caleb Williams has a tendency to bail out his OL at times, especially on the blindside, Jones will still need to keep the speedy Turner in front of him to keep Williams clean. Love showed that it is possible to beat the Brian Flores blitz in the first three quarters of the game, with a 60% completion, 227 yards passing, and 2 TD passes against it. The blitz eventually overwhelmed him and the Packers’ OL in the 4th quarter, leading to 1 INT, 2 FFs, and 3 sacks. With that said, if Flores is concerned about Ben Johnson’s ability to scheme pass catchers open quickly, he could rely on Turner to beat Jones outright. If this is the case, Braxton Jones’ ability to withstand the pressure will be critical to a Bears win.

title: Caleb Williams Week 1 QB Grade: Bears @ Panthers Film Breakdown
summary: Note: As you may recall, I like to do select play breakdowns from each week. However, this week I’m away from my usual editing setup, so I won’t be able to put those together. Instead, I’ll be linking to breakdowns of some plays I’d like to highlight from a few of my favorite Bears and […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Carolina Panthers during the first half of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Note: As you may recall, I like to do select play breakdowns from each week. However, this week I’m away from my usual editing setup, so I won’t be able to put those together. Instead, I’ll be linking to breakdowns of some plays I’d like to highlight from a few of my favorite Bears and football content creators. People, it feels so good to be back. The long hibernation from Chicago Bears football is finally over, and boy did we wake up with a roar. In a game that featured very little defense, the Chicago Bears took down the Carolina Panthers 59-37. I’m sure many of you have already heard some of the gaudy numbers and records put up by a Bears offense led by Caleb Williams and coached by offensive guru Ben Johnson, but for those who may have missed a few of them, let’s do a quick recap. It was the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history, with both teams combining for 96 points , breaking the previous mark of 88 set by the Buccaneers and Saints in 2018. The 59 points scored by Chicago set a franchise record for the most points in a season opener. They were also the most points the Bears have scored in any game since December 7, 1980, when they absolutely smoked the Green Bay Packers 61-7. And the records didn’t stop there. Chicago racked up 552 yards of total offense, the most the franchise has ever produced in a season opener and tied for the seventh-most in Bears history. It was also the second time in Ben Johnson’s tenure that Chicago has eclipsed 500 yards of offense, joining the ridiculous 576-yard performance against Cincinnati last season. Among those 552 yards, the Bears saw both D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai rush for more than 100 yards, marking the second time in just seven regular-season games that the duo has accomplished the feat. Before Swift and Monangai first did it against Philadelphia last November, you had to go all the way back to 1985, when Walter Payton and Matt Suhey each rushed for more than 100 yards against the Lions. Not to be outdone, or left out of the record book, Caleb Williams set a Bears franchise mark of his own. With another two touchdown passes against Carolina, Williams has now thrown for at least two touchdowns in eight consecutive games, including the playoffs. The streak dates all the way back to December 7 against the Packers at Lambeau Field and is now the longest such streak by a quarterback in Bears history. And somehow, after scoring 59 points and piling up 552 yards, the prevailing feeling inside the Bears locker room was that they still left points on the board . That might be the craziest part of all of this. For me personally, it was one of the most memorable opening games to a Bears season since 2012, when Chicago kicked off the year with a 41-21 win over the Indianapolis Colts. For more information including scoring key, game-by-game grading sheets, weekly grading scorecards, and an overall look at his 2026 season, you can view Caleb’s entire season workbook here . Benchmarks Stat Formatting Key: (Last Season totals are underlined , Last Season averages in Italics , and this week’s stats appear in regular text.) C/A: 330/568 (58.1%) | 19.4/33.4 (58.1%) | 21/29 72.4% Yards: 3942 | 231.9 | 269 Touchdowns: 31 | 1.8 | 4 Turnovers: 8 | 0.5 | 0 QB at Fault Sacks: 1 3 | 0.8 | 0 aDOT: 8.9 | 10.7 Passer Rating: 90.1 | 124.1 True Passer Rating : 125. 8 | 173.6 Time to Throw: 3.00s | 3.04s Time to Pressure: 2.67s | 2.56s Pressure Rate: 30.84% | 41.46% On-Target Rate: 67.6% | 84.0% Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 9.0 % PPR / 7.6% BPR | 4.7% PPR / 11.6% BRP EPA per dropback: +0.11 | +0.54 ANY/A : 6.8 | 9.7 Game Scorecard The full grading sheet for each play can be found here. Game Notes Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score , which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward. NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN:IS: 124.1 / 173.6 / 87.7 The average NFL passer rating through Week 1 of the 2026 season sits at 95.3 , putting Williams’ 124.1 NFL Passer Rating well above the league average and firmly in the range of a very good to near elite performance based off that metric. A 173.6 TPR represents an elite game in my model, with 100 serving as the baseline for “Average.” Caleb had just one start during the 2025 season north of a 170 TPR, when he posted a 187.7 against the Dallas Cowboys in Week 3. He has now already matched that total in one game. On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying quarterback and 90 represents elite territory, Williams’ 87.7 Impact Score was one of the best performances of Week 1. His 87.7 ranked third among all quarterbacks for the week. Williams averaged a 74.9 Impact Score during the 2025 season, which ranked 20th among quarterbacks. Needless to say, he’s off to a much hotter start in that metric this year. On-Target Throws: 2025 Season Average: 67.6% | Week 1 vs. Panthers: 84.0% Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. On-target throws are only measured on aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line of scrimmage are excluded. Drops, however, can still count as on-target throws. Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 15/15 | 100.0% On-Target Deep-Level Passing (10–20+ yards): 6/10 | 60.0% On-Target Williams had just one start during the 2025 season in which he topped an 80.0% On-Target Rate: Week 15 against the Cleveland Browns, when he also finished at 84.0% . One start into the 2026 season, and he has already matched his best mark from a year ago. It also represents a massive improvement from where he started last season. Against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 1 of 2025, Williams posted just a 41.7% On-Target Rate . One year later, he more than doubled that number in his season debut. Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 4.7% PPR / 11.6% BPR Williams averaged a 9.0% Poor Play Rate in 2025 compared to a 7.6% Big Play Rate . He’s off to a much better start in both categories this season, recording just two poor plays across 43 graded plays while producing five big plays against Carolina. The best of the bunch was his 22-yard touchdown throw to Cole Kmet, a perfectly placed ball with linebacker Devin Lloyd draped over Kmet in coverage. Time to Throw: 3.19 seconds Williams posted a 3.19-second Time to Throw, 0.19 seconds higher than his 2025 season mark. As we know by now, that number can be somewhat deceiving with Williams. A portion of it is inflated by his uncanny ability to extend plays, escape pressure and keep his eyes downfield rather than simply taking what would otherwise be a dead play. Under Pressure: +0.66 EPA per dropback Williams was particularly dangerous when pressured against Carolina, leading all quarterbacks in Week 1 in EPA per dropback while under pressure , according to PFN using TruMedia data, at +0.66 EPA/dropback . Using the same pressure charting for a more traditional look at his performance, Williams completed 4 of 8 passes for 96 yards and a touchdown, good for a 133.3 passer rating. And that doesn’t account for what he did with his legs, where he added two rushing touchdowns on scrambles. A Tale of Two Halfs?: Well, not really. Despite a pretty jarring difference between the scores for each half (6.60 vs. -0.30) Caleb was tasked to do less within the second half, sticking to underneath routes that focused on moving the chains while the ground game took over. 6 of his 9 second half…

title: Bears-Panthers Upon Further Review: A Closer Look at the Referees
summary: Hello Chicago Bears Fans!  Welcome to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag, that’s right – the refs.  Every week when the Bears end up in the loss column, Bears fans leave Soldier Field (or the living room) with the same two questions: Did we actually lose that game, or did […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 6: A detail view of a flag on the field during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game between the Carolina Panthers and the Chicago Bears, at Soldier Field on October 6, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello Chicago Bears Fans! Welcome to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag, that’s right – the refs. Every week when the Bears end up in the loss column, Bears fans leave Soldier Field (or the living room) with the same two questions: Did we actually lose that game, or did the officials take it from us? And when we are in the win column, we will inevitably hear from opponents’ fans that they were robbed by the refs. Well, were they? Upon Further Review exists to answer these questions with film, the rulebook, and a consistent grading scale: Each week I’ll isolate the flags and no-calls that went against Chicago and against the opponent, grade every one as Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, or Horrible, then roll those grades into four numbers: a Calls-Against-Bears rating, a Calls-Against-Opponent rating, an overall referee performance score, and a differential that shows which sideline got the better of the crew. I’ll also pull the most controversial calls from around the league so we can see what call this year will have NFL fans screaming, “wait, what?” and NFL rules analysts assuring us, “always has been.” Chicago beat Carolina 59–37 on Sunday in Charlotte. Official totals: Bears 12 penalties for 57 yards, Panthers 11 for 84 yards. Below are all accepted flags, in order, with the player named, the yardage, the game clock, and the score when the penalty was enforced. First Quarter CHI 0, CAR 0 Rome Odunze (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 15:00, first play from scrimmage. Swift’s 17-yard run came back; ball spotted at the CHI 19. Dayo Odeyingbo (CHI), roughing the passer, 1 yard — 12:54. After Young’s 26-yard completion to Coker at the CHI 2. Half-the-distance; first-and-goal at the 1. Montez Sweat (CHI), defensive offside, 0 yards — 12:44. Already at the 1; replay first-and-goal. Darren Waller (CAR), offensive pass interference, 9 yards — 12:29. Waller’s 1-yard TD catch wiped off. First-and-goal from the 10. CHI 0, CAR 7 Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding, 9 yards — 10:09. Swift’s 9-yard run on 3rd-and-1 nullified. Cairo Santos (CHI), kickoff short of landing zone — 5:52. Ball placed at the CAR 40 (no yardage in the official 57-yard total). CHI 14, CAR 7 Isaiah Simmons (CAR), offensive holding, 10 yards — 1:59, on the kickoff return. Carolina started at its 17. M. Freeling (CAR), false start, 5 yards — 1:27. Second Q uarter CHI 14, CAR 7 Mitchell Evans (CAR), unnecessary roughness, 15 yards — 15:00. After Raymond’s 23-yard punt return to the CHI 44; Bears started at the CAR 41 and scored two plays later (Kmet 22-yard TD). CHI 21, CAR 14 S. Snapshot: Flags For and Against In our inaugural UFR, I’m glad I’m not in a position to analyze the flags that cost us the game. In fact, it was flags against the Carolina Panthers that were pivotal – the first-ever “roughing the passer” call for Caleb Williams, erasing a 2 nd and 20 near the red zone, and an interception at the goal line that was erased by an offside. Both of those flags were on Carolina Panthers defensive lineman, Derrick Brown. Carolina also had two touchdowns called back for offensive pass interference (Waller in Q1, Coker/Evans in Q4). That said, while those penalties were certainly the most impactful, in my evaluation none of them were incorrect calls. Chicago’s flags were more volume than impact—two landing-zone kickoffs, two holdings that were overcome, and a pair of small defensive infractions near the goal line—except Odeyingbo’s first-quarter roughing, which put Carolina at the 1, and arguably Rome Odunze’s holding call on the first snap of the game, which killed a first down run, and on the next play Luther Burden would fumble the football, leading to a Carolina touchdown. Flag of the Game: The “Roughing the Passer” on Derrick Brown Panthers called for roughing the passer for this hit to Caleb Williams pic.twitter.com/I8GD65igAT — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) September 13, 2026 Rule that matters: once the passer leaves the pocket and throws on the run, he loses the one-step protection. He still cannot be hit late with no attempt to avoid, stuffed, or driven through. Williams is outside the pocket, retreating, then dumps the ball toward the sideline. Brown (#95) is still coming. Contact is after the release. Williams goes down hard. Brown said he thought it was one step. Canales called it the two-step rule and “tight.” From video review, it is more than one step. Both from a forcible contact perspective (forearm to Caleb’s sternum) and from the differential between when the pass left Caleb’s hand and when Brown made contact (close to two full steps) – this is classic RTP. I rate this call correct. Brown had plenty of time to pull up and instead he delivers a blow to the quarterback. Upon Further Review — Week 1: Bears 59, Panthers 37 Crew: Brad Allen . Official totals: Chicago 12–57 , Carolina 11–84 . Scale: Correct / Arguable / Incorrect / Horrible . title: Midweek Musings: Buckle Up, Bears Fans
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: The summer of 2026 was mostly a hot and humid mess in the Midwest. It rained a lot, the temps got uncomfortable early, and we were offered […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears looks on against the Carolina Panthers during the fourth quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: The summer of 2026 was mostly a hot and humid mess in the Midwest. It rained a lot, the temps got uncomfortable early, and we were offered few reprieves. Then football started, and cooler weather arrived. We’re close to hoodie season. You can almost taste the apple cider. I love autumn, mainly for the football, but give me all the other good stuff that comes with it too. I’ve never correctly advocated for a Chicago Bears head coach candidate before Chicago landed Ben Johnson – and I was extremely early. It was early in the 2023 season I started pushing it and when I dropped the idea on a Lions podcast, the hosts about kicked me off the show. I knew I had something at that moment. It’s given me an added layer of enjoyment to this new era of Bears football. I was extremely confident the Bears would be getting an offensive mastermind. I had no idea he’d be such a badass. The new Nike Bears logo is incredible. I love this thing so freaking much . I might need to get another writing gig to help pay off all the gear I’m going to buy. Don’t tell my wife. I was wrong about D’Andre Swift. I said he was a supercharged RB2 or a decent lead in a committee but he wasn’t a guy who could dominate in the run game. While that was the book on Swift before he landed in Chicago – and a fair representation of his work in 2024 – he’s been a much improved back under the Ben Johnson regime. It’s not often you see this type of growth this deep into a player’s career. Kudos to him for making it work. I liked the Panthers jerseys – the black and Carolina Blue (or whatever they’re calling it) is a fun look. I just can’t understand choosing to wear dark colors on a hot day in September while letting your opponent where the traditional away whites. The temps were brutal. I wonder if they regret their uniform choice. Speaking of the hot Carolina temps – did you catch Caleb Williams wiping his hand off mid-play to get a better grip on the football? I don’t think I’ve ever seen that before. Caleb wipes his throwing hand mid-play pic.twitter.com/u3rIOUC44h — Adam Hoge (@AdamHoge) September 15, 2026 PFF put out a grade on Caleb Williams that sure looked like they didn’t watch the same game the rest of the world saw on Sunday. Really good reminder that the grades are an invention for engagement, as explained by their founder years ago. Engage in those grades at your own risk, positive or negative. I said on Bear & Balanced this week that I thought that might’ve been one of Caleb’s best games as a pro. He looked completely in charge and had a steady, high-level performance. There are a couple of throws and runs that will make his end of season highlight reel, yes, but there were so many smart decisions on when to run, when to throw away, and when to check the ball down that were a work in progress last season. This is big trouble for the rest of the league and for those Caleb haters in your group chats. If you’re just coming back to the site and missed my story on the history of the Chicago Bears mascots , I promise you it’s worth your time. These niche history dives are fun but always take more time than I think they will. I thought the TD pass to Jahdae Walker was beautiful. The pass itself was a nice little schematic win, but the fact that Ben Johnson schemed up Walker after he did all the dirty work all game was one of those football moments where you know that guys are buying in and Johnson understands how to reward hard work. Football euphoria. Did you notice that Carolina wanted nothing to do with Zavion Thomas on their kickoffs? I’m curious if that’s a trend we’ll see and, if so, whether there’s a way to call a better return play knowing they’ll be targeting the non-Zavion returner. Plenty of hand-wringing over the defense, and I get it; we’ve come to expect a certain standard of living on the defensive side of the ball over the years. Let’s see where it goes over the next few weeks, but I want those of you who can’t help but lead with the negative to do me a favor and look up at the scoreboard once in a while. This is fun if you’re willing to join the rest of us. I’m eager to get to the Vikings game. I have a lot of Vikings fans in my general orbit, and while we can all be happy for them reveling in their big win against Green Bay last week, it’s time to start making a statement with a divisional victory. I don’t really care who is playing quarterback; jump on this team early and dare them to play in the track meet with you. Pushing teams to get out of their comfort zone puts the ball in harm’s way and will allow the Bears to continue their dominance in the turnover differential. Only 548 more points to break the 2013 Broncos mark…

summary: After lighting up the scoreboard in week one, the Chicago Bears are generating headlines and catching the attention of the NFL world. Week one of the season is always full of surprises, and this week was no different. Beyond surprising results like the Chargers losing to the Cardinals or the Giants beating the Cowboys, bigger […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears hands off the ball to Kyle Monangai #25 against the Carolina Panthers during the second quarter of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images After lighting up the scoreboard in week one, the Chicago Bears are generating headlines and catching the attention of the NFL world. Week one of the season is always full of surprises, and this week was no different. Beyond surprising results like the Chargers losing to the Cardinals or the Giants beating the Cowboys, bigger storylines emerged. Scoring was way, way up. And the Bears were part of it. We know the Bears are going to move up the ranks after such a headline-grabbing performance. And they were assisted by the likes of some of the week one national darling teams laying eggs (shoutout Green Bay!). Let’s see where Chicago lands this week. WCG – Aaron Leming 7. Chicago Bears (1-0) Initial Week 1 Thought: The offense’s Year 2 jump under Ben Johnson is evident, but the defense might keep them from being a legitimate Super Bowl contender. The Bears must find some defensive balance, and it must happen in a hurry. Better health will help, but for now, the offense will face continued pressure to produce 30-plus points per game. The Athletic – Josh Kendall and Chad Graff 4. Chicago Bears (1-0) Last week: 10 Sunday: Beat Panthers 59-37 What we learned: Best offense in the NFL? Ben Johnson told our Dan Pompei this offseason that he wanted to build the highest-scoring offense in league history. It seemed outlandish at the time. Then the Bears hung 59 on the Panthers in Week 1, and suddenly anything seems possible. The defense carries plenty of questions, but that offense was unbelievable. Yahoo Sports – Frank Schwab 10. Chicago Bears (1-0, LW: 11) The Bears are going to be fun to watch. The offense was fantastic against a Panthers defense that isn’t great but not that bad (22nd in defensive DVOA last season). They put up 59 points, a franchise record for a season opener, and 552 yards. That’s great. They also allowed 37 points and 478 yards against a Panthers offense that was 25th in DVOA last season. Every game might be a pinball machine. And the Bears’ offense might be so good it doesn’t matter how much the defense allows. It’s why they’re not higher in the top 10. NFL.com – Nick Shook 8. Chicago Bears (11) Ben Johnson stated his intent to rewrite the offensive record books with his team in 2026. After one week, the Bears are on pace to do so. They detonated the Panthers in a style that mirrored their 2025 success, running the ball authoritatively and letting Caleb Williams make superstar plays in an incredible offensive explosion. The one drawback: They gave up 37 points, a concern tied to a defense that still might be a persistent weakness. CBS Sports – Pete Prisco 9. Chicago Bears (15) Maybe Ben Johnson is right and this team will break the single-season scoring record. They looked unstoppable in rolling up 59 points against the Panthers. USAToday – Nate Davis 4. Chicago Bears (5): The Windy City Cowboys? The Bears barely played a lick of defense Sunday in Charlotte but nevertheless looked like a team very much capable of making a run to Super Bowl 61 − especially with Caleb Williams, fresh off his first game with multiple TD passes and runs (even he’s not Allen-esque … yet), at the helm. What do you think of this week’s rankings? Are the Bears getting the respect they deserve following their win?

title: Hot Take Tuesday: Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson have put everyone on notice
summary: Holy Bleep. We will keep it PG today for the kiddos, but my oh my, what a difference a coach and a quarterback make. What the Chicago Bears did on Sunday was historic. The Bears put up numbers never seen in week one of the NFL season. It was the 12th highest-scoring game of all-time. […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after their 59-37 win against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Holy Bleep. We will keep it PG today for the kiddos, but my oh my, what a difference a coach and a quarterback make. What the Chicago Bears did on Sunday was historic. The Bears put up numbers never seen in week one of the NFL season. It was the 12th highest-scoring game of all-time. The Bears scored the 23rd-highest points by a single team of all-time, and if you go over the last 50 years, that number moves up to 7th. In short, it was bananas. Yes, we could criticize the defense, and it deserves criticism. But we will save that for another time when the defense costs them a victory, because no matter how bad the defense was, it simply didn’t matter. The Bears offense was that good. Think about the growth of Caleb Williams. Don’t think about it from where it was last year in the playoffs. Roll the clock back 365 days and think about where it was when last season started. Do you remember the frantic pace of Caleb’s play against the Vikings? Look at how much more relaxed and in control he is one year later. Look at the growth of Ben Johnson as a head coach. In week one, he made a special teams decision that might have cost the Bears a victory. In week two, he got smashed by his former team. A year later, he’s the one doing the smashing. Look at the buy-in from this team. Did you see the receivers? Jahdae Walker was blocking everyone. D’Andre Swift was an animal in pass protection. Luther Burden and Rome Odunze were putting bodies on everyone. No block, no rock. It’s a full buy-in. Ben Johnson has the beautiful tape to back it up now. You want to have explosive plays when the ball is in your hand? Your teammates will block for you and make that happen. But if you want them to block for you, you need to block for them. I can’t remember a skill position group, as a whole, blocking like this. That is a group of bad mother, you know what. They are a tough group that is going to make secondaries sore on Monday morning. Think about the offensive line. No Drew Dalman, no problem. This line didn’t skip a beat; it controlled the line of scrimmage and allowed the Bears to rush for nearly 300 yards on the ground. D’Andre Swift is now an animal. He’s one of the top 10 backs in the league. He isn’t the same guy who played soft in Detroit. You know what’s amazing? The Bears gained almost 600 yards on offense, and their big three of Luther Burden, Colston Loveland, and Rome Odunze averaged about 35 yards each. They weren’t the focal parts of the offense. They didn’t need to be. The ground game dominated. Caleb Williams dominated. Cole Kmet scored. Jahdae Walker scored. Kaliff Raymond led the receivers on Sunday. It was a full team effort, and their big offensive weapons barely had to carry a load. They scored 59 points anyway. Their time will come. Ben Johnson is a Madman. I say that in every complimentary way possible. He says he wants this offense to be the highest-scoring one of all time, and I believe him. Will they get there? Probably not, but it’ll be fun watching them try. The highest-scoring Bears team is the 1985 Bears. They scored 456 points. They scored 7 defensive TDs and Special Teams TDs that year (not to mention the number of short fields the offense got on turnovers). That offense scored 407 points without the defensive TDs. The 2013 Bears scored 445. This offense will destroy both those teams. They will easily surpass 500 points this season. 540 points would make them one of the 10 greatest offenses of all time. Who would they be with? Peyton Manning’s 2013 Denver Broncos, two Tom Brady Patriots teams (including the 2007 team that went undefeated in the regular season), Ben Johnson’s 2024 Lions offense, Patrick Mahomes 2018 Chiefs offense, Aaron Rodgers and the 2011 Packers, the 2011 Saints with Drew Brees, the 1998 Vikings with Randall Cunningham launching bombs to Randy Moss, and Washington in 1983, that was a ferocious ground attack led by John Riggins. Of those nine teams listed, six of them have all-time QBs. That’s not bad company for Caleb Williams to be in if they can get there, and I think they just might. The Bears offense has arrived. Defensive coordinators around the league are about to see how good Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams are. Get ready for a wild ride this year, Bears fans, and guess what? Get used to this. For the next decade, the Bears are going to be an elite offensive team, something that no one has said about the Bears since FDR was President. Holy Bleep.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Bears-Panthers Stock Watch: Swift & Walker up, Stevenson down
summary: With an opening weekend 50-burger, the Chicago Bears have announced they are not going to let regression come to them. A record-setting 59-37 victory sets the tone for the 2026 Bears. For better or worse, the game sets the tone for this team and what the league and the fans are going to expect the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the first quarter against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images With an opening weekend 50-burger, the Chicago Bears have announced they are not going to let regression come to them. A record-setting 59-37 victory sets the tone for the 2026 Bears. For better or worse, the game sets the tone for this team and what the league and the fans are going to expect the rest of the way. But it wasn’t all good. It rarely is in football. However, there was plenty worth revisiting, too. If you’re new to this piece, I pick three players I see as rising and three I see as falling. It’s a week-to-week exercise, but the performance over multiple games plays a part, too. With that said, let’s get to this week’s stock watch. Stock up Ben Johnson, coach – I wasn’t sure my stock in this man could go up, but here we are. The man crush is deep. I knew he was the real deal as a coach and coordinator. But seeing the team put up 59 points , all on offense, is mind-boggling to me as a longtime fan of this team. Johnson is an incredible play designer and caller. D’Andre Swift, RB – Fresh off his contract extension, Swift scored three TDs to start the season with a bang. On his way to 124 yards and three rushing touchdowns. His yards matched his Bears career high and the touchdowns were a new high for his entire career. Jahdae Walker, WR – Walker was a three-phase contributor on Sunday. He had a highlight block on special teams, multiple great blocks on offense and Ben Johnson rewarded him with a 1-yard touchdown later in the game. With the receiver shuffling that was done in the offseason, there was some question about what kind of role Walker might have. But if this week was any indication, the Bears will be asking him to be a role player a lot this season. Stock down Tyrique Stevenson, CB – Stevenson enters a contract season with the opportunity to really carve out a role and earn his future in Chicago. But his first game felt like a lot of what we’ve seen over his first three seasons. Moments of flash, moments of getting beat and moments of getting banged up. Stevenson has to be more consistent to earn that second deal. Luther Burden, WR – Burden’s game was solid overall. He made good catches and even had a couple of big pass plays. But his fumble on the opening drive set up a Carolina touchdown and was a terrible way to start the game and his season. I’m not worried long term, but this is still a mistake that has to be cleaned up. Colston Loveland, TE – I think this was a one week blip. He had two targets and one of them was a miss by Caleb, so it’s hard to even get down on Loveland too much. But finishing the game with zero catches is surprising. And he was flagged for a holding penalty, too. Again, this isn’t one to be worried about, but someone has to land here. Who’s stock do you think is up or down after week one? Let us know in the comments.

title: Evan McPherson named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after historic performance
summary: Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson has been named the AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after helping his team score a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 1. McPherson converted all four field-goal attempts and three extra points, accounting for 15 of Cincinnati’s 33 points. He led all NFL kickers in […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson talks with Tampa Bay Buccaneers Evan Deckers before the opening of NFL regular season at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Cincinnati Bengals kicker Evan McPherson has been named the AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after helping his team score a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 1. McPherson converted all four field-goal attempts and three extra points, accounting for 15 of Cincinnati’s 33 points. He led all NFL kickers in Week 1 scoring, and his four field goals led all AFC kickers. McPherson’s kicks came from 20, 55, 58, and 32 yards. He became the first player in Bengals history to make multiple field goals from 55+yards in a game, and his 58-yarder tied for the fourth-longest kick in team history. That kick also came in the fourth quarter of a game the Bengals ultimately won by just six points. McPherson has now made 123 career field goals, surpassing former kicker Horst Muhlmann (120) for fifth in Bengals history. Money Mac also extended his streak of made field goals to 16, dating back to Week 11 of last season. That marks the third-most consecutive field goals in team history, trailing 21 by former kicker Shayne Graham in 2007 and 17 by Graham from 2005-06. This is McPherson’s fifth career AFC Special Teams Player of the Week award. He previously received the honor in Weeks 1 and 11 of the 2021 season, Week 4 of the 2022 campaign, and Week 13 of 2025.

title: Bengals vs. Buccaneers: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly
summary: The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it. There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium. Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things. Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win. The Good […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) checks in with head coach Zac Taylor between plays in the second quarter of the NFL Week 1 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals opened the 2026 season with a win, and for once, the defense had a lot to do with it. There were some familiar warts along the way, but Cincinnati made enough plays to hold off Tampa Bay, 33-27, at Paycor Stadium. Whew. A Week 1 game that actually ended with the Bengals on the happy side of things. Here are the best and worst from Cincinnati’s season-opening win. The Good The defense came to play Well, hello there. After everything we heard about Cincinnati’s rebuilt defense during the offseason, we finally got to see it against an actual NFL offense. And the unit immediately made its presence felt. The Bengals forced fumbles on three consecutive Tampa Bay possessions in the first half. Myles Murphy strip-sacked Baker Mayfield, and Demetrius Knight Jr. scooped it up and returned it 27 yards for a touchdown. Then Bryan Cook forced a fumble from Bucky Irving, with Boye Mafe recovering. A few plays later, Joe Burrow found Mike Gesicki for a touchdown. On the next Tampa possession, Barrett Carter forced another Mayfield fumble near the goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone. Three straight possessions. Three turnovers. Cincinnati eventually forced four fumbles and recovered all four, while also sacking Mayfield four times. The Bengals turned those takeaways into 24 points. That’s a pretty good way to start a new defensive era. Mike Gesicki was exactly what Cincinnati needed Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins weren’t exactly having their usual Sunday. So, naturally, Mike Gesicki decided to have a day. Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. He also came up big late in the first half, catching three passes for 52 yards on the drive that ended with an Evan McPherson field goal. The Bucs spent plenty of attention on Chase and Higgins, and Burrow simply went somewhere else with the football. That’s what makes this offense so interesting. If defenses want to take away Cincinnati’s two star receivers, there are going to be opportunities for guys like Gesicki to make them pay. Chase Brown and the run game This was not the old-school Bengals running the ball 40 times and winning 17-13. But it was a much more balanced attack. Cincinnati ran the ball 27 times and threw it 35 times, and Chase Brown finished with 16 carries for 56 yards and a touchdown. He also caught five passes for 23 yards. More importantly, the Bengals showed a willingness to use the run as something other than a change of pace. Brown’s five-yard touchdown run capped an 80-yard, 12-play drive in the second quarter and pushed Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3. If Dan Pitcher’s offense really is going to lean into a more balanced approach in 2026, Sunday was a pretty encouraging first look. Money Mac is back Evan McPherson had himself a day. Four field goals. Four makes. Twenty yards. Thirty-two yards. Fifty-five yards. Fifty-eight yards. Those last two are particularly important because Tampa Bay had started to make things uncomfortable. Cincinnati wasn’t consistently finishing drives with touchdowns, but McPherson kept adding points. He accounted for 12 of the Bengals’ 33 points and gave Cincinnati some breathing room when the offense wasn’t quite clicking. Oh, and the 58-yarder was just ridiculous. It’s nice having that in your back pocket again. The offensive line quietly did its job This probably won’t generate nearly as many headlines as a scoop-and-score or a 58-yard field goal, but it might be one of the more important things to come out of this game. Joe Burrow was sacked just once. He finished 25-of-35 for 254 yards, one touchdown and one interception, while completing passes to nine different receivers. There were still some issues, but Burrow generally had enough time to work through his reads. Considering how much of Cincinnati’s success ultimately depends on keeping No. 9 upright, that’s a pretty significant development. Sometimes the best thing an offensive line can do is make you forget it’s there. Sunday was one of those days. The Bad Joe Burrow’s pick-six There’s no way around this one. Burrow had a pretty solid afternoon overall, but his third-quarter interception was brutal. With Cincinnati leading 27-13, Burrow tried to hit Andrei Iosivas, and Tampa Bay linebacker Josiah Trotter stepped in front of the pass and took it 27 yards for a touchdown. Just like that, a 14-point game became a seven-point game. It wasn’t the kind of mistake that cost Cincinnati the game, but it absolutely gave Tampa Bay life when the Bucs needed it. Burrow finished with 254 yards and a touchdown, so this wasn’t some disaster of a performance. But that interception was a bad one, and he’ll know it. The good news? The Bengals responded. The defense still missed too many tackles Four forced fumbles and four sacks will get you a lot of attention. But this wasn’t a flawless defensive performance. Cincinnati missed tackles, and Tampa Bay was able to move the football despite the turnovers. The Bengals also committed multiple offsides penalties, which is the kind of self-inflicted stuff that can become a real problem against better teams. That’s the tradeoff with an aggressive defense. You want guys flying around trying to make plays. You also need them to know where the line is. Cincinnati found that line a few times Sunday—and stepped over it. Ja’Marr Chase was basically a decoy Two catches. Twelve yards. Four targets. That’s it for Ja’Marr Chase. Obviously, this isn’t going to happen every week. Tampa Bay made a concerted effort to take Chase away, and Burrow responded by distributing the ball elsewhere. That’s actually a positive development. Still, there’s a difference between taking Chase away and simply not getting him involved. The Bengals didn’t need Chase to win this game. But there will be Sundays when they absolutely will. The offense left some points out there Cincinnati scored 33 points, so complaining about the offense feels a little ridiculous. Still, there were stretches where the Bengals had opportunities to put Tampa Bay away and couldn’t quite do it. The Bengals went 2-for-5 in the red zone, according to the game statistics. That’s an area that could come back to bite them against a team that doesn’t hand them four turnovers. The offense did enough. But it didn’t exactly leave the Bucs’ defense picking up the pieces. The Ugly That pick-six made this way too interesting This is where things got uncomfortable. Cincinnati was up 27-13. Tampa Bay had struggled to protect the football. The Bengals’ defense was flying around. Then Burrow threw the pick-six. Suddenly it was 27-20. The Buccaneers had momentum, the crowd had gotten a little quieter, and everybody watching was thinking the same thing: Please don’t do this. Fortunately, McPherson answered with a 58-yard field goal, and the defense eventually forced its fourth turnover of the afternoon. But Cincinnati turned what could have been a comfortable fourth quarter into a game that required some actual late-game execution. Tampa Bay wouldn’t go away Credit to the Bucs. After falling behind 24-10 at halftime, Tampa Bay kept hanging around. The Buccaneers cut the lead to seven in the third quarter, and Baker Mayfield eventually ran for an eight-yard touchdown with 3:19 left to make it 33-27. That’s when Cincinnati finally got the kind of close-out drive it has been looking for. The Bengals possessed the ball for the final 3:19 and didn’t give Tampa Bay another opportunity. So, yes, it got ugly. But Cincinnati actually finished the job. And honestly, after some of the fourth-quarter endings Bengals fans have endured over the years, I’ll take an ugly close-out over another…
