title: Bengals Week 1 awards from 33-27 win vs. Buccaneers
summary: The Bengals are 1-0. That’s a pretty good place to start. Cincinnati opened the 2026 season with a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and while there were certainly some things that need cleaning up, there were also plenty of individual performances worth recognizing. The new-look defense stole the show, Evan McPherson reminded everyone […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals center Ted Karras (64) celebrates with place kicker Evan McPherson (2) after McPherson made a field goal in the 4th quarter over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Bengals are 1-0. That’s a pretty good place to start. Cincinnati opened the 2026 season with a 33-27 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and while there were certainly some things that need cleaning up, there were also plenty of individual performances worth recognizing. The new-look defense stole the show, Evan McPherson reminded everyone why they call him “Money Mac,” and a few guys who probably weren’t at the top of anyone’s bingo card made some big plays. So, without further ado, let’s get into this week’s award nominees. Most Valuable Player (MVP) Criteria: This award goes to the player whose performance had the greatest direct impact on securing the victory. Nominee 1: Demetrius Knight Jr. — Linebacker Stats / Moments: Knight Jr. opened Cincinnati’s scoring with a 27-yard fumble return touchdown after Myles Murphy forced a Baker Mayfield fumble. Why MVP-worthy: Talk about making an entrance. Knight’s defensive touchdown gave the Bengals their first points of the season and immediately gave the new-look defense some life. He wasn’t just in the right place at the right time, either. Knight was flying around all afternoon and looked very comfortable in his first regular-season game with a much larger role. When you’re trying to change the identity of a defense, plays like this are exactly what you’re looking for. Nominee 2: Evan McPherson — Kicker Stats / Moments: McPherson connected on all four of his field-goal attempts, including kicks from 55 and 58 yards. He finished with 12 points. Why MVP-worthy: When the offense couldn’t quite finish drives, McPherson did. The 58-yarder in the fourth quarter was especially important. Tampa Bay had just cut Cincinnati’s lead to seven, and the Bengals needed something to stop the momentum. Enter Money Mac. That kick pushed the lead back to 10 and gave the defense a little more breathing room. Four-for-four with two 50-plus yarders is a pretty strong way to start the year. Nominee 3: Bryan Cook — Safety Stats / Moments: Cook forced a fumble and recovered a Tampa Bay fumble, which was Baker Mayfield’s goal-line gaffe in the first half. Why MVP-worthy: Cook was simply around the football. His fumble recovery came after Mayfield coughed the ball up near the goal line, preventing Tampa Bay from potentially coming away with points. He also forced another Buccaneers fumble, helping Cincinnati maintain control of a game that ultimately became much closer than it looked at halftime. After spending the offseason talking about what Cook could bring to a revamped secondary, Bengals fans got a pretty good first taste. Nominee 4: Mike Gesicki — Tight End Stats / Moments: Gesicki caught five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown on seven targets, leading Cincinnati in receiving. Why MVP-worthy: When Tampa Bay made it difficult to get Ja’Marr Chase involved, Burrow went elsewhere. Gesicki was the primary beneficiary. His two-yard touchdown reception gave Cincinnati its first offensive touchdown of the season, and he consistently found ways to move the chains. You don’t necessarily need your biggest stars to dominate every week. Sometimes you need the guys underneath them to make the defense pay for all that attention. Gesicki did exactly that. Unsung Hero of the Week Criteria: Awarded to a player whose efforts were significant yet flew under the radar, often stepping up in a rotational role, making an impact that doesn’t necessarily show up in the box score, or taking advantage of an opportunity created by injuries. Nominee 1: Dexter Lawrence II — Defensive Tackle Why Unsung-worthy: The stat sheet doesn’t really tell the story here. Lawrence didn’t need a bunch of sacks or splash plays to make his presence felt. He consistently affected what Tampa Bay wanted to do up front and helped create opportunities for the players around him. Nuggets from #Bengals PFF grading data: -Dexter Lawrence with 11 true pass set rushes. His win rate was 36%. That's best in the NFL among all DI (min. 10 attempts). – CBs did a nice job tackling in run game, Jalen Davis and Dax Hill, both graded out 84+. Hill with 2 stops. -… — Paul Dehner Jr. (@pauldehnerjr) September 14, 2026 And that’s exactly why Cincinnati went and got him. The Bengals invested heavily in their defensive front this offseason, and Lawrence’s Week 1 performance was one of those games where the tape was more impressive than the box score. Not exactly a bad debut in stripes. Nominee 2: Barrett Carter — Linebacker Stats / Moments: Carter finished with a team-high eight tackles, recorded a half-sack, and forced a fumble at the goal line. Why Unsung-worthy: Knight Jr. gets the highlight-reel touchdown, but Carter was everywhere. The goal-line forced fumble was enormous. Tampa Bay was threatening to turn a Bengals defensive stop into points, and Carter simply took the football away. Eight tackles, a half-sack and a forced fumble is a pretty busy afternoon. And unlike the defensive touchdown, this is the kind of production that can get lost when one side of the ball generates four turnovers. Nominee 3: Boye Mafe — EDGE Stats / Moments: Mafe recovered a fumble after Bucky Irving lost the ball and was part of a defensive front that helped force four Tampa Bay turnovers. Why Unsung-worthy: Mafe wasn’t necessarily the guy getting all the headlines, but he was involved in the chaos up front. The Bengals wanted a more aggressive, deeper defensive line rotation in 2026, and Mafe’s ability to contribute in that rotation is going to matter. Recovering a fumble isn’t glamorous. It is, however, extremely useful. Nominee 4: Chase Brown — Running Back Stats / Moments: Brown carried the ball 16 times for 56 yards and a touchdown while adding five receptions for 23 yards. Why Unsung-worthy: Brown wasn’t spectacular statistically, but he was steady. His five-yard touchdown run extended Cincinnati’s lead to 21-3 in the second quarter, and he was involved throughout an offense that ran 27 times compared with 35 pass attempts. More importantly, the Bengals didn’t abandon the running game when things weren’t perfect. Brown is going to be a major part of that balance if Cincinnati sticks with this approach. Play of the Game Criteria: The single most impactful or memorable moment that significantly shifted the game in Cincinnati’s favor. Nominee 1: Demetrius Knight Jr.’s Scoop-and-Score Myles Murphy knocked the ball loose from Baker Mayfield, and Knight Jr. picked it up and raced 27 yards for the touchdown. It’s hard to beat a defensive touchdown for this award. It was Cincinnati’s first score of the season and the first big statement from a defense that has spent the offseason trying to change its reputation. Something poetic about Demetrius Knight Jr. being the first to score a touchdown for the Bengals this year. After getting a ton of hate last year & this offseason, nice to see him get his moment. If you believe in omens, this’d be a great one for his sophomore year… pic.twitter.com/QKY2PbonmF — Bengalscentre (@benga1scentre) September 14, 2026 Nominee 2: Bryan Cook’s Goal-Line Fumble Recovery Mayfield lost the football near the Cincinnati goal line, and Cook recovered it in the end zone. Tampa Bay was knocking on the door. Instead of seven points—or at minimum a field goal—the Bengals walked away with the football. That’s the kind of play that can completely change a game. Bryan Cook with a great debut for the Bengals. Flies all around the field, is physical, and made some huge splash plays with a forced fumble and a fumble recovery on two separate plays. pic.twitter.com/YUCHzyKULl — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 15, 2026 Nominee 3: Evan McPherson’s 58-Yard Field Goal With Tampa Bay having cut Cincinnati’s lead to 27-20, McPherson drilled…

title: AFC North Roundup: Ravens and Steelers start fast while Browns stumble
summary: The first week of the 2026 season offered an early reminder that nothing is likely to come easily for the Cincinnati Bengals in the AFC North. Baltimore and Pittsburgh both opened with victories, although they got there in very different ways. The Ravens overwhelmed Indianapolis behind Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry, while the Steelers leaned […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: T.J. Watt #90 of the Pittsburgh Steelers warms up prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first week of the 2026 season offered an early reminder that nothing is likely to come easily for the Cincinnati Bengals in the AFC North. Baltimore and Pittsburgh both opened with victories, although they got there in very different ways. The Ravens overwhelmed Indianapolis behind Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry, while the Steelers leaned on a familiar formula as T.J. Watt helped rescue an uneven offensive performance. Cleveland was the lone division rival to stumble out of the gate, with turnovers, penalties and protection problems contributing to a difficult opening day. T.J. Watt still has plenty left in the tank Anyone expecting age to finally catch up with T.J. Watt may have to wait a little longer. Coming off a disappointing 2025 season by his lofty standards, the 32-year-old linebacker looked much more like the player who has spent the better part of a decade wrecking opposing offenses. Watt recorded two sacks and provided the biggest play of Pittsburgh’s 20-13 victory over Atlanta when he intercepted Cooper Rush and returned it 35 yards for a fourth-quarter touchdown. It was an impressive start for a player whose seven sacks last season represented one of the lowest totals of his career. Against Atlanta, however, there was little evidence that the four-time All-Pro has lost his ability to take over a football game. That was fortunate for Pittsburgh because its new-look offense was hardly dominant. Aaron Rodgers began what he says will be his final NFL season by passing for 221 yards and a touchdown. The Steelers struggled to run the ball effectively, and several dropped passes contributed to an inconsistent afternoon. Rodgers was at his best when Pittsburgh needed to put the game away, completing three passes on a final possession that consumed the remaining 4:16. Ravens offense comes out firing Baltimore’s opener wasn’t nearly as suspenseful. The Ravens piled up 506 yards of offense in a 41-23 victory over Indianapolis, with their two biggest stars doing most of the damage. Henry showed that turning 32 hasn’t made him much easier to tackle. He carried 24 times for 144 yards and three touchdowns. The performance also pushed him farther up the NFL’s career record lists, giving him 125 rushing touchdowns and 130 total scores. Jackson was equally impressive after a 2025 season that fell short of his usual standard. He completed 17 of 25 passes for 324 yards while adding 40 yards on seven rushing attempts. He accounted for touchdowns both passing and running. Perhaps the most encouraging sign for Baltimore was how quickly the offense took control. Jackson threw for 229 yards before halftime, and Zay Flowers accounted for 150 receiving yards on only five catches. The one concern coming out of the performance was Flowers’ hamstring, which kept him out of the second half, but he’s listed as day-to-day, so it doesn’t appear serious. Another downer was that Baltimore lost promising rookie wideout Ja’Kobi Lane to a wrist injury and is set to have surgery that will sideline him for a month. Rough beginning for Cleveland Things went considerably differently for the Browns. Deshaun Watson’s first start in nearly two years began with an interception on Cleveland’s opening possession and never really settled down. Jacksonville’s defense sacked Watson five times and kept him under pressure throughout the game. Cleveland compounded those problems with mistakes of its own. Rookie receiver KC Concepcion Jr. lost a fumble, the Browns were flagged 11 times for 75 yards, and the offense converted only one of eight third-down opportunities. Two possessions inside the Jacksonville 20 also ended without touchdowns. There were a couple of encouraging moments. Raheim Sanders broke a 74-yard kickoff return that helped produce a field goal, while Watson connected with Denzel Boston on a 46-yard touchdown late in the game. But Cleveland finished with only 272 total yards, and the late score did little to disguise an afternoon filled with problems.

full_text: The Week 2 game between the Cleveland Browns and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers will air on CBS at 1:00 PM ET on Sunday. title: Browns QB Deshaun Watson believes media sets unrealistic expectations for him
summary: When it comes to self-awareness, Cleveland Browns QB Deshaun Watson seems to be lacking, as his infamous press conference proved. On top of that, his play on the field has been even worse, including Week 1’s destruction at the hands of the Jacksonville Jaguars. Now, rarely does one player cause a loss or create a […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 07: Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns speaks during a press conference after the Cleveland Browns mandatory veteran minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 7, 2023 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images When it comes to self-awareness, Cleveland Browns QB Deshaun Watson seems to be lacking, as his infamous press conference proved . On top of that, his play on the field has been even worse, including Week 1’s destruction at the hands of the Jacksonville Jaguars. Now, rarely does one player cause a loss or create a win. When it happens, it is often the quarterback who can pull it off. Right or wrong, the head coach and quarterback tend to get the heavy end of the blame and credit for a team’s performance. HC Todd Monken and Watson earned the fans’ ire after Week 1, which was only added to when Monken backed his starting quarterback . According to Watson, continuing to show a lack of self-awareness, a lot of that is because the media sets unrealistic expectations for him: #Browns Deshaun Watson on if he needs to have a big game to get the nod at home and also build up goodwill for the return to Huntington Bank Field: pic.twitter.com/aA37LoCgpr — Mary Kay Cabot (@MaryKayCabot) September 16, 2026 As pretty much everyone who responded said, at this point fans are just hoping for adequate or average play from the quarterback. Forget 400 yards and five touchdowns. Forget living up to his contract. Forget not being the primary reason the team lost. Average. Adequate. The sunk cost of the trade and the contract, on top of moving on from Baker Mayfield , is water under the bridge at this point. Fans and media would just like to see Watson look like he belongs as one of the best 32 quarterbacks in the NFL, even if it is among the bottom 10. Instead, Cleveland fans rightfully are wishing for a variety of other backup quarterbacks, including their own, because Watson cannot reach that low, low expectation on the field. summary: When Cleveland Browns Hall of Famer Joe Thomas spoke to DBN’s Barry Shuck a couple of years ago, he was open and honest about how difficult it was to play for a losing team. Thomas, like former Browns DE Myles Garrett, put on great performances on the field only to see their team lose over […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - NOVEMBER 27, 2016: Left tackle Joe Thomas #73 of the Cleveland Browns kneels during timeout in the second quarter of a game against the New York Giants on November 27, 2016 at FirstEnergy Stadium in Cleveland, Ohio. New York won 27-13. (Photo by: Nick Cammett/Diamond Images/Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images When Cleveland Browns Hall of Famer Joe Thomas spoke to DBN’s Barry Shuck a couple of years ago , he was open and honest about how difficult it was to play for a losing team. Thomas, like former Browns DE Myles Garrett , put on great performances on the field only to see their team lose over and over again. Thomas and Garrett are locked together as the best modern-day Cleveland players , who both rarely saw any chance of winning championships in the orange and brown. While Garrett was moved in a trade, Thomas continues to talk about the Browns, including comments on Baker Mayfield and, recently, Deshaun Watson . Most of the time, Thomas has presented a measured approach to talking about his career and football. This video, talking about how Cleveland’s struggles broke him after one game, was less measured and spoke to what many Browns fans have also felt, while not actually playing at an all-time great level: Joe Thomas says he cried after playing a perfect game in a 30 point loss to Tom Brady and realized he had spent 10 years fooling himself into believing the Browns were a Super Bowl team before each season “The way I entered every season was like, if I need to get the most out of… pic.twitter.com/i9ksUFXIby — dank (@cptdankkk) September 15, 2026 Later in the interview, Thomas talked about a phone call he received from QB Peyton Manning when the Denver Broncos were trying to trade for him . The Hall of Famer noted he was happy in Cleveland, even if he was broken by the team’s performance, so he would not demand a trade. Manning then had a much more extreme idea: Peyton Manning wanted Joe Thomas to take a 💩 on the GM’s desk so he would get traded 😂 pic.twitter.com/lhu7IlXe2E — Bussin' With The Boys (@BussinWTB) September 15, 2026 Putting the two videos together, you have to wonder if Thomas now regrets not asking for the trade when he could have joined a Super Bowl-caliber team. From a heartfelt, sad statement about how he felt after playing a “perfect” game but losing by 30 to a discussion about defecating on GM Ray Farmer’s desk, the Joe Thomas experience. summary: It is Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season, and there is no drama about the Cleveland Browns’ position in national power rankings: they are pretty much dead last. A few sites still have them at No. 30 or No. 31, but overall, the average dropped 0.8 spots to 31.4. Some sites have the likes […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: A Jacksonville Jaguars fan poses for a photo prior to the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Cleveland Browns at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season, and there is no drama about the Cleveland Browns’ position in national power rankings: they are pretty much dead last. A few sites still have them at No. 30 or No. 31, but overall, the average dropped 0.8 spots to 31.4. Some sites have the likes of the Dolphins, Titans, or Falcons in consideration of being worse than Cleveland. Here is a summary of how the Cleveland Browns are viewed across mainstream media outlets in NFL Power Rankings heading into Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season. CBS Sports – No. 31 (no change) How much longer can they go with Deshaun Watson? He wasn’t the only reason they lost to the Jaguars, but he wasn’t good either. ESPN – No. 32 (down 1 spot) Non-QB newcomer debut: WR Denzel Boston The second-round pick’s production — two receptions for 59 yards and a TD — came in garbage time, but Boston’s 46-yard touchdown catch on a deep post was the kind of play he made throughout training camp. He also had the most snaps (47) and routes run (26) of any Browns receiver in Week 1, a sign of the big role that the team has planned for him going forward. NFL.com – No. 32 (down 2 spots) Last year, Cleveland’s defense managed to keep the Browns competitive in a bunch of games. Week 1 informed us that a different story will play out in 2026. The offense was horrendous with Deshaun Watson under center. The Browns hurt themselves by committing 11 penalties, and their defense resembled little more than a sieve against Trevor Lawrence’s Jaguars. It’s looking like it’ll be a long season on the shore of Lake Erie. Sporting News – No. 32 (no change) The Browns’ quarterback situation is bad, but the state of the running game and defense is even worse to begin the Todd Monken era. They were no match for the Jaguars and may struggle to beat anyone for a while. Yahoo Sports – No. 30 (no change) The Browns’ defense is supposed to keep them in games, even with Jared Verse replacing Myles Garrett. That wasn’t the case in the opener as the Browns looked like they really missed Jim Schwartz as defensive coordinator. Trevor Lawrence had four touchdowns and Jacksonville had 31 points with 12:08 left in the third quarter. If Cleveland’s defense is bad, there’s no hope at a respectable season. Bleacher Report – No. 32 (down 2 spots) It is going to be another long season at the Factory of Sadness. Deshaun Watson’s stats weren’t bad in a blowout loss to the Jaguars, but his lone touchdown throw came in garbage time and for most of the game the Browns had no vertical passing attack. That let the NFL’s best run defense from a year ago tee off on running back Quinshon Judkins, who averaged less than three yards per carry. The even bigger disappointment was a Browns defense that ranked inside the top-five last year. Sure, Myles Garrett is gone. But the Jaguars did whatever they wanted offensively in Week 1, whether it was on the ground or through the air. It was an ugly performance all the way around. And the Browns are the NFL’s worst team. Again. USA Today – No. 31 (down 1 spot) Shedeur SZN (Week 3?) is surely almost here, Browns fans − particularly if Baker Mayfield finally exacts revenge on the franchise that dumped him in favor of Deshaun Watson four years ago. title: Cleveland’s defense could adjust some snap counts after first game
summary: The Cleveland Browns’ defense looked lost to open the season, and looked like a shadow of its former self from when Jim Schwartz was the defensive coordinator. There was hardly any pressure, the tackling was poor, and the playmaking was lacking. I know Myles Garrett is gone, but one player shouldn’t turn a defense to […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - SEPTEMBER 13: Mason Graham #94 of the Cleveland Browns reacts after a play during the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Cleveland Browns on September 13, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cleveland Browns’ defense looked lost to open the season, and looked like a shadow of its former self from when Jim Schwartz was the defensive coordinator. There was hardly any pressure, the tackling was poor, and the playmaking was lacking. I know Myles Garrett is gone, but one player shouldn’t turn a defense to complete trash. Looking at the snap counts, there are a couple areas where some adjustments could be coming next week. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on defense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Defensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats DL Jared Verse 37 65% 3 tackles, 1 assist (4 combined). 1 TFL. DL Isaiah McGuire 37 65% 2 assists (2 combined). DL Mason Graham 34 60% 3 tackles, 2 assists (5 combined). 1 sack, 2 TFL, 1 QH. DL Adin Huntington 29 51% 2 assists (2 combined). DL Mike Hall 29 51% No stats registered. DL Sam Williams 23 40% 1 tackle, 3 assists (4 combined). DL Maliek Collins 22 39% 1 QH. DL Derek Barnett 17 30% No stats registered. We expected a lot from Jared Verse , and we got complete mediocrity, at least for one week. Verse graded out to around a 57.2 by PFF and did not generate any pressures. I thought Mason Graham made one of the bigger impacts defensively. It’s nice to see that right out of the gate after he started a bit slow as a rookie. PFF graded him as a 63.0. One of the biggest surprises with snap counts was how much action Adin Huntington saw. Perhaps we will see that number go down as veteran Maliek Collins gets more acclimated to football again. For what it’s worth, Huntington, Collins, and Mike Hall all graded poorly by PFF. Linebacker Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats LB Carson Schwesinger 57 100% 3 tackles, 7 assists (10 combined). 1 TFL, 1 QH. LB Quincy Williams 55 96% 3 tackles, 1 assist (4 combined). LB Easton Mascarenas-Arnold 19 33% 2 assists (2 combined). LB Winston Reid 1 2% No stats registered. It was a pedestrian game for Carson Schwesinger , who was around a 52.5 with his PFF grade. Quincy Williams , the new linebacker to the group, received the worst grade on defense with a 29.7. Maybe this is one of the reasons why: In all the years of watching football film this is a first from a LB in coverage. Zero movement for the first 2s. That's a choice from Quincy Williams (#5) pic.twitter.com/ipKErUGBDn — Browns Film Breakdown (@BrownsFilmBDN) September 15, 2026 Tackling in general was an issue for Cleveland: The Browns defense had 17 missed tackles against the Jaguars, per @NextGenStats , which only trailed the Denver Broncos for the most in the NFL in Week 1. Cleveland's missed tackle rate (21.8%) was also the third highest. Todd Monken was asked about the tackling effort on Monday:… — Daniel Oyefusi (@DanielOyefusi) September 15, 2026 Cornerback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats CB Tyson Campbell 57 100% 3 tackles, 4 assists (7 combined). CB Denzel Ward 57 100% 1 tackle, 4 assists (5 combined). 1 FF. CB Myles Harden 25 44% 1 tackle, 1 assist (2 combined). Denzel Ward was the Browns’ top-graded player defensively, grading out to a 90.5. At least one player remained consistent on this defense. Myles Harden seemed to be picked on a bit early. He was one of the Browns’ lowest-ranked defenders on the day. Safety Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats S Ronnie Hickman 57 100% 3 tackles, 5 assists (8 combined). S Grant Delpit 57 100% 1 tackle, 2 assists (3 combined). 1 pass defended. S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren 14 25% 1 tackle, 2 assists (3 combined). Last, but not least, one of the surprises in terms of snap counts came at safety, where rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren only played 14 snaps (25%). It’s not that I expect him to be an everydown player, but I was envisioning his role being between 40-60% of the snaps each week as a big part of the defense. For the reps he did receive, he graded out to a 69.2, which was the third-highest on defense. It’ll be interesting to see if the team works him more into defensive packages moving forward. Ronnie Hickman did not have a good day. It wasn’t a great day for Grant Delpit either, but he at least made a play on a couple passes.

title: Despite Week 1 loss, one group on the Browns offense improved
summary: The Cleveland Browns played a terrible game in Week 1, with a lot of blame going to QB Deshaun Watson on offense, and then the team’s defense in general. full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - SEPTEMBER 13: Quinshon Judkins #10 of the Cleveland Browns runs the ball against the Jacksonville Jaguars during the first quarter of the game at EverBank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Don Juan Moore/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns played a terrible game in Week 1, with a lot of blame going to QB Deshaun Watson on offense, and then the team’s defense in general. But were other areas responsible for the low output offensively too? There was one unit that actually played at a very high level, believe it or not. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on offense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Quarterback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats QB Deshaun Watson 51 100% 16-of-22 (72.7%) for 205 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT. 6 carries, 38 yards (6.3 YPC), 1 fumble. We can’t just look at the stat line for Deshaun Watson and think he wasn’t a problem. With that said, there are two sides to this. Fans are fed up with Watson. We thought we were done with him after the owner’s comments last year, and yet here he is, starting again. How many empty scoring halves of offense under Watson have we been subjected to? And then when you listen to the clip below, they’re exactly right, what the hell are we doing here, Todd Monken ? We are coddling Watson with kid gloves. "Listen to that. It that not something you'd say to your QB in 6th grade? I'm serious. We're all gonna have to deal with it for the rest of the season. This is just an abomination." 🚨 @KenCarman to @SportsBoyTony on #Browns head coach Todd Monken's comments on Deshaun Watson's… pic.twitter.com/thcnHKHElX — 92.3 The Fan (@923TheFan) September 14, 2026 Now, with all of that in mind, sure, there were a few positives I saw from Watson. I thought his deep ball in garbage time was thrown well, and he had some nice scrambles. He is certainly not tentative about running after his two Achilles injuries. The problem is, this is what, year four of us seeing Watson with the Browns? We’re sick of trying to cherry pick a few highlights to hope he’ll be better. That’s stuff you’d want to point out with Shedeur Sanders as a youngster, not Watson at this point, who has proven he is too turnover prone and doesn’t put points on the board. Running Back Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats RB Quinshon Judkins 33 65% 12 carries, 33 yards (2.8 YPC). 2 catches, 17 yards (2 targets). RB Raheim Sanders 18 35% 1 carry, 1 yard (1.0 YPC). 3 catches, 25 yards (3 targets). FB Michael Burton 6 12% No stats registered. The Browns were blown out so early that it again made it difficult to rely on the running game. Also, this is a Jaguars front that thrived at stopping the run a year ago. Nonetheless, there was nothing really special about the way Quinshon Judkins ran in Week 1. His backup, Dylan Sampson , is out with an injury now. Fullback Michael Burton got six snaps in. title: The Parker Report: How the Cowboys defense fared in week 1
summary: With NFL Week 1 in the books, lets take a look at how first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker and his revamped defense looked against the Giants. Team stats allowed In their first week of action, the Cowboys defense gave up 394 total yards, 29 first downs, and allowed an 82% third down conversion rate (9/11). […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Skattebo #44 of the New York Giants runs against three Dallas Cowboys defenders during the game on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With NFL Week 1 in the books, lets take a look at how first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker and his revamped defense looked against the Giants. Team stats allowed In their first week of action, the Cowboys defense gave up 394 total yards, 29 first downs, and allowed an 82% third down conversion rate (9/11). The team recorded two sacks and took advantage of one turnover on a forced fumble. The real gut punch here is the quantity of turnover worthy plays on defense (five) while only walking away with just the one. The main storyline is of the game, however, is time of possession. The Giants offense was also their best defense, as they controlled the ball for over 36 minutes. The inability of the Cowboys defense to get off the field kept Dak and the high powered offense on the sideline, seeing the field just twice in the second half. Individual stat leaders Second-year edge Donovan Ezeiruaku had one of the better nights on defense. He led the team with ten tackles, had a half sack, two hits on the quarterback, and one forced fumble. Caleb Downs was the only player to finish with a full sack on the stat sheet. The quarterback takedown came on a well disguised slot blitz. The devastating blind side hit forced a Jaxson Dart fumble, conveniently landing in the waiting arms of a Giants offensive lineman. This was exactly the playmaking ability Downs showcased throughout his time at Alabama and Ohio State. Speaking of fumbles, the team forced four of them but only recovered one. Donovan Ezeiruaku, Caleb Downs, Cobie Durant and Quinnen Williams each had their turn jarring the ball loose. The lone fumble recovery came on the Quinnen Williams punchout, which bounced right into Shavon Revel’s lap. Advanced analytics The Cowboys rolled out their 3-4 base on 28 snaps (41.2%), allowing 112 yards. They lined up in nickel on 24 snaps (35.3%) but allowed a whopping 215 yards. It’s interesting to see that the extra DB is what spurred the leaky defense. The coverage split was 77.8% zone and 22.2% man. Dallas lived in a two-high or three-deep zone structure throughout most of the day. The Cowboys blitzed at the seventh highest rate in week one, but that translated to just the 21st ranking in pressures. And when Dallas rushed only four, Jaxson Dart went 17-of-19 for 200 yards and two touchdowns. Dallas bit hard on the play-action. Dart was 5-of-7, had a touchdown, and ran for 26 yards on off the play fake. The young edges consistently crashed hard, opening outside lanes for Dart on the rollout pass or to take off and run. How’d the rookies look? Caleb Downs played nearly every snap on defense. The young star made his presence known with a huge hit on Jaxson Dart, forcing a fumble that was recovered by the Giants. His final stat line would read eight tackles, one sack, one forced fumble, and one QB hit. Where he could improve would be his pass coverage win rate. Great start for the rookie, but there is still much improvement to be had. Malachi Lawrence was not good enough. He was involved in more than one negative big play on Sunday night. Too many times we saw him bite on play fakes, crashing down while leaving a huge void to the outside. His pass rush was nearly non-existent. Lawrence ended the night as the fourth lowest rated player on defense against the Giants. Jaishawn Barham finished the night with six tackles as a rotational linebacker. He had one noticeable hit in the backfield, but outside of that was somewhat forgettable. There were questions about his effort late in the game as the Giants connected in the flat multiple plays in a row on their way to a game sealing touchdown. With Overshown potentially missing up to two weeks , we should see more of Barham against the Commanders and Ravens. LT Overton played a small role Sunday night but did finish with one tackle and one pass breakup at the line. With a strong preseason and a solid first game with limited snaps, expect to see his role grow as the season continues. Final grade: D- The Cowboys came into MetLife Stadium with high expectations surrounding a fresh start on a rebuilt defense. What the Cowboys got was more of the same. There is no nice way to put this: this team was dominated on the defensive side of the ball. While they limited the explosive plays of over 15 yards, they allowed the Giants offense to methodically work their way down the field for touchdowns while chewing up so much clock that their own offense saw the field just twice in the second half. We witnessed large voids in coverage more than once, resulting in touchdowns and first downs. Some mental mistakes are to be expected for a new defense, but too many of the same misses can be seen on film. Dallas will need to get this corrected in a hurry if they want to keep pace in the NFC. The only reason this defense doesn’t get an F is because they forced four fumbles. The law of averages did not apply as the ball seemed magnetized to Giants players after being stripped on more than one occasion. If the Cowboys can tighten up but also keep their intensity around punchouts and strip sacks, the football will bounce their way and win them some games. The Cowboys have a ton of work to do on the defensive side of the ball. Their next test comes at home against the Washington Commanders this Sunday. Jaxson Dart’s mobility was crucial for the Giants victory and Dallas faces another one coming to town in Jayden Daniels. It’s imperative this defense doesn’t overcommit to the inside play fakes because Daniels will take the run option every single time. We’ll see if Parker will make the proper adjustments in week two.
author: Dyllan Rivers

title: Cowboys opponent: A look at the Commanders for Week 2
summary: The Dallas Cowboys dropped their Week 1 game and are looking to bounce back. They don’t have to wait long for another NFC East opponent. After opening the season with a 28-20 loss to the New York Giants, Dallas returns home Sunday to face the Washington Commanders, who are also coming off a one-score loss […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Jacory Croskey-Merritt #22 of the Washington Commanders runs the ball against the Dallas Cowboys in the third quarter of a game at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Greg Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys dropped their Week 1 game and are looking to bounce back. They don’t have to wait long for another NFC East opponent. After opening the season with a 28-20 loss to the New York Giants, Dallas returns home Sunday to face the Washington Commanders, who are also coming off a one-score loss in Week 1. Washington fell 24-22 to the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, but the final score doesn’t tell the entire story. The Commanders showed some promising things in their first game under a new offensive coordinator and with a revamped defense, including some impressive physicality on special teams. This may be the greatest punt coverage you’ll ever see from a gunner 😤 pic.twitter.com/SmYgIV9A2g — Footballism (@FootbaIIism) September 14, 2026 They also showed some of the issues that helped produce a 5-12 record last season. Now, Washington heads to Arlington for its first road game of 2026. Here’s what Cowboys fans need to know. A lot changed in Washington this offseason The Commanders spent the offseason rebuilding a team that finished 5-12 in 2025. The biggest changes came on defense, at the behest of former Cowboys DC Dan Quinn. Washington brought in several new pieces and entered the season with a revamped unit under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. The Commanders also added to their offense including veteran receiver Stefon Diggs, giving quarterback Jayden Daniels another established weapon alongside Terry McLaurin. The Commanders’ offense also has a new play caller. David Blough took over as offensive coordinator, meaning Daniels is operating in his third offensive system in three seasons. That transition looked uneven in Week 1. Washington also added rookie linebacker Sonny Styles with the seventh overall pick. He immediately made an impact in Week 1, recording a sack against Philadelphia. Sonny Styles NFL Debut vs Eagles. 4 TKL, 2 TFL, 1 SACK, 1 QBH. https://t.co/ma4aR4UFim pic.twitter.com/jZH8wB8udC — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) September 14, 2026 Jayden Daniels is back, but he wasn’t quite himself yet This is still Jayden Daniels’ team. After an injury-plagued 2025 season, Daniels returned to regular-season action Sunday, September 13, against Philadelphia and finished 18-of-34 for 164 yards and two touchdowns, adding 31 yards on five rushing attempts. The numbers weren’t spectacular, but the fourth quarter offered a glimpse of what Washington hopes its offense can become. Daniels threw touchdown passes to Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams as the Commanders scored 13 fourth-quarter points and turned a 24-9 deficit into a two-point game. The problem was everything that came before it. Washington had just 50 yards on its seven non-scoring drives, struggling to sustain drives for long stretches. That’s something Dallas’ defense will have to account for Sunday: Which Washington offense shows up for four quarters? And can they make enough plays to keep the Commanders’ offense off-balance? Washington can run the football If there was one thing the Commanders did consistently against Philadelphia, it was run the football. Washington finished with 132 rushing yards on 32 attempts, averaging 4.1 yards per carry. Jacory Croskey-Merritt led the way with 63 yards and a touchdown on 16 carries. Rachaad White added 22 yards on seven carries, while Daniels contributed another 31 yards. If Week 1 was a sign of things to come, this is obviously a cause for concern for Dallas. The Cowboys just watched the Giants control the game on the ground and through time of possession in Week 1. New York ran 68 offensive plays to Dallas’ 52, held the ball for more than 36 minutes in the 28-20 victory, and, as many have pointed out, limited the Cowboys to two possessions in the second half. If the Commanders can establish their running game, they can keep Daniels out of obvious passing situations while pressuring a Dallas defense that allowed 394 total yards to New York in Week 1. Stefon Diggs is already involved One of Washington’s biggest offseason additions made an immediate impact. Diggs caught four passes for 55 yards and a touchdown against Philadelphia. He also drew attention for a costly unsportsmanlike conduct penalty after his touchdown celebration, a mistake that affected Washington’s late-game two-point strategy. Still, his presence gives Daniels something the quarterback didn’t have for much of last season: another veteran receiver capable of winning matchups outside of McLaurin. McLaurin caught only two passes for 14 yards in Week 1, but one came during Washington’s fourth-quarter comeback. The combination of McLaurin and Diggs will be one of the things to watch on Sunday whenever Washington’s offense takes the field. The defense looked better in spots Washington’s defense had a respectable opening week against Philadelphia. The Commanders held the Eagles to 318 total yards, including 203 passing yards and 136 rushing yards. Washington generated three sacks, and the pressure came from multiple places. Frankie Luvu, Odafe Oweh and rookie Sonny Styles each recorded a sack. The defense also did a good job limiting Philadelphia’s offense for long stretches. But the Commanders gave up several explosive plays and struggled with communication in the secondary. That’s where the matchup with Dallas will be interesting. The Cowboys struggled to generate sustained offense against New York, producing just 244 total yards and 20 points. Dak Prescott threw for 175 yards, while Dallas averaged only 3.8 yards per rushing attempt. So, Week 2 presents a straightforward question for the Cowboys. Can Dallas create more explosive plays against a Washington defense that has also shown it can give up opportunities in the secondary? Antonio Williams is worth knowing Keep an eye on Antonio Williams. The rookie receiver wasn’t even listed as one of Washington’s three starting receivers on the team’s initial depth chart. Still, he led the Commanders in receiving against Philadelphia, catching four passes for 64 yards and a touchdown. His touchdown was part of Washington’s fourth-quarter comeback. Williams also fits the profile of the young players Washington is trying to develop around Daniels. The Commanders have praised his route-running ability and his versatility to play both inside and outside. After one game, he has already given Washington another name for opposing defenses to account for, and could be part of a suddenly deep Washington receiving corps with the potential to damage any defense. Jayden Daniels to the rookie, Antonio Williams, for a TD ‼️ WASvsPHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rznfyftIjU — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 This is a different Washington team than Dallas saw last year The Cowboys swept the Commanders last season, winning the final matchup 30-23 at Washington, but this year’s Commanders look different. There’s a new offensive coordinator, a revamped defense, a healthy Daniels and a new veteran weapon in Diggs. Washington is also trying to establish a more balanced offense built around its quarterback’s ability to threaten defenses with both his arm and legs. So far, returns are mixed, but it’s just Week 2. The Commanders moved the ball for 295 yards against Philadelphia but converted only 5 of 15 third downs. They scored 22 points despite producing only 20 first downs. Both teams are 0-1. Both have new questions after Week 1, and both have already seen enough of their new-look teams to know that some changes need to be made. The Cowboys and Commanders will meet Sunday at AT&T Stadium, with both teams looking to put their first loss of 2026 behind them.

title: 3 things we learned about the Cowboys in Week 1 loss
summary: The Dallas Cowboys kicked off the season against the New York Giants, and it gave them a shot to get a big win in the NFC East. Many thought it would happen due to the Cowboys dominance against the Giants over the last decade, but things didn’t turn out that way. For the game, Dallas […]
full_text: Sep 13, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; Dallas Cowboys running back Javonte Williams (33) carries the ball for a touchdown against the New York Giants during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys kicked off the season against the New York Giants, and it gave them a shot to get a big win in the NFC East. Many thought it would happen due to the Cowboys dominance against the Giants over the last decade, but things didn’t turn out that way. For the game, Dallas only amassed 244 total yards and they held the ball for just over 23 minutes. The running game was virtually nonexistent as the Cowboys gained a pedestrian 69 yards while averaging only 3.8 yards per carry. Defensively, the gave up nine conversions on eleven third down plays by the Giants. Not ideal at all. The Cowboys have a lot to clean up before playing the Washington Commanders this Sunday in their home opener. Before that takes place, let’s dive into three things we learned about Dallas in Week 1. It’s going to take time for Christian Parker’s defense to gel One of the additions to the Cowboys that had people the most excited during the offseason was defensive coordinator Christian Parker. However, many forgot the fact that although he has a great football mind, Sunday night was his first time calling plays for a defense in a real game, and it showed. Parker was thoroughly out coached by Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy, and the most alarming part was the lack of adjustments he made when things weren’t going well. It’s only the first game for Parker in this role, which does give him some grace. Plus, there’s a ton of new players and his system is also new, and running it in training camp and the preseason isn’t the same as when the regular season starts. So, Parker has to get back to the drawing board before Week 2, and even if they do play better, it will take some time to get everything flowing the way he wants it to. Penalties are still an issue In 2025, the Cowboys lead the NFL with 133 penalties and they were second in most yards penalized with 1,136. They didn’t get off to a good start this season in that regard as they were called for nine penalties against the Giants which totaled 90 yards. This is glaring issue that somehow keeps plaguing Dallas regardless of who the coach has been over the last decade. The biggest, and without question the most costly penalty, came late in the fourth quarter when running back Javonte Williams got a taunting penalty after he scored a touchdown which led to a missed extra point by kicker Brandon Aubrey. The Cowboys had planned to go for a two-point conversion there, but the penalty changed their minds. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer has got to find a way to get this problem rectified. Lack of pass rush is concerning Dallas simply could not make life difficult for Jaxson Dart on Sunday night. The rushed him with four players on 20 plays, but the only generated two pressures. Whenever they decided to blitz him, he either made plays with his legs or found wide open targets. It routinely happened as the Giants carved the Cowboys up third down which led to over 36 minutes of time of possession. This issue is one that the Cowboys will have a hard time overcoming because they don’t have the talent up front defensively to consistently get pressure although they have Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark on the interior. They have time to make improvements, but how much they can do so without the right type of players is the question. This will likely be a season long thing.

title: Cowboys positional rankings reveal where accountability needs to start
summary: For me it’s quite simple: Because the expectations for the offense and defense were quite high, and both units were outcoached and outplayed by the Giants, the accountability falls squarely on Brian Schottenheimer and Christian Parker. Alas, if only simple answers were the right answers – they almost never are. One of the team captains, […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Brian Schottenheimer head coach of the Dallas Cowboys during the third quarter of the game against the New York Giants on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For me it’s quite simple: Because the expectations for the offense and defense were quite high, and both units were outcoached and outplayed by the Giants, the accountability falls squarely on Brian Schottenheimer and Christian Parker. Alas, if only simple answers were the right answers – they almost never are. The Cowboys went from two red-flag performances retained from the entire 2025 season to 12 in one game . And perhaps even more strikingly, the team went from 13 starter-quality performances retained or acquired from 2025 to just four against the Giants . This wasn’t simply a bad game. It was a remarkable concentration of bad individual performances . One of the team captains, Quinnen Williams, has spoken up and announced the team would take accountability . I think the takeaway is this: Quinnen wanted to make sure he said certain things into a microphone, and a lot of it centered around the idea of the team embracing criticism this week. That doesn't mean things will get better, but it means they aren't delusional about last night. https://t.co/hwe1E4RZca — Bobby Belt (@BobbyBeltTX) September 14, 2026 The idea today is to look at positional rankings (or percentile rankings) to identify which players and units need to take a little more constructive criticism than others. We’ve covered positional rankings extensively this offseason, go here if you need a quick primer . The idea is that instead of using a player’s raw PFF Grade, we look at where a given player is ranked relative to the other players in the league at his position. Relative positional performance gives us a way to separate the players who actually hurt the Cowboys from those who merely looked bad because the team lost. Example: Jalen Thompson has a 43.7 Grade for the season opener, which suggests he had a slightly below-average game. But he ranks 71 out of 84 qualifying safeties, which would give him a positional ranking (1 – position rank / total qualifying players) * 100 of just 15, an indication of a red flag or bottom 20 performance. Based on the overall ranking scale provided by PFF, the results can be split into quintiles, which delivers the following positional ranking groups: body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 0px 6px !important; } Positional Ranking Description 100-80 Blue-Chip Peromance 79-60 NFL starter quality performance 59-40 Slightly above or below average performance 39-20 Underperformer 19-0 Red Flag Be aware though, that we’re talking about the performance in just one game, the sample sizes in terms of snap counts can be quite low, and we understand the vagaries of PFF grades. With that out the way, we’ll start with a top-line view of the roster performance, take a deeper look at the good and bad per position unit, and then move on to a view of the entire roster. title: Cowboys defense is still the problem after loss to Giants
summary: Football is back, and for Dallas Cowboys fans around the world, so is the disappointment that is often associated with this team. For the better part of 60 minutes, the Dallas Cowboys were taken to task by their division rival, the Giants. Both sides of the ball struggled, leading to a season-opening loss, but today […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 13: Defensive coordinator Christian Parker of the Dallas Cowboys looks on during the fourth quarter against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on September 13, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images Football is back, and for Dallas Cowboys fans around the world, so is the disappointment that is often associated with this team. For the better part of 60 minutes, the Dallas Cowboys were taken to task by their division rival, the Giants. Both sides of the ball struggled, leading to a season-opening loss, but today we are going to talk about… that’s right, the defense. This defense still has a long way to go This level of effort from Barham is wild. I think the kid has a ton of potential, but he will never reach it playing like this. pic.twitter.com/WA2ydf3ewU — Massey (@TheJAMassey) September 14, 2026 The play above can sum up the sputtering start to what was supposed to be a vastly improved defensive unit in 2026. Over the offseason, the Cowboys spent a lot of draft capital trying to revamp what was statistically the worst defense in franchise history last season. Dallas even hired a new defensive coordinator, Christian Parker, and many fans and pundits alike believed that this defense would not, could not, reach the levels of profound doom that this unit sank to last year. People expected Vic Fangio; instead, they got Eberflus 2.0, and the Giants essentially did whatever they wanted, limiting the Cowboys to two offensive possessions in the entire second half. By the third quarter, players were already worn out; their effort was questionable, and they couldn’t stop the Giants’ offense. The defensive line was bad. They sacked Dart twice, but one of them came from Caleb Downs on a blitz. The Cowboys rank 21st in Week 1 pressure rate despite blitzing at the seventh-highest rate. The ends constantly failed to set the edge, got lost in coverage and were completely ineffective at rushing the passer. The linebackers may have been worse. Winters had a horrible game, rating in the 40s by PFF; he was consistently lost in coverage and did little to make up for it. Overshown got hurt again, but did little to move the needle when he was in. Barham pulled up, inexplicably, on the Giants’ last touchdown that you saw earlier, after they spammed a checkdown four straight times. The secondary was okay, only to be diced up by Dart when they needed stops on third down the most. They were close but never in good positions to make plays; Dart made them pay as the Giants converted a nearly record-high clip of third downs (9/11). What’s more concerning is that new Dallas Cowboys DC Christian Parker is supposed to be a secondary guru. His nickel package had the second-most snaps and gave up eight yards per play. What’s the bright side The bright side is, it’s week one. Caleb Downs looked solid; he gave up seven yards on two receptions when targeted, led the team in sacks with one, forced a fumble and, at times, seemed to be the only player on the defense interested in playing. Caleb Downs with a HUGE hit on Jaxson Dart 😤 DALvsNYG on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/6x4h1EbLxb — NFL (@NFL) September 14, 2026 The alarm bells don’t necessarily need to be sounding yet, but there are very scary signs that this defense may not have gotten any better. The regular season isn’t the time to make major adjustments; it is the time to show what you’ve done in the offseason. If week one is any indication, these mental lapses and poor play are bad habits carried over from last year. It will once again be a very long year in Big D unless Parker can make some quick fixes.
author: Jorge Guajardo

title: Cowboys news: Jerry Jones wants better communication on defense

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 13: Owner of the Dallas Cowboys, Jerry Jones, acknowledges the crowd prior to the game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on September 13, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. We had some guys play hard, and we had some guys do some good things on both sides of the ball, offense and defense. But I was really surprised and dismayed, as all fans were, that we couldn’t basically stop some of that outside stuff.
