title: Cowboys report card: Grading Week 1 vs. the Giants
summary: The Dallas Cowboys’ chances of winning Sunday night against the Giants felt gone in a New York minute. Dallas’ opening drive ended with the offense looking out of rhythm, while the New York offense, led by Jaxson Dart, couldn’t be stopped. Jerry Jones and the front office invested a ton of resources into the defense […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys’ chances of winning Sunday night against the Giants felt gone in a New York minute. Dallas’ opening drive ended with the offense looking out of rhythm, while the New York offense, led by Jaxson Dart, couldn’t be stopped. Jerry Jones and the front office invested a ton of resources into the defense to overhaul a unit that was at the bottom of the league a season ago. All that personnel change couldn’t change the fact that the defense picked up right where it left off at the end of 2025. There is plenty of blame to go around for what went wrong for the Dallas Cowboys. There won’t be any grading on a curve here as we hand out the report card for Week 1. A grades: Zero No one will get an ‘A’ for their performance this week, as it took a total team effort to look as out of sorts as Dallas did. ‘A’ efforts usually help a team win ball games, and that didn’t happen on Sunday night. B grades: Tyler Guyton (B+): The Cowboys’ left tackle fared pretty well against the 14th-ranked player in the NFL , Brian Burns. The Giants edge rusher had a career year in 2025 with 16.5 sacks, so Guyton didn’t have an easy matchup with a player who usually beats tackles with his speed. Guyton stood his ground and did not allow a pressure across his 20 pass-blocking matchups against Burns. It wasn’t perfect, but fans should feel good about left tackle coming away from Sunday night Cobie Durant (B): Durant looked like the best corner for the Cowboys on Sunday night. Dart didn’t attack Dallas’ defense through the air as much, but Durant stuck close to his man, played physical, and even broke up a pass that should have been an interception. Caleb Downs (B): Downs’ first regular-season game had a splash play where he sprinted untouched on a blitz and hammered Dart for a sack, causing a fumble. Unfortunately for Dallas, they couldn’t recover the ball and give it back to their offense. It wasn’t a bad performance by Downs, but looking back at his rookie season, it won’t be a memorable game. Donovan Ezeiruaku (B): The Cowboys’ second-year outside linebacker may not have gotten to the quarterback, but he was certainly one of the most active defenders in the game. He led the team with ten tackles and had two pressures. His biggest play came with a forced fumble, but like the Downs play, the ball bounced in the Giants’ direction, and Dallas couldn’t recover it. He had the one really bad read on the Dart roll out to the left where he bit inside on the play fake, but overall he was one of the better defenders on a bad night for the Dallas defense. Dak Prescott (B-): The Cowboys’ starting quarterback wasn’t the reason why they lost on Sunday. However, his one interception before halftime set the team back in a big way: the Giants scored a touchdown before halftime, then came back to start the third quarter and scored again. The big plays in the passing game just weren’t there, and George Pickens’ deep-ball drop wasn’t great either. The INT brings his grade from a B+ to a B-. Javonte Williams (B-) Williams would have been the only player in the A category, since he scored twice for Dallas and ran hard all night. It just shows how much a poorly timed penalty can bring down your grade. Williams’ second touchdown was capped by an unsportsmanlike penalty that put Brandon Aubrey in a bad spot to kick a long extra point instead of going for two, as Brian Schottenheimer wanted. Can’t happen for a veteran player. C grades: Terence Steele (C+): Even with someone gunning for his job before the season started, Steele played pretty well given the circumstances. The Giants pass rush may be among the best group of players the offensive line sees all season. He won a couple matchups vs. the edges, but Abdul Carter was making life difficult for Steele. He didn’t allow a sack, but pressure from the right side got to Prescott for most of the night. Jaishawn Barham (C): This one hurts to hand out. Unlike Downs, Barham looked like he had a few learning moments in his NFL debut. His first play on the field was a stop in the backfield, but it almost turned into a WWE suplex, which would have caused a penalty. After that, his angles in run defense weren’t always 100 percent, and then on the Devin Singletary touchdown, it looked like he stopped running before the back crossed the goal line. Hope hasn’t been lost for a player with his skill set and tenacity because he may have to be the next man up with DeMarvion Overshown expected to miss time with his hamstring injury. D grades: Rest of Cowboys pass rush (D): When a “D” grade is handed out in this exercise, it means a player didn’t impact the game the way they were supposed to, or their performance or moment outright cost them the game. It could also be a collection of players, like it is here with Dallas’ pass rush. Yes, the Giants put resources into overhauling their offensive line, but the Cowboys couldn’t get close enough to Dart consistently to make a difference. Rashan Gary, Quinnen Williams, Malachi Lawrence, and Kenny Clark need to take pressure off the secondary. The lack of pass rush allowed the Giants offense to operate with a clean pocket all game The communication on defense (D): It’s not great to hear Schottenheimer come out of his Monday review thinking the defense needs to communicate better. The Cowboys spent the entire offseason saying communication was their No. 1 priority, and that’s what plagued them last year. Well, players not being in the right position or not being told the right call is what inevitably broke the camel’s back on Sunday night and led to Dallas walking out of MetLife Stadium with their first loss of the season. Christian Parker has a lot of work to do this week. #Cowboys Brian Schottenheimer talked about how the film showed communication issues on defense, especially in the red zone. A little concerning, considering the team spent the entire offseason talking about communication and its importance. (🎥: @dallascowboys ) pic.twitter.com/K0AoATEeYJ — Brandon Loree (@Brandoniswrite) September 14, 2026
author: Brandon_Loree

title: Brian Schottenheimer report card: Cowboys culture crashes in Week 1
summary: After a disastrous 2025 season, the Dallas Cowboys hoped to rebound in the 2026 season bringing back the entire starting offense in 2026, and completely new look defense and coaching staff. Things could not have started out worse for the 2026 Cowboys, after dropping their week one game on the road in MetLife against the […]
full_text: After a disastrous 2025 season, the Dallas Cowboys hoped to rebound in the 2026 season bringing back the entire starting offense in 2026, and completely new look defense and coaching staff. Things could not have started out worse for the 2026 Cowboys, after dropping their week one game on the road in MetLife against the New York Giants. While a lot of attention is being put on Christian Parker’s defense after the Cowboys 28-20 loss, today we will take a look at how head coach and offensive coordinator Brian Schottenheimer performed in the Cowboys week one loss. As expected, after not playing any of the offensive starters in preseason action, the Cowboys offense started out relatively slow. The Cowboys first play from scrimmage in 2026 was quite an odd one. Lining up in 11-personnel with Jake Ferguson as the lead blocker lined up at fullback in the backfield, the Cowboys ran a inside-toss play to Javonte Williams that went nowhere due to Jake Ferguson and Ryan Flournoy missing their blocks on Abdul Carter. On second down, the Cowboys ran a comeback route to CeeDee Lamb on the sideline. From the All-22 angle, the ball was put in good position on the boundary, but Lamb was unable to haul it in. On third down, the Cowboys ran their patented George Pickens slant, but Pickens came up just short of picking up the first down. My first Brian Schottenheimer critique starts here. On 4th-and-inches, the Cowboys offense attempted to get the Giants to jump offsides before taking a delay of game and punting the ball. This was the first mistake of the game and the season for the Cowboys, who at the time expected much better results from their defense. According to ESPN Analytics, the “go” in this scenario was +1.7%. We saw last season that Schottenheimer leaned on the conservative side with his fourth-down decision making and there were deep conversations last year about that being a negative impact on the team considering how bad the defense was. Well, this defense doesn’t look much different through one week, and the decision to punt ended up putting the Cowboys in a quick hole after a six-minute touchdown drive by the Giants. The Cowboys next drive showed a bit cleaner operation, but a George Pickens drop on third down (illegal shift penalty declined) led to another stalled drive with no points. The Cowboys final two drives of the half led to a CeeDee Lamb touchdown reception, after a 15-play, 6:44 second drive and a Dak Prescott interception on an attempted throwaway on 3rd-and-5. The Cowboys only had two other drives the remainder of the game due to how poor the defense played. The Cowboys scored touchdowns on both of those drives thanks to some penalties on the Giants defense and the Cowboys passing game starting to find their rhythm. Fans reacted strongly to Schottenheimer burning a timeout on the Giants opening drive out of the half; it was later reported that the Cowboys defense only had 10-men on the field at the time. The Cowboys had a balanced approach coming into the game. The actual game ended up differently due to self-inflicted wounds. All-in-all, the play-calling in this game from Schottenheimer wasn’t a disaster. The Cowboys interior offensive line had struggles generating running lanes all night, so in have-to-have-it scenarios (like the CeeDee Lamb touchdown) Schottenheimer put the ball in Prescott’s hands to get points. What was a problem was the lack of aggressiveness early in this game, the amount of penalties on the offensive side of the ball, and the lack of toughness, focus, and physicality the unit played with for a majority of the game. We have heard so much about culture since Schottenheimer was hired, and over the course of the offseason, but last night the Cowboys culture looked timid, conservative, and showed extreme lack of discipline. Javonte Williams taunted the Giants secondary after scoring to get the game within one possession with an Aubrey extra-point or two-point conversion (which Schottenheimer did say was his plan in the post-game). Week one can tell lies due to everyone throughout the league knocking rust off. At the end of the day, the Cowboys offense found its rhythm in the second-half and should rebound to be near the top of the league in points scored and offensive EPA sooner rather than later. Monday morning quarterbacking this one, the decision to punt on 4th-and-inches on their opening drive was a massive turning point in this game. Who knows what would have happened, but now knowing the Cowboys defense’s inability to get any stops when needed, that feels like a massive mistake that early in the football game. The main concerns come down to Schottenheimer seemingly not trusting his offensive line (punts on fourth-downs and lack of faith in running it on the goal-line). Also, the lack of explosive plays (Pickens had two drops on explosive play attempts), Schottenheimer’s overall faith in his defense to get stops after punts instead of setting a tone early with his offense, and the boneheaded mistakes Cowboys fans are way too used to seeing over the 30-year drought. Play-Calling C+ Fourth-Down Decisions F Timeout Usage B Team Preparation F What grades would you give to Brian Schottenhiemer on Sunday?
author: Connor Livesay

title: Concern around Brandon Aubrey feels fair right now
summary: Brandon Aubrey missed an extra point on Sunday night against the New York Giants. No harm, no foul. Extra points are missed all of the time in the NFL, right? We shouldn’t be freaking out over a single kick. This isn’t like early in Aubrey’s career where he was automatic and the out-of-nowhere miss was […]
full_text: Aug 28, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Dallas Cowboys place kicker Brandon Aubrey (17) looks to attempt a field goal during the game between the Cowboys and the Saints at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Brandon Aubrey missed an extra point on Sunday night against the New York Giants. No harm, no foul. Extra points are missed all of the time in the NFL, right? We shouldn’t be freaking out over a single kick. This isn’t like early in Aubrey’s career where he was automatic and the out-of-nowhere miss was almost funny because it was so rare. The thing is, we are definitely not in those days anymore. There isn’t any real need to panic at this point in time, but Brandon Aubrey’s misses are becoming a bit of a thing now. And that has to be discussed. Concern around Brandon Aubrey feels fair right now It should be noted that the extra point that Brandon Aubrey missed was made more difficult by the extra yardage applied to it following Javonte Williams’ ridiculous taunting penalty . It was literally harder than your average extra point is the overall point. Aubrey struggled in his most recent NFL game before Sunday night, last season’s finale which was also against the Giants at MetLife Stadium. In fact, Aubrey has now missed a kick of some kind in three straight games. This is the first time in his career that this is the case. Again, no one is suggesting panic. Aubrey has a very large body of work that suggests this all might be an aberration, even if admittedly a sort of a large aberration which is a bit of an oxymoron. It bears mentioning that the last two games took place in the same stadium, MetLife, and that it is outdoors and also known for not having the most quality playing surface in the NFL. None of these things are excuses, to be clear. They are simply data points in talking about the overall subject at large. When you throw out terms like “concern” and “worried” people tend to take them at their most intense definitions. It is fair to say that you, me, or anyone is concerned/worried about Aubrey given his recent form, but that doesn’t have to mean that we are ready to totally freak out. So you be the judge. How concerned and/or worried are you? A lot? A little? None at all?
author: RJ Ochoa

title: Cowboys rookie report: Caleb Downs had one big moment in Giants loss
summary: The Dallas Cowboys opened their season with a disappointing 28–20 loss to the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium. There were flashes from the rookie class, but also reminders of how much work remains. Caleb Downs produced the standout moment, while several other newcomers picked up their first meaningful NFL experience. Here is how each […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Downs #13 of the Dallas Cowboys prior to the game against the New York Giants on September 13, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys opened their season with a disappointing 28–20 loss to the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium. There were flashes from the rookie class, but also reminders of how much work remains. Caleb Downs produced the standout moment, while several other newcomers picked up their first meaningful NFL experience. Here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. Caleb Downs (Defensive snaps: 61 | Tackles: 8 | Tackles for loss: 0 | Sacks: 1 | Interceptions: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | QB hits: 1 | Pressures: 1 | Forced fumbles: 1) Downs supplied the rookie class’ biggest highlight, flying in unblocked on a blitz and delivering a crushing hit on Jaxson Dart to force a fumble. That play showed the speed and aggression Dallas hoped it was getting. Starting in the slot, Downs was heavily involved, although his individual flash could not solve the defense’s problems getting off the field. There was plenty to like about his debut, but he acknowledged afterward that the unit needs to execute its assignments better. Malachi Lawrence (Defensive snaps: 30 | Tackles: 5 | Tackles for loss: 0 | Sacks: 0 | Interceptions: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | QB hits: 0 | Pressures: 2) Lawrence generated two pressures on 11 pass-rushing snaps, giving Dallas some encouraging disruption despite finishing without a sack. Getting near the quarterback was the positive, finishing plays more consistently is the next step. PFF also recorded a missed tackle against the run. Setting the edge and not getting caught out of position is something he needs to work on for the next games. Jaishawn Barham (Defensive snaps: 34 | Tackles: 6 | Tackles for loss: 1 | Sacks: 0 | Interceptions: 0 | Passes defended: 0 | QB hits: 0 | Pressures: 0) Barham contributed a stop behind the line and received meaningful playing time. His six tackles gave him a useful statistical start, although that alone does not establish how well he handled every assignment. There was little opportunity to assess his pass rushing with just two rushes attempts. He did commit a costly penalty by jumping offsides. Drew Shelton (Offensive snaps: 3 | Pressures allowed: 0 | QB hits allowed: 0 | Sacks allowed: 0) Shelton participated, but three offensive snaps leave little room for a meaningful evaluation. He was mainly used as a jumbo TE for blocking purposes. This was a small introduction to regular-season action. LT Overton (Defensive snaps: 18 | Tackles: 1 | Tackles for loss: 0 | Sacks: 0 | Interceptions: 0 | Passes defended: 1 | QB hits: 0 | Pressures: 0) Overton made an early contribution by getting his hands into a passing lane and batting down a throw. It was a useful reminder that defensive linemen can affect the passing game without reaching the quarterback. His pressure production was quiet, but that breakup gave him a positive moment in a limited role.
author: Mike Poland

title: Stock Up, Stock Down After the Broncos’ Loss to the Chiefs in Week 1
summary: We’re a few days out from the Broncos’ Monday Night loss to the Chiefs, and it still stings. The Broncos opened up the season with a disappointing and downright embarrassing 31-10 loss to the Chiefs. The debut of offensive coordinator Davis Webb was a failure, and the Denver Broncos defense had a historically high missed […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs attempts to evade Que Robinson #51 of the Denver Broncos as he looks to pass during an NFL football game on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a few days out from the Broncos’ Monday Night loss to the Chiefs, and it still stings. The Broncos opened up the season with a disappointing and downright embarrassing 31-10 loss to the Chiefs. The debut of offensive coordinator Davis Webb was a failure , and the Denver Broncos defense had a historically high missed tackle rate It was all bad. Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos roster and give you stock-ups and stock-downs on every player currently on the 53-man roster. After a game like that on Monday Night, we are looking at a lot of stock downs. So, with all that said, here are your stock-ups and stock-downs for the Denver Broncos after their blowout loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. Quarterback Bo Nix – Stock down: Monday Night was one of the worst games of Bo Nix’s career thus far. He had an opening-drive interception, later fumbled the ball, was lucky not to fumble the ball again, and was sacked a total of 4 times. Not all the blame falls on Nix; he was put in a bad situation by his coaching staff (no run game), his protection sucked, and there were drive-killing drops and penalties throughout. Still, it was not a great game for Nix, and he and the Broncos need to bounce back next week. Jarrett Stidham – Unchanged: He was the backup to Bo Nix, as expected Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged: He was the emergency third-string QB, as expected Running Back JK Dobbins – Unchanged: I thought about stock down here, but he played well when given the ball. He had 8 carries for 36 yards and averaged 4.5 yards per carry. That’s what you want to see from Dobbins, just more of it. The Broncos ran the ball 6 times at halftime, and then the game got away from them in the second half. RJ Harvey – Stock up: I thought Jonah Coleman was going to be the Broncos’ RB3, but RJ Harvey seems to be firmly their RB2 or even their 1B with JK Dobbins. He out-snapped Dobbins (likely due to game script and all the passing) and played well when given the ball. His pass blocking looked questionable at best, but overall, he seems like someone who’s going to be featured in their offense moving forward. Jonah Coleman – Stock down: Coleman saw 3 offensive snaps and returned a kick. I expected to see the rookie used a little bit more, but he’s clearly behind Dobbins and Harvey right now. Tyler Badie – Unchanged: He was inactive and is their RB4. Adam Prentice – Unchanged: Only saw 6 offensive snaps and did most of his work on special teams. There was a key 3rd-and-1 where his lead blocking or short-yardage ability would have come in handy. Wide Receiver Jaylen Waddle – Stock down: All that hype, and we get 3 targets and 1 catch for 2 yards. Waddle himself was not bad, though he did have a drop on 3rd down, but his lack of targets and usage was odd to me. I would have expected the Broncos to feature the new weapon they traded for and hyped up all offseason. Yet, just 3 targets and 1 catch for 2 yards. Courtland Sutton – Unchanged: Sutton wasn’t featured much either, but we know what he and Nix can do, so I am not going to overreact here. Still, he didn’t get his first target until the 3rd quarter, I believe, which is a very odd game plan. Pat Bryant – Stock up: He played 59% of the offensive snaps and led the way for the Broncos receivers with 6 targets and 4 catches for 42 yards. He came up big for them on their lone touchdown drive and showcased why he will be a key part of this offense moving forward. He did have a couple of holding calls, which I thought were mostly BS, so I am not holding them against him. His drop on a screen play that would have led to a 1st down did suck, though. Marvin Mims – Unchanged: Mims had another injury scare, but thankfully seemed to be okay. He didn’t do much on offense but did have a few nice kick returns. We did see Troy Franklin play more offensive snaps than him, so that will be something to watch moving forward. Troy Franklin – Stock up slightly: I thought Franklin was in danger of being inactive due to the Broncos going with Lil’Jordan Humphrey, but that did not happen. LJH played the procedural off and on the roster game this week, and Franklin was active and played 33% of the offensive snaps. However, he did see just 1 target, and it was a rather bad OPI call, which set the offense back. His usage gives him stock up, but that OPI was not great. Lil’Jordan Humphrey – Unchanged: It was reported prior to the game that the Broncos released Lil’Jordan, but it was simply a procedural move and that he would rejoin the team soon. On Tuesday, it was reported that LJH re-signed with the team. I would anticipate him being active and utilized a little more moving forward, but we shall see. Tight End Adam Trautman – Unchanged: He did catch 2 passes for 10 yards, but that’s not why he’s on the roster. He’s a run-blocking tight end, one that is being paid decently by a team that refuses to run the ball. Make that make sense. Evan Engram – Stock up: Engram led the Broncos in receiving yards and caught their lone touchdown on a well-drawn-up play that left him wide open in the end zone. This was the lone bright spot for the Broncos on Monday Night, but I think we’ll see Engram used a bit more moving forward. Nate Adkins – Unchanged: Played 13 snaps and is a blocking specialist for a team that does not run the ball. He did have 8 special teams snaps as well. Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: The rookie was inactive. Offensive Line Garett Bolles – Unchanged: I am no OL expert, but it was a rough night for the Broncos blockers. Bolles has earned the benefit of the doubt. Ben Powers – Stock down slightly: From the clips I did see, Powers had a rough night and gave up some pressure up the middle of the Broncos’ offensive line. Luke Wattenberg – Stock down slightly: In the same boat as Powers but also had a few iffy snaps. It was humid, and the ball was likely slippery, so hopefully that was the reason for that. Quinn Meinerz – Unchanged: Like Bolles, Meinerz has earned the benefit of the doubt from me. Mike McGlinchey – Stock down: I did notice a lot of pressure coming off that edge, and in the clips I did see, McGlinchey was having a rough time. Again, I am not an OL expert, but he’s the one loser I am going with from this group. Matt Peart – Unchanged: Reserve OT/Swing tackle and played 2 special teams snaps Alex Palczewski – Unchanged: Reserve OL and likely 6th offensive lineman, but saw just 2 special teams snaps. Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: backup center and saw 2 special teams snaps Kage Casey – Unchanged: The rookie OL was inactive Defensive Line Zach Allen – Unchanged: It was a rough night for the defense, but Allen gets the benefit of the doubt from me. I am sure he missed some, but I don’t recall him missing any notable tackles. DJ Jones – Stock down: When you’re a run-stuffing nose tackle and a team runs for over 200 yards on you, your stock is going down. The Broncos’ run defense has been leaky dating back to the playoffs, and Jones is the man in the middle of their defensive line. They need better play from him. Malcolm Roach – Unchanged: I went back and forth here, but settled on unchanged. He’s a run-stuffing DL on a team that sucked vs. the run, but he made some plays, including a nice PBU on 3rd down. Run defense needs to be better/ Eyioma Uwazurike – Stock down slightly: Need more from the Broncos’ big man. He was supposedly unblockable in camp, but that didn’t seem to be the case vs. the Chiefs. I am not sure if he played badly or not, but again, 200+ yards rushing. Everyone has a bit of stink on them. Sai’vion Jones – Stock up slightly: This is just based on usage. He played 15 defensive snaps and 7 special teams snaps…
author: Scotty Payne

title: Broncos vs Jaguars Week 2 preview: Denver looks to drastically improve
summary: The Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged in their opener. What makes it even tougher is that it came against a hated rival. Now the Broncos have to learn from this, improve, and get ready for another tough matchup this Sunday. Teams face adversity, and Denver has that in spades early in the season. How do […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - DECEMBER 21: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos walks off the field after a 34-20 loss against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field at Mile High on December 21, 2025 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged in their opener. What makes it even tougher is that it came against a hated rival. Now the Broncos have to learn from this, improve, and get ready for another tough matchup this Sunday. Teams face adversity, and Denver has that in spades early in the season. How do the Broncos respond? What improvements do they make against the Jacksonville Jaguars? To add a little flavor to the mix, you have the result from last season’s game between these two teams when Denver got whopped by the Jaguars in Week 16, 34-20. FanDuel Sportsbook currently has the Broncos as the -2.5-point home favorites on Sunday. The total sits at 45.5, with a lean towards the under at -115. Offensive Rankings Jacksonville : Fourteenth in total offense (360 yards per game), 11th in rushing offense (126 YPG), 10th in passing offense (234 YPG), sixth in scoring offense (34 points per game). Denver : Thirty-second in total offense (176 yards per game), 31st in rushing offense (61 YPG), 32nd in passing offense (115 YPG), tied for 28th in scoring offense (10 points per game). Defensive Rankings Jacksonville : Tenth in total defense (272 yards per game), ninth in rushing defense (87 YPG), tied for 13th in passing defense (185 YPG), tied for second in scoring defense (10 points per game). Denver : Twenty-fourth in total defense (392 yards per game), 31st in rushing defense (220 YPG), 10th in passing defense (172 YPG), tied for 23rd in scoring defense (31 points per game). Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Sunday’s game. Do the opposite of whatever Denver just did Whatever the hell we witnessed in Kansas City, the Broncos must do the complete opposite against Jacksonville. That starts by looking and playing like an NFL team. For Denver to do that, it needs to really hammer down the preparation this week. Bo Nix called the loss to the Chiefs “an ugly wake-up call.” Here’s hoping the Broncos got the message and don’t hit the snooze button. Come together as a team, do the little things, limit the costly mistakes, and execute. — Ian St. Clair Tackle! Watching Kenneth Walker embarrass the Broncos defense was eye-opening. Patrick Mahomes constantly escaping on that reconstructed knee was baffling. It wasn’t that the defense played horribly; it just found ways to miss tackles, making it impossible to win. If Denver can’t wrap up the Jaguars, mark down 0-2 and a major uphill climb to the playoffs. — Adam Malnati Better play on third down The Broncos struggled to stop the Chiefs on third down on Monday Night Football. Moreover, they kept shooting themselves in the foot on offense and were dreadful in that aspect. This was also an issue for them last December, when they lost to the Jacksonville Jaguars. If they can’t do better at extending drives or getting off the field in key situations, they’ll continue to be their own worst enemies. Their performance in these situations has to get better to be successful. — Christopher Hart Better offensive game plan We need to make sure the Jaguars don’t coat themselves in oil, making it impossible for our defenders to tackle them as the Chiefs did. Seriously, though, we need a better offensive game plan to counter what the Jags will do on defense. The Bronco offense looked completely unprepared for the funky blitz packages that Spags always uses. Also, the Broncos need to do a better job of convincing the refs not to call holding on them when they are blatantly holding. The Broncos should ask the Chiefs what their secret is. — Joe Mahoney Score more points than the other team Data and analytics tell you that the Broncos are winless when they score less than their opponent and are undefeated when they score more. So, the game plan is simple! Score more points than the Jaguars. You didn’t do that against the Chiefs, and we’re all angry and disappointed. Do that vs. the small-market Jags, and we’ll be happy again. — Scotty Payne What are your keys to Sunday’s game?

title: Broncos at Chiefs: The No Bull Review
summary: The Denver Broncos decided to run it back with the best continuity in the NFL, brought in a top-tier wide receiver free agent, and had a healthy Bo Nix for week 1 of the NFL season. What did we get for all the chatter about being a Super Bowl ready team?  An absolute butt stain […]
full_text: The Denver Broncos decided to run it back with the best continuity in the NFL, brought in a top-tier wide receiver free agent, and had a healthy Bo Nix for week 1 of the NFL season. What did we get for all the chatter about being a Super Bowl ready team? An absolute butt stain of a performance from the Broncos on offense and defense. 31 – 10 is an embarrassment. Some may take great joy at digging into the failures and faults at every orifice of an abomination of a game, but I honestly find less and less joy doing that the more years I add to my belt. I’ve got some points to make worth talking about, but largely we’ll use the review to talk big picture (kinda my normal routine in recent years when the Broncos lay an absolute egg). Head Coach Sean Payton, for some strange reason, doesn’t understand how to get his teams ready to hit the gates running. He runs a complex offense that is scheme-dependent (which I honestly love because it works well when executed properly). He doesn’t seem to value playing starters much in the preseason, with many vets getting a couple of series in the warm-up games. It is hard to analyze this performance and not cast some doubt on the process being used when his teams year after year have problems executing early in the season. This team on both sides of the ball looked very unprepared for this game. The offense had no clue how to find a groove and keep it or how to execute any 3rd down play effectively. The “best offensive line in the NFL” pass blocked like a car full of clowns at a diarrhea fiesta. The defense looked like a unit full of undrafted rookies trying to make a big turnover on every play and forgetting that this is the kind of football where they have to tackle. Payton often takes the fault immediately in his pressers when the team plays this poorly, and I’m sure he did this week as well. Yes, Payton. It indeed is your fault. You did not prepare your team properly to play this game. You were outcoached in the most predictable ways. I’m a friggin nobody fan chugging Mountain Dews and eating Cheetos, and I knew the Kansas City Chiefs were going to run multiple tight ends / extra offensive linemen like the Bills did last year and run the ball with Kenneth Walker on repeat as their one and only way to create offensive production. Your team had no plan for that. Bo Nix’s one biggest weakness is his reluctance to throw the ball over the middle, and yet another offseason went by without any evidence of work being done to address that weakness. It kinda makes it easy to defend the pass when your QB only uses ⅔ of the field the majority of the time. Offense So let’s just say that all the talk about how awesome Davis Webb is and how ready he is for the play-calling duties is looking quite sus at this point in time. That looked like a weaker version of the offense we saw last year, with a play caller abandoning the run when it didn’t need to be, getting fancy on 3rd and short when you could have just run the friggin ball for an easy first down, and leaning on underneath throws when you just traded for one of the most potent downfield threats in the NFL. I do know that not all the calls were terrible. I liked a lot of the plays that they threw to Pat Bryant. I thought Waddle and Sutton both dropped catchable balls. I thought Nix lost plays quite often by trying to go outside instead of simply stepping up and throwing the ball. The execution on offense was lacking from the player side of things. Also, why are we still having to use timeouts and getting delays of game when we have this nifty young play caller? I thought this move was put in place to address that? One small pass I give the offense and Bo Nix that is worth mentioning is the wind. In the 2nd and 4th quarters, when the offense played its worst was when the wind was in their face, which is going to make most QBs more timid about throwing over the middle or deeper down the field. Those would have been great quarters to lean on the run game in my mind, but hey…the game plan called for check downs and screens…right? Quarterbacks Bo Nix looked like a rookie, plain and simple. The moment of this game was far too big for him. His early interception was horrendous, unforgivable, and pathetic. He stared down the only option on that side of the field, watched a guy with perfect technique defend it. Then Bo decided to throw him the ball (because there was a 0% chance of our guy ever catching that ball). The happy feet are back big time. The line did him no favors (regardless of how much Payton wants to crow about sacks being a quarterback stat). If Bo was audibling out of runs or choosing the pass option in RPOs, he needs coaching because we have backs who can run effectively now. Line Mike McGlinchey had an awful night and owes the offense a dinner or two. He got worked multiple times and was a core piece of many pressures on the night. Running Backs I’d love to crow about our running backs. JK Dobbins averaged 4.5 ypc, and RJ Harvey averaged 6 (small sample size). It seems like we maybe could have done better than 30% of the plays on the night being runs if we wanted to. Before anyone says a word about the game going sideways, please note that the team had 17 passing attempts vs. 6 runs in the first half, with the game being within one score. Don’t take that excuse from Sean Payton, other fans, or silly announcers. Receivers The good news is that the team seems to have figured out how to make Evan Engram a part of the offense. Also, Pat Bryant is currently the best wide receiver on the team, and it isn’t close. Cortland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle seemed to be largely placeholders on the field that Nix wasn’t interested in throwing to when coming open (which they were through the night constantly). Oh yeah, and Troy Franklin still sucks. Let’s rotate Lil’Jordan Humphrey back in and let the potato get picked off the waiver wire. Defense We need to stop all talk about Vance Joseph being one of the best defensive coordinators in the NFL right this second. He can’t even get his team ready to stop a team that can only run their bell-cow back on repeat to gain yards. Heck, the team outside of Zach Allen and Patrick Surtain doesn’t even understand the fundamental process of how to tackle in the NFL at any level. The effort of this defense was absolutely pathetic. The execution of this defense was what I would expect from a team of Pop Warner youths doped out on barbiturates. Positive notes for the defense: Kansas City was holding on damn near every pass play, and it was insulting to the game of NFL football that they were allowed to get away with it…I had not seen this level of holding abuse since 2015. If you are worried about our pass rush, don’t be. They still have it, but the refs decided Kermit gets different rules than other more common quarterbacks in the NFL. Front 7 The continued story of Alex Singleton being a liability at inside linebacker is alive and well. He was an embarrassment at linebacker with 2 good tackles out of his 15 in the game (let me point out again that getting a lot of tackles does not equate to a linebacker being good…where they make the tackle is rather important). We extended the worst starter on the team. I’m glad he’s a team captain and a feel-good story. I have never felt good about his play over any three-game stretch of his time here and have quite regularly thought he was a liability and a minus player for this defense. Secondary I had notes on many defensive backs in this game with good plays, but sadly had just as many of the same players missing a tackle. I’m not giving your name time when you can’t even square a player and wrap up properly on an NFL field. Hit the tackle dummies, boys…you need the work. Special Teams Jeremy Crawshaw has a phenomenal leg. He was the most effective player on the whole roster on Monday Night. Now pardon me while I go puke after typing that. Final Thoughts Now that we’ve exercised the demons of this game,…

title: Stat was a bad way to start the season
summary: The Denver Broncos lost the game in two of three phases on Monday – offensively and defensively. I would say that special teams was the only phase that the Broncos won. Jeremy Crawshaw forced the Kansas City Chiefs to start three drives inside their 10 (9, 6 and 3 yard lines). The Broncos only started […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Nick Bolton #32 of the Kansas City Chiefs knocks down a pass against Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos during the fourth quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos lost the game in two of three phases on Monday – offensively and defensively. I would say that special teams was the only phase that the Broncos won. Jeremy Crawshaw forced the Kansas City Chiefs to start three drives inside their 10 (9, 6 and 3 yard lines). The Broncos only started one drive inside the ten (on the 8). Marvin Mims averaged 18 yards on his two punt returns. That was about the end of the good for the Broncos. The offense finished the game 2 of 12 on 3rd downs and 0 for 1 on 4th downs. The offense got only 9 first downs in the game and fumbled three times (only losing one). As crazy it seems, the Broncos are not the worst in the NFL after week 1 in terms of 3rd down conversion. The Browns are worst going 1 of 8 on first team in their game. When only the Browns are worse, you know it’s bad. On the other side, the Chiefs had 19 first downs, and were 9 of 17 on third down. Defensively the Broncos are only seventh worst in 3rd down conversion rate allowed. The Cowboys allowed the Giants to convert on 9 of 11 which is crazy. The Broncos had 58 actual defensive plays (KC had 3 kneel-downs) and somehow managed to miss a tackle on 29.8% of those plays. There were 34 solo tackles for the Broncos and 40 assisted tackles. Since missed tackle percentage does not delineate what play the missed tackle happened on (two can and did happen on multiple plays on Monday) we don’t know how many of those plays involved a missed tackle, but the Broncos had 24 missed tackles last night. Their were at least two on the TD pass to Rashee Rice. However bad you thought the Broncos' tackling was against the Chiefs, it was even worse Denver's 248 missed tackle yards allowed were the most in a single game in @NextGenStats ' database. Their 29.8% missed tackle percentage is the third worst single-game score since 2018 https://t.co/Kd0zQjfUFl — Trevor Sikkema (@TampaBayTre) September 15, 2026 According pro-football-reference.com the Broncos only had 85 missed tackle s in the regular season in 2025. The defense did end up getting two sacks (both by Zach Allen) who also had three QBhits to go with those sacks, meaning that he had at least five pressures in the game. The rest of the defense combined for two QBhits, one by Que Robinson and one by Jonah Elliss. Nik Bonitto did not show up in either stat, though he might have had a pressure. Admittedly he should have had plenty of them given that he was going up a player in Kahlil Benson who had never played a snap at LT above the high school level. Admittedly, the Chiefs were getting rid of the ball quickly on Monday, but he still should have had something to show. It’s possible that he had a pressure since those have not been tabulated yet. According to NFL Next Gen stats, the Chief runners last night we getting -0.1 yards before contact, meaning that they were getting hit at or behind the LOS on most plays. They still managed to gain 223 yards on 35 actual runs on Monday (taking out the kneel-downs). That’s 6.37 yards per carry. That’s the second worst run defense in the league right now. Only the Panthers defense, which allowed 291 yards on 39 carries (7.46 ypc), was worse in week one.

title: Drew Brees thought about returning?
summary: Supposedly, Adam Schefter reported that Drew Brees flirted with the idea of helping save the Broncos’ playoff run last year when Bo Nix broke his ankle. This is a great talking point. We get to wistfully wonder, “What if?” But let’s be real, Broncos Country. There’s no way that would have ever worked. First of […]
full_text: CANTON, OHIO - AUGUST 08: A New Orleans Saints fan holds a cutout of Drew Brees during the 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame Enshrinement Ceremony at Tom Benson Hall Of Fame Stadium on August 08, 2026 in Canton, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Supposedly, Adam Schefter reported that Drew Brees flirted with the idea of helping save the Broncos’ playoff run last year when Bo Nix broke his ankle. This is a great talking point. We get to wistfully wonder, “What if?” But let’s be real, Broncos Country. There’s no way that would have ever worked. First of all, Brees left the game well cooked at quarterback. He got every possible iota of play out of his body before retiring. He was also still technically a Saint. Finally, would you really trust a guy who has sat out of football for the better part of 5 years over your backup who’s been drilling and prepping with the team all year long? Sure, the Sean Payton system is still very similar to what they ran in New Orleans. You can not tell me that there’s not a lot of nuance that has been moved about in the years since Brees was last playing the game. While it may be a fun talking point, it seems rather far-fetched…especially when we hear after the fact that Brees tested his arm and had problems with his wrist. title: Day after Broncos: Picking up the pieces
summary: Well, its Tuesday evening and I think most of us have gone through all of the emotions from last night’s butt whoopin’. Few things hurt worse in the regular season than having a division rival put belt to ass for 60 minutes, but that’s exactly what the Kansas City Chiefs did to the Denver Broncos […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos looks on against the Kansas City Chiefs during the third quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, its Tuesday evening and I think most of us have gone through all of the emotions from last night’s butt whoopin’. Few things hurt worse in the regular season than having a division rival put belt to ass for 60 minutes, but that’s exactly what the Kansas City Chiefs did to the Denver Broncos on Monday Night Football . The good news is the NFL season does not allow anyone to linger too long on one bad game. It’s on to the next one. There a plenty of questions about this team on offense and defense, but the biggest one that will be answered first is ‘how will they respond’ when the Jacksonville Jaguars come to town on Sunday? Broncos daily recap Sean Payton’s Broncos struggle in September; he’s also shown an ability to turn things around Denver’s endured tough September losses under Payton. But his teams have consistently improved as the season progresses. The Broncos’ poor run defense and tackling are major concerns The Denver Broncos’ defense was atrocious last night vs. the Chiefs. They allowed Kenneth Walker to rush for 173 yards, including a 60-yard 4th-down touchdown run, and average 7.5 yards per carry. They also allowed a hobbled Patrick Mahomes in a knee brace to rush for 23 yards, including a 15-yard first-quarter touchdown. Davis Webb’s debut as a playcaller was an epic failure There was a lot of hype and anticipation about Webb’s debut as a play caller, and well, his debut was an epic failure. Potent quotables Sean Payton On QB Bo Nix’s fumbles and sacks against the Chiefs “I think part of it was certainly the downs and distances that we put ourselves in. So when you end up in some of those second-and-long or third-and-longs, however you get there, minus plays, penalties, there’s a number of reasons. Then all of a sudden, the job description for him gets much more difficult. So if there was one thing that gave you a pretty good reflection on how the game went, and how poorly we played, and how well Kansas City played, if you just look at the third-down numbers, those guys were converting third-and-2, 3, 4 at a pretty good rate. I don’t think we converted a third down in our last 10 attempts.” On if he would characterize last night’s game as a ‘wake-up call’ “Certainly a slap in the face. When you come off training camp and your offseason program, it’s one thing to lose in a hard-fought game where you feel like you played well. I don’t feel like we played up to our standard, and certainly that starts with us as coaches, myself. So yes, it’s disappointing. That would be a great way to describe it.” On if it’s easier or more difficult to flush games like this “Honestly I think it’s more difficult because you have to have that honest day where you come in as coaches. We first meet and we go through everything and discuss, ‘What are the things we would’ve done differently?’ Then you have to have that… I know it’s a shorter week, but there’s no way we can get past today without looking at the tape and looking at the things that we have to improve on before we even play the next opponent. So I would tend to always rather see your team play well than not play well. So that’s why I would say it’s more difficult.” On media reports regarding Pro Football Hall of Fame QB Drew Brees “When this topic came up at the [Pro Football] Hall of Fame, I kept thinking they were discussing the COVID season. Drew [Brees] had reached out, I think, right after the championship or right after the playoff win against Buffalo. I think he called [Bills Offensive Coordinator] Pete [Carmichael], probably texted Pete or [Ravens Senior Offensive Assistant] Joe [Lombardi], those guys. None of it even came to my attention. So, when the story came up in Canton, I kept thinking they were just talking about the COVID season. Even in the COVID season when he and I discussed possibly coming back for a Monday night game, he had trouble throwing it. So, I don’t think really anything really came of it. I think in Drew’s mind, there’s that competitor in him. So, I was kind of out of the loop. I don’t think it’s a big story, but nonetheless, certainly one that once they described it to me, it just never got to my level, I guess. He had reached out to Pete, I think, and then Joe.” On lessons he learned at the start of his own play calling career that he can share with Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb “I think there is always that experience element as you continue to do that, there are certain things you learn, things you prefer. I think most importantly is how’s the game unfolding on the other side of the ball. It’s so important to understand what’s happening with our defense and the opponent’s offense. A lot of that can guide you sometime relative to the risk tolerance you’re willing to have on certain plays or series.” On if Kansas City did anything in particular to generate pressure on QB Bo Nix “I think a lot of it, we were in one-dimensional phases. Our run-pass ratio was skewed and off. As that unfolds and you get into where you’re throwing the ball, then it becomes more challenging. The way that game unfolded, all of the sudden there were a number of series where you felt one-dimensional. I think that added to the problem.” On QB Bo Nix being pressured by a three-man rush while trying to get the ball to WR Jaylen Waddle “You focused on a shot play. They did a good job with mixing up the rush. We got some pressure. We probably got a little bit more man-to-man maybe on third down then maybe in the past. Last year’s studies in both games where K.C. defended our offense, there wasn’t as much pressure anticipated. There was some man-to-man. So [Chiefs CB L’Jarius] Sneed does a good job of timing up his pressures, but then also giving you some looks that… It’s entirely different when you’re playing that game and you’re in Kansas City with the silent snap count and when the pressures unfold then sometimes when you play at home and the timing of a verbal cadence and how much that carries weight. They have to show the pressures a little earlier. You point to a good snap where he [QB Bo Nix] is certainly looking to get the ball downfield. They’re doing a good job of staying on top.” Under the radar In what everyone proclaims to be the best offensive line in the league, Bo Nix was pressured on 45.5% of his dropbacks against KC Whenever protection did hold up, he was 15-18 for 126 yards and a TD We're used to him carrying the offense, but was too much in the season opener pic.twitter.com/hy4NRKmBx0 — Jordan Lopez (@JordanTLopez) September 15, 2026 Week 1 defense: -RB yards before contact per carry (run defense stat) -Average time to pressure pic.twitter.com/zDNrouPH3r — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) September 15, 2026 The Feed Post your own thoughts on MHR’s Feed . Holy smokes! There are a lot of good posts from the community today. The Feed is chalk full of them and I even missed a few because its been so busy in there. I just curated a list of them above, but I’m sure I missed some. Way back in the day – 2007 – these were called “Diaries” and that is where I began raging against those Mike Shanahan defenses at the end of his career. Hopefully we see all of us turn more positive after this first game. I was comforted a bit by this tweet from Scotty on the main account today: Sean Payton has a 4-8 record in the month of September with the Broncos 28-12 in the rest of the months pic.twitter.com/et1PKpibHw — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 Just got to get through September, people.

It is just one game, but boy do we have a lot of concerns heading into Week 2 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Let’s vote and discuss the disgusting performance from last night and how they might be able to […]

title: Sean Payton’s Broncos struggle in September; he’s also shown an ability to turn things around
summary: The Denver Broncos looked downright ugly in their opener. And that’s being nice. In the season opener with a national audience watching, Bo Nix, Sean Payton, and the Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged. If it were a boxing match, people would have begged someone to throw in the white towel. Some still did. This also […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Head coach Sean Payton of the Denver Broncos scratches his head during the third quarter against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Denver Broncos looked downright ugly in their opener. And that’s being nice. In the season opener with a national audience watching, Bo Nix, Sean Payton, and the Denver Broncos were unmercifully flogged. If it were a boxing match, people would have begged someone to throw in the white towel. Some still did. This also isn’t anything new. Payton-coached teams struggle in September. That’s the case for his time in Denver, but his entire coaching career. After Monday night’s 31-10 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, Payton is 31-31 in September. Sean Payton has a 4-8 record in the month of September with the Broncos 28-12 in the rest of the months pic.twitter.com/et1PKpibHw — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 15, 2026 With the Broncos, Payton is now 4-8 in September: 2023: 0-3 2024: 2-2 2025: 2-2 2026: 0-1 Last season in particular, Denver had two crushing, last-second losses to the Indianapolis Colts and Los Angeles Chargers. The Broncos held on for the win against the Tennessee Titans in the opener. The Chargers’ loss was especially infuriating since Denver blew a fourth-quarter lead. The key to remember from all of this: Payton is 28-12 with the Broncos when it’s not September. “Obviously, not a good evening,” Payton said to the media after Monday’s game. “We didn’t do a lot well at all in the game, so we will have to look at the tape tomorrow. I felt like all the key factors: they rushed the ball well, we didn’t. It starts with me. It starts with our coaching staff. I thought they won, really, in every phase.” So the panic after the loss to Kansas City is justified. The poor tackling. The horrible run defense for the third-straight game. The inept play-calling by Davis Webb. Nix looked disoriented most of the game. With all of that in mind, it’s also a terrible time to make sweeping conclusions about this team. Payton consistently gets his teams to improve. He’s shown an ability to diagnose the problems (see above), make adjustments, and have his team playing its best football late. “I think you learn how important it is not to kill yourself,” Nix said to the media after the game. “That goes without saying, but when you do that in a game like today, it just raises that a little higher. I just felt like it was penalty, after penalty, after penalty. Nobody has good plays to call when you are in 2nd-and-long, 3rd-and-long. The play sheet is very small. We didn’t put anybody in a good spot today. We really didn’t.” What sucks is that this happened in the opener against a bitter division rival. But it doesn’t change the fact that Denver has some serious issues to fix. It also doesn’t mean the season is over. After all, this is September, and we’ve seen this movie from Payton before. Since his teams have a knack for starting slow, let’s let this one play out before making any bold proclamations about the Broncos or the season. In other words, don’t panic. “I think we just let ourselves down,” Nix said to the media after the game. “I think it’s more disappointing than frustrating. I’m not necessarily filled with rage; we just let ourselves down, shot ourselves in the foot, literally gave ourselves no chance to succeed today. We made it easier for them, point blank period. We know we have to be better. There are a lot of guys in that locker room who are going to take ownership and be better. It starts with me, and it starts with our offense. We’re going to be better. We don’t have a choice but to get better. It was a nasty wakeup call today.”
author: Ian St. Clair

title: 5 Lions vs. Bills thoughts after watching Buffalo’s Week 1 game
summary: To prepare for my “On Paper” preview between the Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills, I watched Week 1’s game between the Bills and the Houston Texans. Taking notes along the way, I came up with five observations about Buffalo’s performance, and how it may impact Thursday night’s showdown. 1. Their run defense may be significantly […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 13: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills passes the ball against the Houston Texans during the third quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images To prepare for my “On Paper” preview between the Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills, I watched Week 1’s game between the Bills and the Houston Texans. Taking notes along the way, I came up with five observations about Buffalo’s performance, and how it may impact Thursday night’s showdown. 1. Their run defense may be significantly improved I’m feeling pretty darn good about the Detroit Lions’ rushing attack after a strong Week 1 outing against a Saints run defense that was excellent last season. Heading into Week 2 against a Bills’ run defense that ranked 31st in both DVOA and EPA/rush, I figured this could be a huge advantage for the Lions to exploit. However, there were signs the Bills defense could be significantly improved this year under new coordinator Jim Leonhard. Yes, the Texans ran for 124 yards and two touchdowns, but it came on 32 carries, averaging just 3.9 yards per carry. What was particularly impressive was the Bills’ ability to generate negative plays in run defense. The Texans had the seventh-highest “stuffed” rate per FTN Fantasy—with 24% of their rushes being stopped at or behind the line of scrimmage. Now, the Texans rushing attack was terrible last year (27th in stuffed rate, 29th in DVOA), so this wasn’t the biggest test for the Bills run defense, but it was a promising start. 2. Jared Goff could have some time in the pocket On the other side of the Bills’ defensive front, they surprisingly did not produce much pressure against a questionable Texans offensive line. Per NFL Pro, C.J. Stroud faced the lowest pressure rate (21.4%) of any quarterback in Week 1, despite taking three sacks (and two forced fumbles). Now, when the game was on the line and the Texans were in the red zone to win it, the Bills pinned their ears back and picked up two of those sacks and the game-winning fumble recovery. But for most of the game, the Bills’ pass rush was largely invisible. 3. Josh Allen, Joe Brady are psychopaths Okay, this is nothing new, but Josh Allen was an absolute menace on Sunday vs. the Texans—throwing caution to the wind. It’s beautiful… pic.twitter.com/JckrAPPT5i — Nate Geary (@NateGearySports) September 14, 2026 It’s only been one game, but #Bills Josh Allen is: – 1st in air yards per attempt (12.6) – 1st in deep pass percentage (24.1%) – 3rd in EPA/drop-back (+0.49) – 11-of-16 throwing further than 10 yards Vertical passing game so far 📈📈 #BillsMafia @BuffTrenchTalk pic.twitter.com/2nyZPZ5Z0A — Carson Hayek (@CarsonHayek) September 15, 2026 Allen is every bit of the gunslinger he has been for the entirety of his career, but I also think Joe Brady’s promotion from offensive coordinator to head coach is enabling him even further. Take, for example, when the Bills got the ball up 24-21 at the end of the first half. They were on their own 17-yard line with 18 seconds left and the Texans had only two timeouts. Any sane coach would take a knee and go to halftime with a lead, but apparently not Brady and Allen. They dialed up a bomb to D.J. Moore, and while it fell incomplete, it just goes to show you they are going to be aggressive in any and all situations. They also lined up to go for it twice in field goal range on fourth-and-short. They failed to convert one and committed a penalty on the other, but expect them to be a little more aggressive than they were last year—although they’ve always been pretty aggressive on fourth down. Oh, and there was a hook-and-ladder thrown in there during the first half. The good news is that aggressiveness can can also get the Bills in trouble. Allen made an absolutely bone-headed throw during their game-winning drive that would’ve—and should’ve—been the game-losing pass. Kamari Lassiter Just Sold So Hard Bruhhh. Josh Allen Just Threw Up A Shot, And It Should Have Been Picked. pic.twitter.com/HMc5uXF1Yx — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) September 13, 2026 4. Tight ends could be a problem By now, you may have seen the graphic that shows the Bills were in 13 personnel (one running back, three tight end) 50 percent of the time . And while that puts a ton of pressure on the defense, I’m more concerned about what Dalton Kincaid can do to a defense on his own. He hauled in five catches for 130 yards against the Texans, displaying his elusiveness and athleticism. “He’s a mismatch in the pass game, man,” Dan Campbell said Tueday. “He’s one of these big skill, get through the defense, one-on-one matchups.” Last week, the Lions did an okay job against the Saints tight ends. Noah Fant caught four catches for 33 yards and a touchdown, while Juwan Johnson had three for 54 and a score. Perhaps the assumed debut of Lions nickelback Christian Izien will help, but with the threat of Allen running, a decent run game, and a lethal play-action pass, Kincaid feels like a nightmare matchup. 5. Penalty prone? It’s a one-game sample size, but the Bills committed 10 penalties for 85 yards—five of which gave the Texans a first down. They were particularly handsy in the secondary, committing four defensive holding penalties and a defensive pass interference. Five different defensive backs were called for a penalty, but that may just be something the Bills will live with, because they were sticky in coverage, allowing the seventh-lowest separation rate of all Week 1 teams.

title: Before the Roar: Previewing Week 2 against Buffalo
summary: After a Week 1 win over the New Orleans Saints came down to the wire, the Detroit Lions travel to Western New York to take on the Buffalo Bills in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season. Coming off of a close win against the Houston Texans in Week 1, Buffalo will be looking to […]
full_text: After a Week 1 win over the New Orleans Saints came down to the wire, the Detroit Lions travel to Western New York to take on the Buffalo Bills in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season. Coming off of a close win against the Houston Texans in Week 1, Buffalo will be looking to get their second win of the year in what will be the first regular season game played in their brand new stadium. To preview the matchup, my good friend Meko Scott and I are back with another episode of, “Before the Roar.” From the beginning, we dive into the player that really makes everything happen in Buffalo, quarterback Josh Allen. As you probably know if you are reading this, Allen is one of the best players in the league, and has been for some time now. Simply put, he can do it all. Extend plays with his size and speed, make tight-window throws with the howitzer that is attached to his right shoulder. Anything you want from a modern-day NFL quarterback, Allen delivers in spades. Combine that with the fact that Buffalo’s skill-players are among some of the best in the league, and it’s easy to see why Buffalo’s offense has been so dynamic over the course of the last several years. On the defensive side of the ball, we discuss the Bills’ talented defensive line, and how their transition to a 3-4 defense under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard could impact how the Lions approach Thursday night’s game. You can watch the entire episode right here , and listen wherever you get your podcasts. If you haven’t already, please be sure to like and subscribe to the Pride of Detroit YouTube Channel. Your support allows us to continue to grow, and reach other Lions fans around the world.

summary: The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills are prepping for a Thursday night Week 2 showdown, and with a short week ahead, they’re doing another set of walkthroughs. On Tuesday, the Lions ran another set of walkthroughs, meaning participation levels for these practices are only estimates based on what the coaching staff projects each player could […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: D.J. Reed #4 of the Detroit Lions walks off the field after an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills are prepping for a Thursday night Week 2 showdown, and with a short week ahead, they’re doing another set of walkthroughs. On Tuesday, the Lions ran another set of walkthroughs, meaning participation levels for these practices are only estimates based on what the coaching staff projects each player could have produced in a full practice. With that in mind, let’s take a look at Tuesday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Injured list updates RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back) — injured reserve, expected to be out until December During his Monday press conference, Lions coach Dan Campbell noted that Pacheco’s back injury required surgery, and it was “going to be a while” before he would be able to get back on the field. NFL Insider Ian Rapoport reported soon after that Pacheco’s surgery was to address a nerve in his back and that his recovery time (roughly 12 weeks) could give him a chance to be back in December. Estimated no practice on Tuesday LG Christian Mahogany (hip) RT Blake Miller (knee) Campbell confirmed on Monday that Mahogany’s injury was not “something serious long-term, but it could be tough to get him ready for Thursday.” That’s Campbell’s way of saying we should probably expect to see Ben Bartch at left guard against the Bills. Campbell also addressed Miller’s absence, noting that his injury was less clear and they would need more information before making a decision on his status. Fortunately, Miller spoke to the media on Monday and expressed a bit more optimism about being able to play on Thursday. “I’m doing everything I humanly can to get my body feeling the best it can feel. Even with the progress just today that I’ve made, I’m happy, and I’m optimistic,” Miller said. Estimated limited practice C Juice Scruggs (knee) CB D.J. Reed (foot) — NEW INJURY Scruggs is estimated to have practiced both days this week, which, even if it’s limited, is a good sign that coaches believe he’ll have a chance to play Thursday. Reed was added to the injury report on Tuesday, suggesting he either injured himself during the walkthrough or was limited by discomfort. Unfortunately, Campbell isn’t scheduled to talk to the media again until after Thursday night’s game, so we will have to wait until Wednesday’s injury designations for an update on his status. Estimated full practice DB Christian Izien (groin) Another full practice is a good sign for Izien, and based on Campbell’s comments on Tuesday, he may be on track to make his Lions debut this week. “Last week, we were close but wanted to give him a few more days,” Campbell said of Izien’s potential return from injury. “He’s looked pretty good through the week, and we’ve continued to run him in preparation, hopefully, for this game. title: Dan Campbell pours cold water on Detroit Lions Joey Porter Jr. trade rumors
summary: It’s no secret that a lot of people are connecting dots when it comes the Detroit Lions and Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The 26-year-old defender is in the midst of a contract dispute with the Steelers, and sat out of Week 1 with a back injury. Per ESPN, the Steelers are open to […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 12: Joey Porter Jr. #24 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on from the field during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Houston Texans at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s no secret that a lot of people are connecting dots when it comes the Detroit Lions and Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. The 26-year-old defender is in the midst of a contract dispute with the Steelers, and sat out of Week 1 with a back injury. Per ESPN, the Steelers are open to hearing trade requests, and Porter is interested as well . Combine that with a thin Detroit Lions secondary—and over $38 million in cap space following a pair of contract restructures —and it’s easy to make a surface-level deduction that Detroit could be one of the team’s interested in courting Porter. Plenty of media outlets have made that connection. On Tuesday, though, Lions head coach Dan Campbell was asked if the significant amount of cap space— estimated to be second-most in the NFL —could be used on some sort of big acquisition now or before the trade deadline. “I don’t see that,” Campbell said. “I would say this, though: it gives us options, whether that be our own guys or—it just gives us flexibility here before the season starts because there’s a lot that can happen.” It’s worth noting that Campbell was not specifically asked about Porter—and he wouldn’t be able to talk about him directly, either, as it would be considered tampering. As for other potential uses of that cap space, the Lions have admitted publicly that they are interested in making both tight end Sam LaPorta and safety Brian Branch long-term players in this organization—both are eligible for contract extensions. Branch remains on the Physically Unable to Perform list after suffering an Achilles injury in December, while LaPorta is back in action after losing the last half of his 2025 season to a back injury. Detroit also likes to have a significant amount of freed cap space to manage their roster in case of injury. So, while things could always change, it doesn’t appear the Lions are currently interested in making a big roster move.

title: NFL Week 2 power rankings: Detroit Lions’ defensive concerns remain despite win
summary: The Detroit Lions opened the 2026 season with a 31-30 overtime win over the New Orleans Saints, and while a win is a win in the “ugly” month of the season, not all national writers were left impressed or optimistic. Let’s take a look at where the national media believe the Lions stand entering the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches a replay against New Orleans Saints during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions opened the 2026 season with a 31-30 overtime win over the New Orleans Saints, and while a win is a win in the “ugly” month of the season, not all national writers were left impressed or optimistic. Let’s take a look at where the national media believe the Lions stand entering the 2026 season in this week’s power rankings. The Athletic: 8 (Previous rank: 9) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : What we learned: A throwing motion negates a fumble The Lions were saved when an apparent Jared Goff fumble was ruled an incompletion thanks to a statute many had never heard of before. The Lions went on to survive a crazy second-half comeback by the Saints that exposed several significant flaws . But, hey, they’re still 1-0 entering a big Thursday night showdown. Yahoo Sports: 9 (Previous rank: 9) From Frank Schwab : The Lions almost blew a 21-0 lead. They held on when they forced an incompletion on a 2-point conversion in overtime. Detroit’s defense had played very well in building that lead, then let the Saints back in the game. Lions head coach Dan Campbell blamed the offense’s inefficiency for the lead slipping away. “I’m like, man, we’ve got to be more efficient on offense,” Campbell said. “We kind of spit and sputtered there and then they … had some tempo going.” The Lions face a very tough Week 2 game against the Bills, who will host their first regular-season game in their new stadium Thursday night. Sports Illustrated: 10 ( Previous rank: 8) From Connor Orr : A slightly more conservative Lions offense than we’re used to, with Jared Goff throwing at about half the average depth of target as Tyler Shough, but an efficient one nonetheless. I liked the Drew Petzing wrinkle of lining Penei Sewell back up on the right side and then rushing opposite to keep the Saints on their heels. The Lions’ secondary is going to be their cross to bear in 2026, but can the offense be so good it doesn’t matter? ESPN: 11 (Previous rank: 8) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Non-QB newcomer debut: OC Drew Petzing Week 1 certainly wasn’t pretty, but Petzing’s offense looked like a well-oiled machine as it marched downfield for a 10-play, 70-yard drive in overtime that was capped by a 4-yard touchdown grab from WR Amon-Ra St. Brown. Petzing spent his past three seasons in Arizona, and in his Lions debut, he helped RB Jahmyr Gibbs record a career-high 34 touches. Quarterback Jared Goff thought Petzing “adjusted good” and “settled us down when we needed it and got us into the right plays. USA Today: 12 (Previous rank: 11) From Nate Davis : If you didn’t think missing starting safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch was a big deal, then you didn’t see Saints QB Tyler Shough raid this defense for 410 yards through the air Sunday. NFL.com: 13 (Previous rank: 15) From Nick Shook : The Lions played with a level of sloppiness typical of Week 1 but still managed to build a comfortable lead before watching it evaporate in the second half and scrambling to hang on for an overtime win. It’s not an ideal way to start the season, but credit Detroit for bouncing back from a dramatic collapse to record the victory. Sporting News: 13 (Previous rank: 15) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions were pushed into an overtime grind with the game Saints, bringing up lingering concerns about their defense outside of Aidan Hutchinson. But the high-priced trio of Jahmyr Gibbs, Jared Goff and Amon-Ra St. Brown saved the day, like they often will need to do. CBS Sports: 15 (Previous rank: 19) From Pete Prisco : They beat the Saints, but it was a lot tougher than expected. The secondary is going to be a problem until they get their starting safeties back. The Ringer: TBD (Previous rank: 16) From Diante Lee: Article not released at the time of publishing.

full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Keisean Nixon #25 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates with teammates after pulling in a first quarter interception against the Minnesota Vikings of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Even though the Green Bay Packers ultimately lost their opening game 39-22 in week one, no one has a leg to stand on if they want to blame the Packers defense for this one. Until the last six minutes of the game, the defense stood firm and kept giving the offense chances with the ball. They only surrendered two late touchdowns to the Minnesota Vikings because of field position surrendered by the offense with turnovers. On the second play of the young season for the defense, they intercepted Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray on an all-out blitz, giving the Packers the ball at their 47-yard line. The pressure forced Murray to hurry his throw, resulting in an errant pass. The play call was a quarters coverage hot blitz where the defense shows cover-0 from a zone alignment, the standard way to present cover-0 these days. Instead of playing straight man-to-man, the corners are reading the route distribution of the receivers and a low hole vision dropper will rob anything short over the middle. The safeties are keying on the inside routes of the slot receivers. The Vikings are in 11 personnel (one running back, one tight end) shotgun empty running a mirrored curl/seam route concept called “HOSS Y-JUKE”. The Packers defensive shell shows man across the board with a zone alignment but they’re actually playing quarters coverage principles in the secondary. The corners are going to play “man on deep” and let anything shallow go underneath. Once they see the receiver sit, they’ll bail to the deep quarter to help the safety. The safeties are going to take anything vertical from the inside receivers. Up front, the pressure brings six and the Vikings have five in to pass block. That leaves one extra free rusher unaccounted for and means Murray has a hot throw. On this throw in the Shanahan/McVay offense, of which Kevin O’Connell is part of, the hot throws are the seam routes and the trips side 6-yard stop route. Zaire Franklin (No. 44) is mugged up in the A-gap and blitzes as the interior rusher in that gap. The offensive right guard should pick up the blitzing linebacker, making the furthest edge defender the widest rusher, but he lets Franklin go unopposed up the middle. This shorter time to pressure causes Murray to heave an errant pass up the seam where it hangs on him and is intercepted by Keisean Nixon, who fell off the shallow curl route to sink under the pass. This was Jonathan Gannon’s most effective pressure call of the game and it gave the Packers the ball at midfield, where they were able to drive into scoring range but only for what ended up being a 59-yard field goal.
