full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Brandon Cisse #2 and Kaleb Johnson #26 of the Green Bay Packers run onto the field prior to the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Nobody really wants to hear about bright spots after the way the Packers started the season, but there were a few in Week 1, and rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse was one of them. Yes, Justin Jefferson got the better of him on one noteworthy play, but Justin Jefferson has a way of doing that. He’s victimized better corners than Cisse well past the first game of their career. But outside of Jefferson’s score, Cisse was on target and on task, playing 49 snaps in his first game in the NFL, the most of any Packers defender that didn’t hit 100% in Week 1. The Packers’ defensive backfield has been the target of no small number of questions this offseason, but if this is what we can expect from Cisse, those questions should largely go away. He and Keisean Nixon will have their problems, I’m sure, but every competent snap helps every other defensive back do his job better. That’s the real takeaway from Cisse’s performance. Rising tides in the secondary tend to carry all boats, and every decent performer takes just that much pressure off of everyone else. If Cisse continues to grow and perform well, it’ll only help a Packers team that can use all the help it can get right now. title: Carrington Valentine got picked on in the red zone vs. the Vikings
summary: While the Green Bay Packers’ defense did well on Sunday — if you can believe it — as the unit ranks among the NFL’s highest in fewest yards per play allowed through Week 1’s action, one glaring issue on the defense did pop up at the end of the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings: […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the Green Bay Packers’ defense did well on Sunday — if you can believe it — as the unit ranks among the NFL’s highest in fewest yards per play allowed through Week 1’s action, one glaring issue on the defense did pop up at the end of the Packers’ loss to the Minnesota Vikings: cornerback Carrington Valentine’s play when the Vikings were on the warning stripe of scoring a touchdown. Valentine played for just 13 snaps as Brandon Cisse’s replacement at left cornerback, as the second-round rookie dropped out of the game due to a cramp. You’ll see it out there that Benjamin St-Juste played one snap of defense on Sunday, but he was only on the field for a kneel-down, not a real play against a live offense. It was Keisean Nixon and Cisse at outside cornerback, and when Cisse left, it was Valentine who subbed in for him. Unfortunately, Valentine had five pretty bad plays in those 13 reps, and they all came when Minnesota was over the 50-yard line. CV pic.twitter.com/ME47WYs76N — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 16, 2026 The first play was an explosive run; Valentine did little at the point of attack. This has been an issue for Valentine since he came into the NFL, and it was why the Packers actually rotated in Kamal Hadden and Nate Hobbs for Valentine on run looks before those two players were ultimately injured last season. If you need a reminder of Valentine’s ability to play strong on the perimeter, here’s another example: a screen-turned-touchdown from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Dallas Goedert in the Packers’ playoff loss from the 2024 season. The second play was a bootleg where Valentine had to follow Justin Jefferson across the field, and Jefferson was able to cut the distance to the goal in half without Valentine ever being a factor on the play. The third play is a pin-and-pull play where Valentine doesn’t set a hard edge until he’s basically out of bounds, making it more difficult for his teammates to be involved. Valentine doesn’t initiate contact with the running back until they hit the goal line, at which point it doesn’t even matter. The fourth play? Another run directly at Valentine. This one starts on the right hash, and Valentine doesn’t set an edge until he’s outside of the numbers, letting the Vikings cut the distance to the sticks in half. And the final play is that same boot action look again, as Minnesota found a call they liked, but this time Jefferson scores a touchdown because Valentine missed a tackle around the seven-yard line. All in all, it was a pretty poor showing for Valentine on Sunday. The worst place to play him is in the red zone, as the Vikings showed, but it’s where the defense spent a lot of time because of the failures of the offensive line . Personally, I don’t think it’s a bad idea to start spelling Valentine with St-Juste, if Valentine does get playing time, in obvious run looks or the red zone. St-Juste was clearly brought in as a CB4 and a special teams contributor, but with a 6’3”, 200-pound frame, I feel like he gives you a better chance on the perimeter than the 5’11”-and-change, 189-pound Valentine in those situations. Valentine is fine as a middle-of-the-field coverage player, but a goal-line threat he is not.

title: Packers Defense: Jonathan Gannon has a lot of answers
summary: While former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley called defenses with pretty predictable structures, as he mostly called in plays out of a 4-3 base and a nickel defense, we were promised a more diverse set of answers under Jonathan Gannon, who runs a 3-4 base. While it wasn’t enough to stop the Minnesota […]
full_text: (Photo by Adam Bettcher/Getty Images) | Getty Images While former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley called defenses with pretty predictable structures, as he mostly called in plays out of a 4-3 base and a nickel defense, we were promised a more diverse set of answers under Jonathan Gannon, who runs a 3-4 base. While it wasn’t enough to stop the Minnesota Vikings from scoring 39 points ( Thanks, offensive line! ), we did get a look at what types of answers Gannon has on defense last Sunday. I want to break down these answers as two sets of families, because there are several defenses that have the same personnel groupings: the 3-4 family and the nickel family. 3-4 Family 3-4 — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:39:24.426Z The photo above is the Packers’ typical 3-4 defense, with two edge defenders on the field, three interior defensive linemen (think 300-pounders) and two off-ball linebackers in the box. I won’t explain this one too much, since you guys are probably well familiar with how this defense works. It’s been around for decades, and it’s what 3-4 teams generally call against two-receiver sets. 6-1 (Cooper dropdown) — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:44:04.424Z One change-up that Gannon has is adding a sixth player to the line of scrimmage, which, in the Packers’ case, is Will linebacker Edgerrin Cooper. This is Gannon’s answer to heavier formations where the offense is in an obvious running situation. The screenshot above is from a situation where the Vikings had two backs and a tight end on the field and only needed three yards to move the sticks. In this look, the weak-side edge defender (in this case it’s Dani Dennis-Sutton at the top of the screen) is “reduced” into a third defensive tackle role and Cooper drops down on the edge to replace him. In short, it’s a way for the Packers to clog up running lanes at the point of attack while not tipping off to the offense that they’re doing so, as they aren’t getting into a new personnel package — only the spacing is changing. Nickel Family Nickel — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:39:57.074Z The photo above is nothing special; it’s just your run-of-the-mill nickel defense. There are two edge defenders (3-4 outside linebackers or 4-3 defensive ends, depending on the scheme), two interior defensive linemen (again, think 300-pounders) and two off-ball linebackers. The spacing is similar to a 4-3 defense, with the major difference being that instead of a strong-side (Sam) linebacker, that player has been replaced by a nickelback (in this case, it’s safety Javon Bullard at the top of the screen). Penny (LVN kick inside) — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:46:32.316Z The Packers have different ways to get into different spacings out of this group, though. In the preseason, Gannon debuted his penny defense , which is essentially a 3-4 defense on the line of scrimmage with just one off-ball linebacker (generally, 3-4 defenses sub out the Will linebacker for the slot defender). Gannon had a couple of new wrinkles for the regular season, though. Because Green Bay’s Will (Cooper) is a player that the Packers want on the field full-time, they play him on the edge. So do the Packers sub out an edge rusher to get the nickelback on the field? No! Edge defender Lukas Van Ness (top of screen), who can hold his own on the interior, has been regularly kicking inside in these nickel subpackages, allowing Green Bay to sub out a 300-pound defensive tackle. That’s how the Packers were able to play penny out of nickel personnel in this game. For what it’s worth, Green Bay used a true slot defender against the Vikings, a different look from their preseason set — when they played split safeties and then Xavier McKinney 15 yards deep in the middle of the field over the split safeties. This formation is used when the Packers want to stop the run (with their spacing) against three-receiver sets, but still want to play coverage (with their personnel, by bringing a slot defender onto the field). Mint (LVN kicked inside) — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:39:40.707Z This is another nickel personnel subpackage that the Packers have. It’s similar to penny, in that Van Ness is kicking inside to a defensive tackle position, but instead of the team playing a five-down front with one off-ball linebacker, the team plays a five-down front with two off-ball linebackers. To make the math work out of nickel personnel, Bullard, the slot defender, actually plays the edge defender position opposite of the true edge rusher (Bullard is at the top of the screen here). The Packers are using this against two-receiver sets (which usually demand a 3-4 base defense) in obvious passing situations. For example, the screenshot above comes from a 2nd and 10 when the Vikings played two tight ends and a running back. The thinking is that a team in Minnesota’s situation would want to pass the ball, but is baiting the defense to get into their base defense to match their personnel. The Packers are comfortable enough with Van Ness inside (something he didn’t do at all in the preseason outside of rush packages) and Bullard on the edge to call opposing offenses’ bluffs. Other 3 LB package (new) on 3rd & XL — Justis Mosqueda (@jumosq.bsky.social) 2026-09-14T19:40:23.789Z This is the final package I want to talk about, and it was sort of a one-off. The Packers called this three-off-ball-linebacker set just one time, on a third and extra long against the Vikings. There’s only one interior defensive lineman on the field, the head-up nose tackle, while two inside linebackers are walked up over the guards and two edge defenders are outside of the tackles. This is Green Bay’s answer to screens and draws: Taking off a 300-pounder for an extra off-ball linebacker, who in this case is Isaiah McDuffie, to help run and chase on a tackle. — There are a lot of different defenses that Gannon called this weekend, and they all have their own specific usage. For the most part, the team matches offensive personnel with defensive personnel — meaning two-receiver sets are matched with a 3-4 base and three-receiver sets are matched with a nickel defense. Certain situations call for different options, though, which is why the Packers played it’s 6-1 against heavy personnel in run downs, penny against light offenses in run downs, mint against heavy offenses in pass downs and their three-linebacker set when a screen or draw was coming on an extra long down and distance. So far, the Packers lead the NFL in yards per play on defense (Thanks again, offensive line!), so it’s hard to make the case that the plan didn’t work in Week 1. We’ll keep an eye on Green Bay’s defense week-to-week and let you all know if anything is changing with their plan.

full_text: (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After releasing receiver Chris Hilton Jr. , the Green Bay Packers had three open spots on their practice squad. The Packers will be filling at least one of those spots on the roster this week, as Sports Illustrated ’s Bill Huber has reported that the team will sign defensive lineman Eric Johnson II . Johnson is an interesting name, as we highlighted him as a possibility for Green Bay after cutdowns, since he was a pre-draft visitor for the team in 2022, when the Indianapolis Colts selected him in the fifth round. At the cutdown deadline, there seemed to be little reason for the addition of Johnson, but clearly things changed when Nazir Stackhouse was claimed off waivers by the Tennessee Titans and Jaden Crumedy was signed off the Packers’ practice squad by the Houston Texans, leaving Green Bay with no bodies on the defensive line on the practice squad. Updated with bench correction. Eric Johnson II was drafted with pick 159 of round 5 in the 2022 draft class. He scored a 9.39 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 90 out of 1459 DT from 1987 to 2022. https://t.co/de2dJlN1US #RAS #Colts pic.twitter.com/eUYwWMaVRg — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 30, 2022 In his NFL career, Johnson has played 51 games in the regular season (40 for the Indianapolis Colts and 11 for the New England Patriots) and has recorded 700 defensive snaps and 132 special teams snaps (mostly on field goal block). This is Johnson’s fourth NFL team, as he was also a member of the Minnesota Vikings and Atlanta Falcons (the Packers’ Week 3 Thursday Night Football opponent) during training camp. Johnson is one of eight players who have worked out with the Packers this week so far. In total, the team brought in three interior defensive linemen, three wide receivers, a quarterback and an international edge defender for tryouts. I would not be surprised if the practice squad is filled with two other signings by Wednesday’s practice.

title: Adam Stenavich explains the Packers’ offensive line woes
summary: On Tuesday, the Green Bay Packers’ coordinators had an opportunity to speak to the media for the first time since the team’s opening-week loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Obviously, coming out of that game, where the Vikings scored 29-straight points but only had to post one drive of over 28 yards during that run because […]
full_text: (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Tuesday, the Green Bay Packers’ coordinators had an opportunity to speak to the media for the first time since the team’s opening-week loss to the Minnesota Vikings. Obviously, coming out of that game, where the Vikings scored 29-straight points but only had to post one drive of over 28 yards during that run because the offense was coughing up the ball on short fields, the center of the Packers universe right now currently revolves around the offensive line position. Early on in his press availability, offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich tried to calm the media storm around the position, stating, “I’m not gonna freak out or overreact or anything like that. This is the first game of a 17-game season.” That makes one of us. I’m very much freaking out! When Stenavich was asked about how the team could have avoided putting quarterback Jordan Love in such a bad position, he said that the majority of the issue on the line came from “miscommunication upfront. The backs and linemen not on the same page.” Hopefully the team pulls it together for the pass-rush plan this week, but they had multiple weeks to prepare for the Vikings, and they’re staring down a stretch where they’ll play two games in five days, as they have the Atlanta Falcons on Thursday Night Football right after they play the New York Jets on Sunday. The other big subject that fans had questions about was how former undrafted player Donovan Jennings earned the start at left guard once Aaron Banks (knee tendinitis) was ruled out, over draft picks like Jager Burton, Anthony Belton, John Williams and Travis Glover, who were either on the bench offensively or were healthy scratches during the game. Stenavich stated that “We felt like Donovan was doing a better job in practice.” Previously, head coach Matt LaFleur said that the team preferred Jennings, who has only gotten extended playing time in one NFL game — six snaps against the Baltimore Ravens in Week 17 last year — in his NFL career, because of his “time on task.” The team generally played Burton at left guard with the starting unit throughout training camp, until the last week of camp, when Burton was cross-trained more as a center (Burton played both positions in college) and Jennings was pushed into the left guard position. Stenavich also mentioned that the team isn’t ruling out transitioning Belton back to guard, the position he played during the 2025 regular season, to help the team. Belton has spent both of his NFL training camps at the tackle position, as the team has been short on bodies there, and could potentially move to guard full-time during both of his regular seasons. This begs the question: Did the staff not think they would struggle at guard for a second season and potentially need to develop their former second-rounder to play that position, rather than one he ultimately wasn’t needed for during the regular season? In other contradictory news, Stenavich stated that ideally the team would have liked tight end Tucker Kraft to run the sneak play on fourth-and-one, but that they didn’t want to use him in that scenario, as Kraft was coming off his ACL tear. LaFleur previously said that Kraft’s injury was not a factor in the decision. When the coaching staff can’t keep their stories straight, it’s hard to know what the truth is.

title: Packers Film Room: Setting up a slant
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ payoff here isn’t huge, but I always love seeing how a call is set up in real time. We’ve got three plays we’re going to look at real quick, with the first two plays informing the third. Play 1: 2nd & 9, 8:28 remaining in the 3rd quarter In their drubbing […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ payoff here isn’t huge, but I always love seeing how a call is set up in real time. We’ve got three plays we’re going to look at real quick, with the first two plays informing the third. Play 1: 2nd & 9, 8:28 remaining in the 3rd quarter In their drubbing of the Rams in Australia, the 49ers made liberal use of a specific type of motion in their offense. I’ve heard a lot of names for that type of motion being thrown around – “Banana” being my favorite – but I believe it’s called Dash motion, so that’s what we’ll use until I learn otherwise. It’s not too different from what we’ve been seeing in Green Bay (and around the league) for years, but it’s different enough to mention it. The blocker will go in motion before the snap, and it’s kind of a long, looping motion behind the line. Arcing behind the line, instead of more of a straight line. At the snap, he’ll start towards the line and block. It kind of looks like a mix between Orbit motion and a TE motion block. When using this motion, the 49ers had the blocker (Kyle Juszczyk) attack different parts of the line, keeping the Rams defense off balance. The Packers used this a handful of times against the Vikings, to middling results. It seems pretty clear that it was not originally in their playbook, but they had a package of plays armed with it for this game. I assume we’ll the use expanded in the coming weeks. When using Dash motion, the Packers basically did one thing: Mark Redman [86] was the Dash blocker (most of the time). He’d go in motion at the snap and kick out the EMOL (End Man On Line), while Jacob Monk [62] would pull from his RG position. The handoff would go to the RB, who would run behind this. They hit a nice run with it early, but, as I said earlier, the results were middling. As they used it a few more times, a trend emerged: the outside defender from the side Redman was originally aligned on would blitz. Play 2: 1st & 10, 7:23 remaining in the 3rd quarter A couple plays after the play we just looked at, the Packers showed the same thing. Redman as the outside TE in YY Wing on the right, going in Dash motion. Redman kicks out the EMOL, Monk pulls and Isaiah Rodgers [2] blitzes. Play 3: 2nd & 4, 1:24 remaining in the 3rd quarter On the next drive, the Packers try something a little different. They’re no longer in YY Wing and the Dash motion man is Josh Whyle [81], but they’re using Dash all the same. Instead of closed side of the field, Matthew Golden [0] is lined up wide outside of where Whyle was originally aligned. The Packers are seeing if the Vikings have an automatic boundary blitz called when Dash motion is called. If it is an auto blitz check, the Packers are running Golden on a slant behind it. Rodgers does a good job of hiding his intentions until the ball is snapped. As soon as it’s snapped, Rodgers makes a beeline for the backfield. Jordan Love [10] takes a glimpse over, sees Rodgers blitzing and fires a quick throw over to Golden. Eric Wilson [55] is buzzing over, but he can’t get to the ball and Golden is able to dip under the tackle to pick up a few more yards. I love it when a plan comes together. I even slowed down the throw so you can enjoy it that way if you prefer. Albums listened to: she’s green – swallowtail ; Tom Waits – Rain Dogs

title: Colts move green dot from Cam Bynum to Akeem Davis-Gaither
summary: The Colts are already making a significant change after their ugly defensive performance in Week 1. After Cam Bynum wore the green dot in the season opener against the Ravens, Indianapolis will now shift that responsibility to linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither. The green dot allows one defensive player to hear the call from defensive coordinator Lou […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Cam Bynum #0 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates after breaking up a pass against the Baltimore Ravens during the second quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts are already making a significant change after their ugly defensive performance in Week 1. After Cam Bynum wore the green dot in the season opener against the Ravens, Indianapolis will now shift that responsibility to linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither. The green dot allows one defensive player to hear the call from defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo and relay it to the rest of the defense. The move comes after the Colts gave up 41 points and 504 yards against Baltimore, with several issues showing up before and after the snap. Indianapolis struggled to get lined up, looked late reacting to motion and repeatedly appeared disorganized against one of the more difficult offenses in the league to defend. “The communication wasn’t where it needed to be Week 1,” Shane Steichen said, according to the Indianapolis Star. “It frees up Cam on the back end to communicate with A.J. and Sauce and Mooney and all those guys, and obviously Akeem’s right there in the middle.” This was something I mentioned after the Ravens game because the Bynum green dot plan always felt a little questionable. Bynum is a good player, and none of this should be viewed as a knock on him individually. The issue is more about the structure of the defense. Safeties can end up 10, 15 or even 25 yards away from the line of scrimmage depending on the play, the coverage and where the ball ends. That makes it harder to get the call, relay it, communicate checks and still get back into position before the snap. Linebackers are usually the green dot players for a reason. They are closer to the nucleus of the defense. They are near the defensive line, connected to the second level and still close enough to communicate with the safeties behind them. When the offense is moving quickly, that positioning is very important. The Colts apparently saw enough in Week 1 to go back to the more traditional setup. Davis-Gaither played 94 percent of the defensive snaps against Baltimore, so if he is going to be on the field that often, giving him the green dot makes sense. It should also allow Bynum to focus more on organizing the back end with A.J. Haulcy, Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward instead of carrying the full defensive communication burden himself. The move also says something about the Colts’ linebacker situation. CJ Allen was drafted in the second round with the belief that he could become an every-down player and eventually handle major communication responsibilities. Chris Ballard even called him a green dot type of player after the draft. Allen, however, did not play a single defensive snap in Week 1, and Steichen noted that the Colts are rotating linebackers. “We’re rotating linebackers in there,” Steichen said. “Only one guy can wear the green dot.” For now, that guy is Davis-Gaither. This does not fix everything by itself. The Colts need to be better at just about everything after Week 1. Changing the green dot is not some magic solution. However, it is a logical correction after the defense looked scattered against Baltimore. If the communication improves and Bynum looks more comfortable focusing on the secondary, this could be a simple but important adjustment. At the very least, the Colts recognized the Week 1 setup did not work. Now they are going back to a structure that makes more sense on paper, with the linebacker in the middle of the defense calling the plays.

title: The Chiefs dismantling the Broncos has some Colts fans sweating
summary: The Denver Broncos had one of the best defenses in 2025. It’s what carried them to a No. 1 seed in the AFC. Sure, it might have been a bit of a down year for the conference but there was no denying their defensive prowess. Teams change and personnel is different every year, but what […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts is tackled by Drue Tranquill #23 of the Kansas City Chiefs in the fourth quarter of the game at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos had one of the best defenses in 2025. It’s what carried them to a No. 1 seed in the AFC. Sure, it might have been a bit of a down year for the conference but there was no denying their defensive prowess. Teams change and personnel is different every year, but what the Kansas City Chiefs did to the Broncos on Monday Night Football should keep some Indianapolis Colts fans up at night. A ton of that concern comes from the Chiefs hanging 31 points on that defense. More concern comes from the fact that the Chiefs’ defense shut down Bo Nix and the Broncos’ offense as well. The most concerning part has nothing to do with either the Chiefs or the Broncos, however. The main concern stems from what we witnessed on Sunday against the Ravens as the Colts were absolutely shredded. 31 points were surrendered by halftime with Lamar Jackson having 324 yards through the air, while he and Derrick Henry picked up another 184 on the ground. Let’s also not forget that Zay Flowers had 150 yards and barely played half a game. Overall, the defense couldn’t get off the field. Third and long was no problem as the Ravens converted with ease, especially in the first half. Justin Walley was targeted on repeat and left the game cooked. The line didn’t generate enough pressure and failed to tackle Jackson when they had the chance. Flowers, Henry, and even Mark Andrews ran free and wild. If the Chiefs took the Broncos to the woodshed, they must be licking their chops after witnessing that incredibly lackluster effort from the Colts. The season isn’t over by any stretch of the imagination, and no one in the organization should panic. One good game gets them right back into things. To be without nerves after watching each team play, however, would be foolish. One team looked primed for another go at a Super Bowl. The other looked like they will be watching the playoffs from home again. Something has to change if the Colts are going to win at Arrowhead.

(Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Tuesday, the Indianapolis Colts announced that the team has re-signed cornerback Johnathan Edwards to their practice squad and waived fellow corner Robert Carter Jr. in a corresponding roster move. After being waived on Monday by Indianapolis, Edwards subsequently cleared league waivers. For now, the 24-year-old cornerback will remain within the Colts organization, with a chance to be eventually elevated again to their 53-man active roster. The former undrafted cornerback out of Tulane was signed as an undrafted rookie free agent by the Colts in the 2025 offseason. Due to injuries at the cornerback position, he even started in 5 games as a rookie last year, while also recording 26 tackles (19 solo) and 3 passes defensed in 14 games collectively during the 2025 campaign. While Edwards struggled during this year’s preseason, the thought was that the Colts would keep him on the active roster as a lower depth backup due to his speed, athleticism, and potential special teams prowess. That being said, he was a healthy scratch this past weekend against the Baltimore Ravens, which didn’t bode well for his 53-man active roster future. With Colts cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt having served his one game suspension, it became a numbers game within Indianapolis’ cornerback room, and Edwards was the casualty. However, the Colts clearly liked him enough to keep him within their organization, and who knows, if another injury or two happen again, he could find himself right back on their 53-man active roster. He did show some initial promise as a rookie—albeit in limited action, even if some more recent struggles have since ensued.

title: Horse Power or Horse Play? Reactions from Colts’ Week 1 blowout loss to Ravens: Nevermore!
summary: On Sunday, the Indianapolis Colts suffered one of those losses that was going to take some time to rightfully recover from. After waiting months for the 2026 regular season to start, Colts fans saw the Baltimore Ravens demolish the Colts at home, 41-23, in a laugher that was already over by halftime. Rather than immediately […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Zay Flowers #4 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates after an pass reception against the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, the Indianapolis Colts suffered one of those losses that was going to take some time to rightfully recover from. After waiting months for the 2026 regular season to start, Colts fans saw the Baltimore Ravens demolish the Colts at home, 41-23, in a laugher that was already over by halftime. Rather than immediately nose myself back into that utter stink of a showing, I wanted to take some time to gather my thoughts on some of the takeaways from Sunday’s opener—and highlight some of the few and far between silver linings, as well as a lot of the bad that was readily apparent. Horse Power Offensive Line Run Blocking : Colts star workhorse Jonathan Taylor rushed for nearly 100 rushing yards, as he had 19 carries for 98 total rushing yards and 2 rushing touchdowns on the afternoon. The unit collectively was able to open up rushing lanes for Taylor, who would’ve made this grouping as well, had it not been for his mid-second quarter fumble—which effectively ended any chance of a realistic comeback. Sauce Gardner : The Ravens manipulated the coverage matchups by having their best wideout Zay Flowers (*5 receptions for 150 total receiving yards and a touchdown reception before halftime) go up against the Colts debuting slot cornerback Justin Walley, and the latter showed his greenness initially in this one before Flowers left early with an injury. Gardner was reportedly only targeted twice in man coverage, surrendering just one catch for 12 total receiving yards. The Colts had their fair share of secondary problems on Sunday, but Gardner wasn’t largely one of them. Rather than have Gardner lock up Flowers, the Ravens just avoided him all together and took advantage of Indianapolis’ other more vulnerable DBs to routinely pick on in the passing game. The Colts really ought to think about having Sauce shadow the opposing team’s best wide receiver going forward, if this is the alternative. Rigoberto Sanchez : The Colts longtime, recently re-signed punter had 5 punts, averaging 52.6 yards per punt. Yes, highlighting a punter shows what type of day it was for Indianapolis, but that’ll certainly play. Horse Play Lou Anarumo and the Colts defense collectively: This was Week 1, and the Colts had months to prepare for this defensive matchup against the Baltimore Ravens, which makes this one so frustrating. This wasn’t a short turnaround ahead of Thursday Night Football or something to that effect. Yes, the Ravens have a new offensive coordinator, Declan Doyle, without the luxury of NFL tape regarding his play-calling, but some of the miscommunication and blown coverage assignments and gaffes were certainly within their control prior to this one kicking off. The run defense was awful, allowing veteran Derrick Henry to rush for 144 total rushing yards and 3 rushing touchdowns, averaging 6.0 yards per carry. The linebackers were either in the wrong spots or non-existent, as starter Jaylon Carlies did not even record a single stat in 42 total snaps. The secondary also got torched, as the inexperience of both rookie safety AJ Haulcy and slot cornerback Walley, as mentioned, clearly showed in particular. Some of the expected reliable veterans such as Charvarius Ward and Cam Bynum didn’t fare all that much better in coverage though. The Colts surrendered 506 total offensive yards defensively, which is their most surrendered since Week 8 of the 2023 regular season. It was nothing short of a disaster of a defensive showing. Colts O-Line Pass Blocking: On the other side of blocking, this was not a banner day for the Colts offensive line as it relates to pass blocking. Returning starting quarterback Daniel Jones was the most pressured NFL passer of Week 1, having been pressured on over half (52.9%) of his passing dropbacks. The plan seems to be to blitz Jones into oblivion , until he and the Colts prove they can consistently handle it, which so far hasn’t happened, since even around midseason of last year—when Jones and the offense arguably began to cool off a bit following their historic hot start, even before his later key injuries.

title: Chiefs film review: Kenneth Walker makes explosive debut
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Denver Broncos 31-10 in a dominating effort at Arrowhead Stadium on Monday Night. In front of a packed house, the Chiefs dominated the Broncos from start to finish in an eye-opening display of firepower. Many players had great games, but newly acquired running back Kenneth Walker had the best. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Kenneth Walker #9 celebrates with his teammate Trey Smith #65 of the Kansas City Chiefs after scoring a touchdown against the Denver Broncos during an NFL football game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Denver Broncos 31-10 in a dominating effort at Arrowhead Stadium on Monday Night. In front of a packed house, the Chiefs dominated the Broncos from start to finish in an eye-opening display of firepower. Many players had great games, but newly acquired running back Kenneth Walker had the best. Walker finished with 173 rushing yards on 23 carries and a touchdown, averaging a whopping 7.5 yards per carry while also catching three passes for 18 yards and a touchdown. His dynamic performance was the most rushing yards a Chiefs running back has ever had in their team debut, and it ranks 15th all time for rushing yards in a game for the team. Walker displayed the power, speed, and explosion of a seasoned Pro Bowl-caliber back, and with head coach Andy Reid’s revamped run scheme, it led to a huge night for Walker. Creating plays Walker wasted no time showing off his cutting ability and vision. The Chiefs haven’t had a back who can make something out of nothing in a long time, but Walker made multiple plays with less-than-ideal run lanes up front. The backside of the zone look isn't blocked well, but Walker slips and slides through the line, and then the movement created by Humphrey and Smith allows him to find space on the front side of the play. pic.twitter.com/pTxKUzFcWd — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 16, 2026 On the snap, the Chiefs go with an offset zone look from under center. The backside double team initially creates movement, but Khalil Benson and Kingsley Suamataia allow their men to slip off as Walker gets to the line. Walker recognizes this and quickly jump-cuts to the outside, plants, and then, as the secondary starts to fill, jukes laterally to find space and break a tackle. This play looks dead in the water once the backside double team gets split, but Walker had the vision and movement to create his own yards. With poorly blocked plays, Walker found nice gains, and with decently blocked plays, he found even more yards. Beautiful pass off from Suamatia to Humphrey on the 3-tech. This gives Walker a little crease, and he does the rest. He gets skinny, slips on the tackle, then blasts into the open field, dragging men with him. Love the run call away from the strength. pic.twitter.com/lMNcGH5ksu — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 15, 2026 The Chiefs go with a zone look to the weak side of the formation, and Suamataia and Humphrey work perfectly in combination to pass the slanting 3-technique from the B-Gap to the A-Gap. Humphrey seals the defensive tackle, while Suamataia works to the next level. The backside linebacker flows hard, but Walker keeps his feet churning, runs through contact, explodes into the second level, and breaks more tackles on his way to a big gain. Walker was a tackle-breaking machine on Monday night, racking up 14 total, and he tallied them with his elusive running style and brute strength. Ken Walker forced 14 (!!) missed tackles last night, per PFF. That tally led the NFL and doubled the total of the next closest player. He racked up 179 yards after contact. Not bad! — Matt McMullen (@KCChiefs_Matt) September 15, 2026 KC's twist on the full house backfield into H counter. The playside double team creates movement, and the kickout from Smith opens the initial lane. The Broncos fill, but Walker cuts and lowers his shoulder, fighting for extra yards. pic.twitter.com/Ipc3WHHPHF — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 15, 2026 Out of a full-house backfield, the Chiefs run counter, and Walker follows the double team from Benson and Suamataia to the next level. The Broncos quickly fill the run, but Walker lowers his shoulder and delivers a big hit to a secondary player before working his way upfield. Walker was excellent at creating his own yards, but his best run of the night came off good execution throughout the game. Setting up the big one Explosive run plays have been few and far between for Kansas City the past few seasons, but a deeper look shows the numbers weren’t just bad for breaking big runs; they were historically bad. The literal worst explosive RB rush rate of this century…two seasons in a row! Hard to overstate how categorically different it is to play the Chiefs when they actually have a back who can damage you https://t.co/NTu3a4sqZw pic.twitter.com/yT3PIJM9IT — Benjamin Solak (@BenjaminSolak) September 15, 2026 During his Chiefs debut, Walker matched the Chiefs’ explosive runs from the 2025 season, but his 60-yard dash to the end zone came from tremendous playcalling and taking advantage of the Broncos’ tendencies. Early in the game, the Chiefs showed off heavy personnel looks, with extra offensive linemen on the field and nose tackle Khyiris Tonga at fullback. On an early fourth-and-short, the Chiefs rolled out this heavy look, and Walker blasted up the middle for a first down. Motion creates a full house look with Tonga in the FB slot. Not a tremendous amount of movement up front, but Walker slips the DT and gets a good seal from Humphrey to pickup the first on 4th down. pic.twitter.com/Kz4Wqa2Vb9 — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 15, 2026 There is nothing too complex about this play: more mass on the field for Kansas City leads to a better push up front, and Walker falls forward for a first down. A few series later, Tonga comes back in on a third-and-short, and again the Chiefs pound the rock up the middle. 3rd and short. Tonga in the backfield with Ezeudu and Nourzad on the left side. Quick-hitting power look; Walker dances behind the big bodies to find space. pic.twitter.com/ZFc5vqd6vs — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 16, 2026 This time, the Broncos are prepared, and slant inside when they see Smith pull. The play is not tremendously blocked, but Walker disappears into the sea of bodies and re-emerges on the other side of the line of scrimmage for a first down. It may not seem like much, but the data the offensive braintrust and Walker gathered from these two plays would set up the “big one.” Big runs don't just happen. It is the culmination of many little things and all the things that make football great. KC runs power on 4th down, and Denver pinches. Why pinch? When was the last time a Chiefs RB bounced on a 4th and short? Walker reads it immediately and is gone. pic.twitter.com/0VGsUcD8mZ — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) September 15, 2026 On fourth and short, the Chiefs come out in an offset I-formation look with the same overload personnel as the previous third-and-short look. Once more, the Chiefs would go with a power play to the left, but this time they took advantage of Denver pinching the inside gaps. With eleven players loaded in the box, the Broncos take away the inside, but with Tonga acting as a lead blocker, Walker reads the defense crash inside, then makes one cut and charges toward the perimeter. The Broncos had grown accustomed to the Chiefs slugging out short yardage plays up the middle and cheating the look, and this time Walker makes them pay. The burst to the outside is impressive, but his ability to break one more arm tackle and his second gear into the end zone sets him apart from other backs in the NFL. The bottom line The Chiefs have not had a back with Walker’s skill set since Kareem Hunt’s second season in the NFL in 2018, but maybe not one as talented since Jamaal Charles’ final season with the team in 2016. This was the most impressive performance by a running back of the Mahomes era, and it is only the tip of the iceberg for what Walker and the Chiefs can accomplish in 2026. The Chiefs have their running back, and it will be fun to see how they continue to plan to use him as the season progresses.
author: Caleb James

title: Week 1 AP NFL Power Rankings: Chiefs make their debut in the top 5
summary: Was this the best Week 1 of an NFL season in recent memory? Normally, the opening week brings sloppy play across the league, as many teams don’t play their starters in the preseason. We are used to seeing offenses struggle to get into sync, with defenses having the advantage early in the season. That wasn’t […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Travis Kelce #87 of the Kansas City Chiefs reacts in a huddle against the Denver Broncos during an NFL football game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Was this the best Week 1 of an NFL season in recent memory? Normally, the opening week brings sloppy play across the league, as many teams don’t play their starters in the preseason. We are used to seeing offenses struggle to get into sync, with defenses having the advantage early in the season. That wasn’t the case in this weekend’s slate of games. Fantasy football managers rejoiced as we saw an offensive explosion across the league. Is this a sign of a historic offensive season upcoming, or will defenses eventually catch up? Some things looked different, but others stayed the same. The NFC South is 0-4. The Cleveland Browns are still the Browns. And oh yeah, Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is healthy, and the AFC West runs through Arrowhead. Like the Chiefs’ running game, the Arrowhead Pride NFL Power Rankings are back this season. This week, along with me, staff voters were Maurice Elston, Caleb James, Ron Kopp Jr., Rocky Magana, Jared Sapp, and Matt Stagner. 1. Seattle Seahawks No Sam Darnold? No problem. The defending champs still looked like the champs in their Super Bowl rematch. 2. Baltimore Ravens Derrick Henry defies all odds of a normal human being. 3. Buffalo Bills Josh Allen has a way of putting his team on his back and playing like Superman. And if his defense keeps playing as they did in Week 1, he’ll have to be Superman every week. 4. San Francisco 49ers This is why we play the games. Seemingly, not much went right for the 49ers this offseason. Written off as the “has-been” in the NFC West. Yet, they dominated in Melbourne. Their travel plan couldn’t have been better. 5. Kansas City Chiefs I don’t know about you, but that was the most fun I’ve had watching the Chiefs since 2023. I wanted to reach through the television and give Kenneth Walker a hug. 6. Cincinnati Bengals The new Bengals? Usually slow starters, they start 2026 with a victory. Their defense looked new and improved, but their franchise stars, Burrow and Chase, played a lackluster game. 7. Houston Texans This Texans’ defense did not live up to their “historic” billing. Superman gave them two turnover opportunities in the second half, but they couldn’t capitalize. CJ Stroud looked like he’s playing for that new contract this season. 8. Chicago Bears Head coach Ben Johnson said his goal for the Bears is to be the top-scoring offense in league history. He wants shutouts and blowouts. He got the blowout, and they’re on track for that scoring record. However, they’ve got some work to do on that defense if we’re going to see some shutouts in the Windy City. 9. Philadelphia Eagles Anyone else thrilled the Tush Push didn’t show up on Sunday? 10. Jacksonville Jaguars Such a sneaky team who could be a sleeper in the AFC. Is Trevor Lawrence a dark horse MVP candidate? 11. Los Angeles Rams The NFL’s offseason darlings were flat-out embarrassed on Friday Thursday night in Australia. Hindsight is 20/20, but I guess it wasn’t a great idea to get off a 16-hour flight and play a football game. 12. Denver Broncos Personally, I can’t wait for the Broncos to (over)pay Bo Nix. 13. Detroit Lions About as disheartening an overtime victory as you can get. The Lions were a Saints’ failed two-point conversion in overtime away from letting a 21-0 lead slip through their fingers. 14. New England Patriots Yikes. Not going to win many football games if your franchise quarterback throws three interceptions in the fourth quarter. 15. New York Giants I’m just trying to imagine John Harbaugh and Cam Skattebo having a conversation. Regardless, this is an exciting young team to watch. They could make a run back to the postseason. 16. Minnesota Vikings Kyler Murray’s Vikings debut didn’t last long. Wily vet Carson Wentz saved the day with a big comeback win over the Pack. QB controversy in Minnesota? 17. Green Bay Packers Is the seat starting to get warm for Matt Lafleur in Green Bay? 18. Pittsburgh Steelers Aaron Rodgers is louder off the field than he is on it these days. 19. Dallas Cowboys More of the same from them. This defense didn’t look any better. 20. Los Angeles Chargers LOL. Chargers gonna Charger. 21. Tampa Bay Buccaneers After dusting himself off from getting sacked four times, Baker’s first thought has to be his revenge game against the Cleveland Browns. 22. Arizona Cardinals The team that knocked you out of your Survivor League before it got started. 23. New Orleans Saints Is Shough enough? There will be highs and lows with him, but such a fun player to watch. He almost completed the remarkable comeback in the Motor City. 24. Indianapolis Colts That’s an awful defensive performance for a team who has invested so heavily in that unit. 25. Washington Commanders Stefon Diggs is continuing his antics in a new city. 26. Carolina Panthers The Panthers have quietly put up 37 and 31 points in their two most recent showings, dating back to the Wild Card Round of last year’s playoffs. Although both games were losses, is this a sign of things to come for the Panthers’ offense? 27. Las Vegas Raiders Ashton Jeanty is a scary running back. Reminder that the Raiders also started 1-0 last season. But they’ve got talent. 28. Atlanta Falcons The NFC South is 0-4 to start the 2026 season. Perhaps no team exemplifies the South more than the Falcons. Some of the most elite offensive talent in the league—except at the most important position on the field. 29. New York Jets The Jets got the win, but a single interception remains elusive. 30. Miami Dolphins I challenge any NFL fan to name five players on this roster. They are in complete rebuild mode. 31. Tennessee Titans Will the Titans have a new stadium and quarterback in 2027? Cam Ward didn’t look great in the season opener. 32. Cleveland Browns Is there a fan base in the NFL you feel worse for? It would just feel impossible to be a Browns fan.

title: The Good and the Bad from the Chiefs’ win over the Broncos
summary: Football is back! The Kansas City Chiefs beat the Denver Broncos 31-10 on “Monday Night Football” in dominant fashion, making it one of my favorite Chiefs wins in years. The crowd and energy were fantastic, and the Chiefs bludgeoned Denver with physicality and power on both sides of the ball. It was an incredibly impressive […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates with his teammates after scoring a 15 yard touchdown against the Denver Broncos during the first quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Football is back! The Kansas City Chiefs beat the Denver Broncos 31-10 on “Monday Night Football” in dominant fashion, making it one of my favorite Chiefs wins in years. The crowd and energy were fantastic, and the Chiefs bludgeoned Denver with physicality and power on both sides of the ball. It was an incredibly impressive performance that was very enjoyable to watch. There’s a ton to analyze, so this season I’ll structure film reviews around two or three topics each week. In wins, I’ll cover two positives and one negative; in losses, we’ll point out two negatives and only one positive. Let’s start with the positives. The Good Chiefs playing extra offensive linemen I absolutely loved what the Chiefs did in the run game against the Broncos. It started from the very beginning. Head coach Andy Reid, notorious for his love of the passing game, came out on national television and sent a message to every NFL team: we’re going to run the ball. Kenneth Walker will get most of the headlines for the improved run game, and rightfully so. You couldn’t have asked for a better debut. Walker showed big-play explosiveness, but also patience and vision between the tackles. His tackle-breaking was elite, and he showed power with his stiff arm and by running through defenders. But that wasn’t my favorite part of the Chiefs’ run game. Four times in this game, Andy Reid checked in backup guard Hunter Nourzad and nose tackle Khyris Tonga on short-yardage plays; reserve lineman Josh Ezeudu also saw time. Every snap of jumbo the Chiefs played against the Broncos pic.twitter.com/GfzOT5mDnE — Chiefs Clips (@ChiefsClip58569) September 16, 2026 Kansas City used the “Jumbo” packages to move the chains, and I loved the decision. Essentially, they had two options: extra offensive linemen or tight ends. They chose the linemen. Normally, the trade-off is that extra linemen reduce the pass threat. Defenses don’t have to account for them in coverage, making the run more obvious and letting defenders attack downhill (although I would like to see a Khyris Tonga touchdown). But with this Chiefs’ roster, the tight ends don’t provide enough of a passing threat to justify keeping them on the field. Teams aren’t worried about covering Noah Gray or Jared Wiley (a gameday inactive) downfield, while Travis Kelce is now limited to a smaller area of the field. The Chiefs simply don’t have enough receiving talent at tight end for defenses to adjust much anyway. So why not just add another lineman and improve your run blocking? There’s obviously a limit to how often you can use jumbo personnel, but I like that the Chiefs are willing to turn to it when needed. An improved pressure plan Broncos quarterback Bo Nix was pressured at the fourth-highest rate in the NFL this week at 45.5% . Last season, the Chiefs’ pressure rate was 34.4% , 15th in the NFL. More pressure was an offseason priority, and they delivered on Monday. Multiple factors contributed. First, some of the young defensive linemen they brought in made an immediate impact. The most noticeable was defensive end R Mason Thomas, who finished with two pressures and a sack on 19 pass-rush snaps . Thomas didn’t get off to the best start, but found his rhythm as the game progressed. Thomas’ sack was particularly impressive, showing the lower-body flexibility to spin back inside after trying to get upfield. R Mason Thomas all true pass rush reps in his NFL debut pic.twitter.com/iiyeCFIS2T — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) September 15, 2026 Huge punchout by Felix Anudike-Uzomah pic.twitter.com/ZsSiTycFtJ — T.J. Randall (@TJ_Randall12) September 15, 2026 Felix Anudike-Uzomah also impacted the game with a strip sack. Surprisingly, the Chiefs had FAU inside at defensive tackle during this game, despite his smaller frame. On his sack, he showed impressive power in a swim move to turn upfield. But more than the defensive line, the Chiefs’ blitzes were outstanding. The team blitzed just 30.3% of the time , 14th in the NFL this week, but were incredibly effective when they did. Early in the game, the Chiefs brought cornerback Nohl Williams on a blitz from a condensed formation as the Broncos looked for a big play. Williams got a sack and changed the tone of this game. From there, the Broncos mostly called short passes against the blitz, but the Chiefs were all over them, dropping defenders into hot zones and forcing Nix to hold onto the ball. Two keys on the early sack. Bringing Nohl Williams and Delane was a nice wrinkle. Williams blitz discourage Nix from slinging it since it didn’t create the desired coverage they hoped for. Bolton’s drop eliminated the only other option. #Chiefs #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/82KM1nOIBK — Nick Jacobs (@Jacobs71) September 15, 2026 Another thing the Chiefs scouted was that they wanted to keep running back R.J. Harvey in pass protection. Harvey is not a big back and struggles in those situations, and the Chiefs picked on that all night. Linebacker Nick Bolton’s sack was a one-on-one with Harvey where he blows him up and then swims around him. Bo Nix just got crushed 😭 pic.twitter.com/LbfpBfDncw — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) September 15, 2026 The speed of the new defensive linemen will help the four-man pass rush and the blitzes. One problem the Chiefs had last year was poor blitz spacing because their defensive linemen couldn’t get upfield to occupy blockers. Thomas now gives them that, alongside a guy who can win one-on-one. The Chiefs defense sent a message to the NFL that they’re going to hit the quarterback more this year. The bad The Chiefs’ passing game Most of the game was outstanding for the Chiefs, but the pass game struggled. Mahomes was 7-for-17 passing at halftime for 56 yards. At one point, the Chiefs had six straight incompletions. Kansas City’s leading wide receiver in receiving yards was Rashee Rice with 19 yards. The Chiefs’ wide receivers had five total catches. Mahomes was 29th in average depth of target this week at 4.7 yards. Patrick Mahomes vs. DEN: 0/5, 1 INT on 10+ air‑yard throws 90% YAC (!!!) 2.27s TTT 4.68 aDOT ‑12.3% CPOE 50.2 Total QBR https://t.co/iQkZQrQN5S pic.twitter.com/oN9sa969DV — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) September 15, 2026 The Chiefs had 18 air yards combined on their completions tonight, tied for their fewest in any game in @sportradar database to 2006. Also had 18 vs Lions in 45–10 win 11/1/2015 — Josh Dubow (@JoshDubowAP) September 15, 2026 Frankly, the Chiefs got lucky on the two best passing plays of the game. Rashee Rice had two defenders in position to tackle him on his touchdown, and both whiffed badly . Tight end Travis Kelce’s catch and run was a great hot read to beat the blitz, but the amount of space he had was crazy and rarely happens in the NFL. Outside of those two plays, the Chiefs’ passing game was inept. The group struggled with quick-game concepts because the Broncos were sitting on every underneath route. At one point, Kansas City ran back-to-back screens to Walker, and Denver blew both up. The Broncos dared the Chiefs to throw downfield, and they couldn’t. Nobody could separate against Denver’s cornerbacks. Rice had virtually no impact outside of his touchdown. Xavier Worthy saw six targets but caught just three for 18 yards, while wide receivers Tyquan Thornton and Cyrus Allen didn’t record a catch. The Chiefs will face less talented secondaries moving forward, and getting left tackle Josh Simmons back should give the quarterback more time for receivers to get open. But the reality is the Chiefs don’t have enough pass-catching talent right now. Teams aren’t threatened by their receivers, and they don’t have a player who…

title: Chiefs Mailbag: How concerning was the passing game against Denver?
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs! Coming off a monster 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds. TheSovereign1587 asks: What specifically stood out the most […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs looks to pass against the Denver Broncos during the second quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs ! Coming off a monster 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds. TheSovereign1587 asks: What specifically stood out the most about the passing game that made it look as rough as it did? Was it Patrick Mahomes being rusty? Did his knee affect his throwing ability/accuracy? Was it the WRs, not getting open, mistakes, etc? Were the pass plays and routes not effective? Tackle play will take the bulk of the blame for the Chiefs’ disappointing results through the air Monday. That certainly played a role as rookie Kahlil Benson’s inexperience at left tackle significantly dictated the game plan. The uncertainty on the left side masked legitimate concerns about Jaylon Moore’s ability to man the right tackle spot. However, I think other factors combined with Benson and Moore to make for a perfect storm against the Chiefs’ passing attack. Mahomes definitely appeared rusty, especially in the first half. He looked like a player who had not been on the field competitively since December. In addition, wide receivers Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy played as they had been in and out of the lineup throughout training camp. Week 1 was essentially the preseason for the full starting offense. Also, the Denver secondary — arguably the league’s best and a group very familiar with the Chiefs — deserves credit. The Broncos’ defensive backs apparently were Denver’s only unit that was aware a game was scheduled for Monday night. I think Mahomes will get at least some of his timing back, the tackle play will improve, and most defensive backfields do not have the talent to match Denver’s game plan. However, I am taking real concerns from Monday night and am unsure how much it can be improved. I will probably wait until after Kansas City’s Week 5 bye to determine how panicked or confident to be. RoyalsFanBill asks: Will the Chiefs continue to feature the running game? Hope this isn’t the ole Marty Schottenheimer trick of starting a game with a deep pass only to not pass the rest of the game. I don’t think we will revert back to the old offense, but it would be my major question going forward. Kenneth Walker is effectively signed to a two-year contract worth $28.7 million with a team option for a third year in 2028. I think the Chiefs plan to make him their workhorse over that period. Outside of Mahomes and defensive tackle Chris Jones, Kansas City’s biggest investment has been on the interior of their line. With the money owed to Walker, center Creed Humphrey and guard Trey Smith, it would be incompetence not to rely on the run game early and often. I do think we will see a bit more balance in the coming weeks. It also won’t surprise me if rookie Emmett Johnson sees more work in the backfield on a short week after Walker’s heavy Monday night workload. But I think the days of the run game being an afterthought in the Andy Reid offense are officially over. ReadyForFBSeason asks: What will other teams see on film that they can exploit? Denver clearly didn’t adjust well during the game. What will the Indianapolis Colts be preparing to do differently in Week 2? The Broncos’ inability to answer Walker may be all that is keeping the Indianapolis Colts ’ struggles against Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens from becoming a major Week 1 story. Indianapolis gave up 324 passing yards and 202 yards on the ground. We will see what adjustments they make, but Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo — a longtime Mahomes nemesis — has a lot to fix in a week’s time. One mistake on Denver’s part was abandoning the run game early and only having 11 rushing attempts by running backs. Expect the Colts to try to work around Kansas City’s rejuvenated pass rush with a heavy dose of tailback Jonathan Taylor — who totaled 121 scrimmage yards and a pair of touchdowns on Sunday. wbenk307 asks: Can we continue to expect that level of domination from our D-line and third down defense? Denver had the best offensive line last season, so I am wondering if this was Week 1 wonkiness or the tone for the rest of the year. Broncos quarterback Bo Nix might still be having nightmares about Kansas City’s newfound pass rush when the teams meet again in Denver during Week 8. I think what the Chiefs did early on should be taken very seriously. The most encouraging sign of the Chiefs’ defensive dominance came via the snap counts. Chris Jones, Peter Woods, R Mason Thomas, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah all made their presence felt while playing less than 60% of the defensive snaps. The timeshare approach may not lend itself to individual players putting up huge sack numbers, but the Broncos’ offensive line quickly proved more tired than the Chiefs’ defensive front, with fresh players constantly switched in. George Karlaftis will assuredly lead the group in defensive snaps most weeks, but I expect his 86% snap count to trend down, likely inversely to Ashton Gillotte’s 27% trending up as his foot heals. The Chiefs have the players in place to imitate the constant rotation that helped the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots advance to last year’s Super Bowl. Health will ultimately determine Kansas City’s defensive dominance. The Chiefs’ secondary worked around the absence of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane after the first defensive series. However, an effective pass rush needs top-notch defensive backs to be maximized. The Chiefs’ defensive line played inspired against Denver, but it remains a group with little depth. With the current roster, even one injury could prove catastrophic to what the Chiefs want to do. Second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott will hopefully return from the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list soon after the bye. We will see if rookie edge rusher Jack Pyburn — recently claimed off waivers — can carve out a role this season. But Monday night’s group missing any round of rotational snaps could leave the defensive line very tired, very fast. Papajazz asks What are reasonable expectations going forward? Week 1 is generally a terrible sample to use for the sweeping predictions people inevitably fire off immediately after. I am not going to predict the Chiefs to win the Super Bowl based on one game. I remain high on the Chiefs as a playoff team that should challenge for the AFC West title. The next few weeks should dictate our expectations. In the short term, Kansas City came out on top of their seemingly toughest early-season matchup. It would be very disappointing if they enter the bye week (with the Colts, the Miami Dolphins , and the Las Vegas Raiders on tap) at anything less than 4-0. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will be back after the Chiefs’ season continues with the Colts on “Sunday Night Football.” Keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.
author: Jared Sapp

title: Chiefs News: Commitment to Jumbo packages paid off in Week 1
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs not only rushed for 220 yards as a team against the Denver Broncos in Week 1, but also ran the ball with physicality, using formations with multiple backs and extra linemen. On some short-yardage plays, defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga and offensive lineman Josh Ezeudu joined the starting offensive line. The latter […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Khyiris Tonga #92 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs against the Denver Broncos during an NFL football game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs not only rushed for 220 yards as a team against the Denver Broncos in Week 1, but also ran the ball with physicality, using formations with multiple backs and extra linemen. On some short-yardage plays, defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga and offensive lineman Josh Ezeudu joined the starting offensive line. The latter was recently acquired from the New York Giants , but it didn’t take him long to understand Kansas City’s offensive philosophy this season. Join the conversation! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Upon Further Review: The Chiefs’ Jumbo Commitment To Run Game Pays Dividends | FOX Sports One of those bonus linemen on the 60-yard touchdown was Josh Ezeudu, acquired from the Giants at the end of preseason for a 2028 seventh-round pick, and he’s quickly learned how much his new team values owning the line of scrimmage. “I’ve only been here about three weeks now, but something that’s emphasized here is being physical,” Ezeudu told me. “We’re going to run that motherf—ing ball. I’m sorry, but it’s something we take pride in.” Kansas City Chiefs’ Week 1 Snap Count Observations: Khyiris Tonga flexes versatility, Cyrus Allen with few opportunities | A to Z Sports “Me and (Khyiris) Tonga, we always talk. I’m saying that’s one of my best friends on the team. Really, you know, he knows my dad and everything. Having everybody come in there, like the bigs, they just make big holes. You just run through them, and you know, they make our job a lot easier.” Tonga also played nearly 50% of the team’s snaps on defense, and played on special teams. That’s quite a Week 1 contribution from the 2026 free-agent signing. Chiefs receive a crucial update on rookie DB Mansoor Delane’s injury | Chiefs Wire The Kansas City Chiefs impressively began the 2026 season with their dominant victory over the defending AFC West champions. The victory was bittersweet as their 2026 first-round pick was injured and unable to return early in the game. According to NFL Insider Ian Rapoport, Chiefs rookie defensive back Mansoor Delane should miss minimal time with his shoulder injury. Delane suffered the injury early in the first quarter in the Week 1 victory over the Denver Broncos. Biggest Winners and Losers From Chiefs’ Week 1 Win Over the Denver Broncos | Sports Illustrated Special Teams The punting and kicking were about the only two things the Chiefs got right in the kicking game Thursday. Matt Araiza boomed four punts for an average of 54.5 yards, pinning two inside the 20, while Harrison Butker went 1-for-1 on field goals and 4-for-4 on extra points. The return and coverage units were another story, and they handed Denver a real edge in field position frequently. Kansas City was flagged seven times, but four of those penalties came on special teams. Kansas City Chiefs’ lopsided victory Monday capped a quirky first in NFL history | The Kansas City Star Andy Reid ties Bill Belichick Tight end Travis Kelce wasn’t the only one to move up on a career NFL list during the Chiefs’ lopsided win. Reid got the 18th win in a season-opening game, which tied former Patriots coach Bill Belichick for the second-most in NFL history. Only former Cowboys coach Tom Landry had more with 21 as X user NFL Researcher noted earlier this month. Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce named victim in $25 million fraud scheme | KY3 A 2021 Forbes article states Kelce was an investor in a fund created by Swiftarc, which the defendant, Sid Jawahar, co-founded. Jawahar pleaded guilty in January to federal wire fraud charges related to an investment scheme. Prosecutors said Jawahar used money made from new investors to repay older financiers “and to fuel an extravagant lifestyle that included flights on private planes, stays at luxury hotels and expensive outings at fancy restaurants.” Around the NFL Sean Payton ‘never heard’ about Drew Brees’ comeback attempt with Broncos in playoffs | The Athletic “I just know that I was the odd man out,” Payton said after the Broncos suffered a 31-10 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Monday. “I never heard anything about it. It never came to anything. I was only told about it later, so I was just like you guys.” No comeback ever materialized for Brees, who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in July, with Payton presenting. Payton said Tuesday he heard the story during the Hall of Fame weekend about Lombardi and Carmichael approaching Brees, but Payton thought they meant it happened during the 2020 season, when Brees missed four games due to injury. Source: Chargers signing Valdes-Scantling to practice squad | ESPN A fifth-round choice in 2018 out of South Florida, Valdez-Scantling spent training camp with the Dallas Cowboys, but the team released him when it cut its roster to 53 players. Valdes-Scantling’s signing comes after Sunday’s loss to the Cardinals in which wide receivers Ladd McConkey (rib), KeAndre Lambert-Smith (hamstring) and Derius Davis (undisclosed) were injured. On Tuesday, the Chargers put Lambert-Smith on injured reserve, meaning he’ll sit out at least four games.​ Ben Johnson suggests he wanted Bears to score 60 points at Carolina | Pro Football Talk In a Monday interview of coach Ben Johnson on ESPN 1000, Jeff Joniak said this about the 59-37 win over the Bears: “At that point I was hoping for 60. I was thinking a two-point try at some point.” Johnson paused, smiled, and said, “I don’t think you were the only one.” It’s on brand for Johnson. He wants to score a lot of points. He wants to blow teams out. Whenever, wherever, however. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride 5 things we learned about the Chiefs from Week 1 win over Denver This team is going to be hard to pass against The severity of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane’s injury hurts this defense. He is a special talent who looks like a cornerstone you can build around for years to come. But even without Delane for most of Monday night, the Chiefs secondary locked down Denver’s vaunted wide receivers, holding Jaylen Waddle and Courtland Sutton to three receptions for 13 yards. Do I think this performance was an outlier? Nope.
