title: There’s one major difference in the Chiefs’ offense this year
summary: There will always be a lot of love for former Kansas City Chiefs running backs Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt from Chiefs Kingdom. The former started for two Super Bowl champion teams, and the latter was easy to root for when he returned to Kansas City in 2024 and helped win the team’s most recent […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Kenneth Walker III #9 of the Kansas City Chiefs dives for a first down against Jahdae Barron #23 of the Denver Broncos during the second quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images There will always be a lot of love for former Kansas City Chiefs running backs Isiah Pacheco and Kareem Hunt from Chiefs Kingdom. The former started for two Super Bowl champion teams, and the latter was easy to root for when he returned to Kansas City in 2024 and helped win the team’s most recent AFC title. So if you’re reading this, Isiah and Kareem, don’t take offense at quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ words after the 31-10 win over the Denver Broncos in Week 1, a dominant victory that featured the most rushing yards (173) by a single Chiefs player under head coach Andy Reid. Running back Kenneth Walker introduced himself to Chiefs fans in as exciting a fashion as he possibly could, even if it didn’t surprise the two-time MVP quarterback. “I told you all, literally, the first press conference,” Mahomes reminded local media after the game. “You all were asking, ‘What is the difference in the offense?’” “It’s K9,” Mahomes emphasized. “It’s that simple.” Kenneth Walker III generated +101 rushing yards over expected against the Broncos, the most by a Chiefs running back since at least 2018. Walker also forced 14 missed tackles, the most by any Chiefs player in a game over that span. #DENvsKC | #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/8K4ldeYFlT — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) September 15, 2026 From the get-go, it was clear that the Chiefs’ offense would be willing to lean on Walker to an extreme. The first four plays of the game were rushing attempts by Walker, and Kansas City needed all four runs to move the chains initially. As Walker’s rushing tally increased, he had more space to burst into the second and third level. By the third quarter, the fifth-year back was streaking down the sideline, shaking off a defensive back on his way to a 60-yard touchdown run on fourth-and-1. “We ran the play a few times” Walker recalled during his post-game press conference. “I knew they were going to crash in, so when they crashed in, I just bounced it out. I was one-on-one with the corner, I outran him, and it was off to the races from there.” The Chiefs’ new lead back finished with 23 carries and 3 catches; head coach Andy Reid knew he had to ride the hot hand on Monday night. “You never know going in how many times you’re going to give him the ball; that’s not a calculated thing that you can do,” Reid said in his post-game press conference. “You have to be making yards. “For him to play the way he did, I thought it was spectacular,” Reid declared. “It was something that you hope for, and you got to see it where he’s the main guy there.” It wasn’t a productive day for the Chiefs’ pass offense, but it didn’t need to be. It’s why the Chiefs paid $28.7 million guaranteed to secure the talent of last year’s Super Bowl MVP. “It’s just a special ability to run the ball tough between the tackles,” Mahomes described Walker. ”Then he does have the speed to go all the way out. We’ll utilize him.“ Sharing the backfield with Walker was rookie running back Emmett Johnson, who contributed 68 yards to the offense over 10 touches. “Emmett did a nice job too when he had an opportunity to get in there,” Reid pointed out. “Both of these guys’ contact balance is ridiculous, so they got a lot of yards after contact, and that’s a special thing to have there.” On a night where Mahomes — 275 days removed from tearing the ACL and LCL in his right knee — was clearly working his way back into full-speed football, Walker made life easier on Kansas City’s superman. Someone else wore the cape for once, as defensive tackle Chris Jones alluded to at the podium Monday night. “If you run like that, you can always be my hero,” Jones said, smiling.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Rashee Rice emphasizes Chiefs’ physicality on display against Broncos
summary: On the surface, the wide receivers on either side of the field in the Kansas City Chiefs’ 31-10 win over the Denver Broncos were not impactful. The Chiefs’ offense ran through tailback Kenneth Walker, who filled up the box score; Walker accounted for 49% of Kansas City’s total yards on “Monday Night Football.” However, the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 14: Rashee Rice #4 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates after scoring a 13 yard touchdown against the Denver Broncos during the second quarter in the game at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images On the surface, the wide receivers on either side of the field in the Kansas City Chiefs ’ 31-10 win over the Denver Broncos were not impactful. The Chiefs’ offense ran through tailback Kenneth Walker, who filled up the box score; Walker accounted for 49% of Kansas City’s total yards on “Monday Night Football.” However, the Chiefs’ No. 1 receiver was all smiles when speaking to Voice of the Chiefs Mitch Holthus on the team’s official postgame show , “Chiefs Rewind,” on YouTube . Rashee Rice scored a touchdown after breaking tackles near the goal line, but he finished with just two catches and 19 yards. He made a point to affect the game without the ball in his hands. Look at Rashee blocking 65 yards downfield https://t.co/TCa4IzOaUo — His DirknesS (@HisDirknesS) September 15, 2026 On the 59-yard gain by tight end Travis Kelce in the third quarter, moving the chains on a crucial third down, Rice can be seen blocking downfield with great effort, preventing the Broncos’ cornerback from getting in on the tackle that brought Kelce down inside the five-yard line. “We ran that ball, and we blocked downfield for everybody to have the ball in their hands,” Rice told Holthus. “We definitely blocked for our brothers today.” Rice, who led all Chiefs receivers in offensive snaps, usually blocked for a handoff to Kenneth Walker on his way to a league-leading 173 rushing yards. With the team’s new talent in the backfield, Rice is learning that, similar to quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ relentlessness on a dropback, Walker has a chance to break into the third level of a defense on every touch. “It’s hard to not watch those guys while the ball is in their hands,” Rice acknowledged. “It’s hard to go get your assignment because those guys are so fun to watch. Sometimes, you get caught up being on the backside of a play, just watching them run the ball — then out of nowhere, [Walker] comes to the backside with the ball in his hands and you have to find a second effort to block the guy in front of you.” Despite the Chiefs’ abysmal downfield passing attack in Week 1, Rice understands what Walker’s big game can do for the unit moving forward. “We have somebody there that’s going to affect the defense,” Rice said of Walker. “It’s going to leave us one-on-one with certain defenders and cornerbacks, so having a running back like that is huge for the offense.” I asked Rashee Rice about what his TD catch meant to him and the Chiefs’ physicality Monday night. “I think we’re a much more physical team than I’ve been on throughout these past three years, and I think that comes with the coaching.” pic.twitter.com/THU3Op8Pia — Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) September 15, 2026 It all comes back to the team’s identity shift this offseason, which was headlined by the re-hire of offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy. The team is clearly more physical, and Rice — in his first season under Bieniemy’s coaching — can see the difference. “I think we’re a much more physical team than I’ve been on throughout these past three years,” Rice told Matt Derrick of Chiefs Digest in the locker room after the game . “I think that comes with the coaching.” “I love it,” Rice emphasized. “[It’s a] mentality.”

title: NFL Power Rankings Week 2 Roundup: The Chiefs are back
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season’s opening weekend wrapped up with the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Denver Broncos and making a statement along the way. Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings: NFL.com: 10 For the first time this decade, the Chiefs have a legitimately fearsome rushing attack. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY , MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Patrick Mahomes (15) of the Kansas City Chiefs hypes up the fans during the fourth quarter of the Chiefs' 31-10 win over the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri on Monday, September 14, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season’s opening weekend wrapped up with the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Denver Broncos and making a statement along the way. Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings: NFL.com : 10 For the first time this decade, the Chiefs have a legitimately fearsome rushing attack. Kenneth Walker III won’t run for a career-high total every week, but he brings a punch that Kansas City’s backfield has lacked for most of the Patrick Mahomes era. That should make folks respect the Chiefs, even as Mahomes shakes off the rust accumulated by a lengthy recovery from knee surgery. — Nick Shook ESPN : 8 Week 1 result: Beat the Broncos 31-10 Preseason ranking: 13 Non-QB newcomer debut: RB Kenneth Walker III For one game at least, Walker was everything the Chiefs could’ve hoped for, bringing more explosive highlights to their rushing attack. Walker produced a career-high 173 rushing yards, with his best moment being a breakaway 60-yard touchdown on fourth-and-inches early in the third quarter. His best trait against the Broncos was his elusiveness, as he forced 14 missed tackles, the most by any Chiefs player in a game since 2018. Walker caught a short touchdown pass, too. — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 7 Last week: 14 Monday: Beat Broncos 31-10 What we learned: They have a running game! After dealing with an inconsistent ground attack last season, the Chiefs went out and signed reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III. It took Walker one game to make a big impact. All eyes in the opener were on Patrick Mahomes’ return, but it was Walker who stole the show, totaling 191 yards of offense and two touchdowns, and adding a new dimension to the K.C. offense. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 8 Kenneth Walker III earned every penny of his contract in his debut, and then some. — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 1 0 Many buried this team, saying the dynasty was over. No it isn’t. Patrick Mahomes didn’t have to do a lot against Denver, but he’s healthy. That’s the good news. — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 7 Kenneth Walker III was excellent and will transform the Chiefs’ offense. He had 173 yards rushing. Patrick Mahomes will be better as he get further removed from a torn ACL. He had just 184 yards passing and was off on many throws, but that didn’t take away from a successful return. But one of the best stories of the opener was left tackle Kahlil Benson. He is an undrafted rookie out of Indiana who got no guaranteed money to sign with the Chiefs and did not play left tackle in college. He was forced into the lineup due to a Josh Simmons injury and there was rightful concern over him protecting Mahomes’ blindside. But Benson, the first undrafted rookie to start Week 1 on the offensive line since Terence Steele with the Cowboys in 2020, played well and the Broncos rarely got any pressure on Mahomes. Offensive linemen don’t get too much attention, but Benson deserves a lot of credit for stepping up when he had to. — Frank Schwab USA Today : 6 Return of the King? Having a Super Bowl MVP tandem backfield of Patrick Mahomes and Kenneth Walker III was even more than it was cracked up to be in the opener, when K.C. made an emphatic statement that it’s ready to reclaim its AFC West throne from Denver. And maybe more. — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 5 I think one of the singular most frustrating parts of covering professional football is spending an entire offseason attempting to understand what will be effective and will not be, and determining that Kansas City—a team starting an undrafted free agent tackle against one of the best defenses in football, having made a wing-and-a-prayer addition of a veteran running back to salvage the offense and starting a QB just nine months after a torn ACL—will struggle. Only to have the Chiefs absolutely demolish last year’s conference runner-up. The prediction game is a painful one, man. Don’t let your kids live this life. — Conor Orr FOX Sports : 1 2 They’re baaaaack. Patrick Mahomes didn’t even look like his old self Monday night and the Chiefs still dominated the Broncos. When Mahomes rounds into form, KC might be ready to reclaim its throne. — Ralph Vacchiano

title: Chargers Power Rankings Roundup: Bolts see drastic fall after loss to Cardinals
summary: The Chargers and their entire fan base were shocked by the double-digit loss to the Cardinals in Week One. For the most part, the Bolts were seen as a potential top-10 team to begin the season and mostly were seen ranked inside the top 16 across the board. However, a sloppy loss to the Cardinals […]
full_text: Inglewood, - September 13: Running back Omarion Hampton #8 of the Los Angeles Chargers runs for the touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals in the first half of a NFL football game at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood on Sunday, September 13, 2026. (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Chargers and their entire fan base were shocked by the double-digit loss to the Cardinals in Week One. For the most part, the Bolts were seen as a potential top-10 team to begin the season and mostly were seen ranked inside the top 16 across the board. However, a sloppy loss to the Cardinals has seen them take a big hit in this week”s updated rankings. There’s only so much to recap as to what led to the drop and most of you likely don’t want to read about it again, so let’s just dive right in to this week’s roundup. Sports Illustrated – #17 I agree with MMQB Podcast co-host Albert Breer who said this on our Monday morning recap show: It’s most concerning to me that L.A. did not dazzle in the run game despite having most conceivable advantages over the Cardinals. Alas, this is the opening week loss no one saw coming (especially the boobs who used ChatGPT for help in their knockout pools. All of you get what you deserve).‘” – Conor Orr Bleacher Report – #19 Are we sure that Mike McDaniel is an offensive guru? Justin Herbert never seemed to find a rhythm, and the Los Angeles Chargers offense looked every bit as disjointed as it did under Greg Roman last season. Unfortunately, the top-tier defense we saw from L.A. in 2025 was nowhere to be found. Maybe the Arizona Cardinals are simply far better than anyone expected. However, the version of the Chargers we saw on Sunday looked like a team that could be headed to the AFC West basement. – Kristopher Knox Yahoo Sports – #19 “There’s nothing good to say about the Chargers’ Week 1 loss. It was so dispiriting that head coach Jim Harbaugh lamented sitting his starters for most of the preseason. The offense, with new coordinator Mike McDaniel, had two plays longer than 15 yards against an Arizona defense that isn’t expected to be good. (Don’t tell Andrew Wingard I said that.) The defense, without last year’s star coordinator Jesse Minter, allowed points or a missed field goal on seven of 10 possessions before a kneel-down at the end. The Chargers’ early-season schedule is brutal, and the Cardinals game was supposed to be a rare easy win.” – Frank Schwab ESPN – #19 The second-round pick out of Florida was put in a tough position. Slaughter spent most of his college snaps at center, but he competed for the left guard spot throughout most of training camp. When starting center Tyler Biadasz suffered a preseason ACL injury, Slaughter was thrust into the starting role. On Sunday, he had as good a performance as you’d hope a rookie center to have, with no major blunders. He allowed just one quarterback pressure, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. – Kris Rhim The Athletic – #19 Maybe that’s an overreaction, but the Chargers lost to the Cardinals, a team that had a preseason win total over/under of 3.5. Justin Herbert wasn’t good, the running game struggled and the defense allowed 393 yards of offense to a team with Jacoby Brissett at quarterback and Kendrick Bourne as its top-producing wide receiver in the game. – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall SB Nation – #19 NFL.com – #20 Did the Chargers take the Cardinals lightly? Perhaps. Their performance suggested they may have, but what I saw from Jim Harbaugh’s crew was evidence of rust. It’s not uncommon in Week 1 — however, it is alarming for a club aiming to improve on its recent postseason one-and-dones. If anything, the uneven showing reminded the Bolts that they cannot underestimate any opponent in the NFL. They better take the field with more fire in the next few weeks. – Nick Shook USA Today – #25 Jim Harbaugh had never lost an opener as an NFL head coach … until Sunday, a defeat that dropped him to 6-1 in Week 1. The Bolts’ putrid performance also makes it worth wondering if Harbs is headed to his first sub-.500 campaign under an NFL headset. – Nate Davis

title: Chargers bringing sense of urgency in Week 2 vs. Raiders
summary: The Los Angeles Chargers have a lot of work to do after their season-opening loss against the Arizona Cardinals. The Cardinals came into the season with low expectations and the Chargers were viewed as a massive favorite going into the game, but that wasn’t reflected in the 26-14 loss. With a chance to start 0-2 […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Head coach Jim Harbaugh of the Los Angeles Chargers looks on in the fourth quarter of a game against the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers have a lot of work to do after their season-opening loss against the Arizona Cardinals. The Cardinals came into the season with low expectations and the Chargers were viewed as a massive favorite going into the game, but that wasn’t reflected in the 26-14 loss. With a chance to start 0-2 at home against the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, the Chargers are attacking this week with more urgency than before. “Just as I would have expected,” Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh said in his press conference. “Everybody really looking at their position, their group, and trying to find out exactly what they can do better to help the cause, just as you would expect a group of competitors to be about.” The Chargers have been in the postseason in each of the last two seasons under Harbaugh, but they have yet to win a playoff game. They know this year can provide that next step forward, but not if they continue to play how they did on Sunday. There was a lethargic energy on both ends of the field, which the Cardinals were easily able to take advantage of. The Cardinals went into the game with nothing to lose, and they played just like that. The Chargers need to zap some of that energy from the Cardinals and apply it to themselves because losing back-to-back games at home at the start of the season to two teams that finished in the top three of the NFL Draft will only set Los Angeles up for failure moving forward. BFTB community, how do you feel about the progress going into this week against the Raiders? Let us know in the comments section below.

summary: The Los Angeles Chargers are boosting their wide receiver room going into Week 2 against the Las Vegas Raiders. According to ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler, the Chargers are signing wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling to the practice squad. The move comes after wide receiver Ladd McConkey suffered a rib injury in the team’s Week 1 loss […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 4: Marquez Valdes-Scantling #11 of the Dallas Cowboys walks off the field during training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 4, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers are boosting their wide receiver room going into Week 2 against the Las Vegas Raiders. According to ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler, the Chargers are signing wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling to the practice squad. Source: Chargers are signing veteran wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling to the practice squad. Valdes-Scantling joins his ninth NFL team. pic.twitter.com/vZ4DTMBDAa — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) September 16, 2026 The move comes after wide receiver Ladd McConkey suffered a rib injury in the team’s Week 1 loss against the Arizona Cardinals. With McConkey potentially missing time, the team promoted Gary Jennings to the 53-man roster and have now moved Valdes-Scantling into his spot on the practice squad. MVS brings a lot of experience to the Chargers organization after he was selected in the fifth round of the 2018 NFL draft out of South Florida. He spent the first four years of his career with the Packers before moving to the Kansas City Chiefs, where he won back-to-back Super Bowls in 2022 and 2023. In the past two seasons, Valdes-Scantling has become a journeyman in the NFL, playing for the Buffalo Bills, New Orleans Saints, San Francisco 49ers, and Pittsburgh Steelers. Earlier in the offseason, Valdes-Scantling signed a one-year deal with the Dallas Cowboys, but he was cut at the end of training camp, ahead of the 53-man roster deadline. It remains to be seen if MVS will ever see the field for the Chargers, but the team is at least giving him a shot to prove himself in practice. BFTB community, how do you feel about the Chargers signing MVS, and where do you think he stands amongst the wide receiver room? Let us know in the comment section below.

(Photo by Harry How/Getty Images)Ladd McConkey #15 of the Los Angeles Chargers | Getty Images The Chargers came out flat, disconnected, and overall sloppy on Sunday. We don’t need to rehash all of it, but we should highlight those who still found a way to standout despite the overall mess on the field. Wideout Ladd McConley was ELITE before leaving the game with his rib injury. Offensive tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt both looked good in their returns to the field. Surprisingly, it was tight end David Njoku who would up being a consistent weapon behind McConkey, as well. Defensively, there wasn’t much to write home about. Much more bad than good, but you’ll see that here in a second. Let’s go ahead and dive in to this week’s best and worst grades from Pro Football Focus. Offense Best WR Ladd McConkey – 90.7 OT Rashawn Slater – 76.3 TE David Njoku – 71.9 OG Kayode Awosika – 71.1 OT Joe Alt – 67.3 McConkey coming out of the gates and catching five passes for 82 yards and a score, including three for 60 on the opening drive, gave us a glimpse of just how good he could be in this new offense. However, that’s if he can return fairly soon from a rib injury that currently has him “day-to-day” per Jim Harbaugh. LADD MCCONKEY 💥 pic.twitter.com/8wUgIknCTS — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) September 13, 2026 Slater was the top offensive lineman in his first game back in over a year and a half. He was the top run blocker (87.4) on the team and third in pass pro (73.1). In his first game with the Chargers, Awosika was solid in run blocking (63.4) and stellar in pass pro with a top grade of 85.1. Joe Alt was behind him in pass pro with an 82.8 in that area. He was also third in run blocking with a 62.9 grade. Njoku caught all five of his passes and was overall the only other consistent offensive player next to McConkey. Worst OG/T Trey Pipkins – 37.1 OG Cole Strange – 41.0 C Jake Slaughter – 42.5 FB Alec Ingold – 47.0 WR Derius Davis – 53.0 The results are in for the “platoon” at left guard and Pipkins was very far-and-away the worse option of the two. He was abysmal in both run blocking (38.9) and pass pro (41.4.) Strange was almost just a road bump on the way to the quarterback. He finished with a 10.9 in pass blocking which is so bad it’s almost impressive. Slaughter unfortunately failed his first real NFL test against a defensive line that did not feature any stars. His 39.0 run block was second worst to Pipkins among offensive lineman and his overall game grade actually made him the worst center in Week One among the 34 players who took at least one snap at the pivot. Ingold, who was added because of his familiarity with the offense, had a rough game as his 36.6 was the worst run block grade on the team. Defense Best S Tony Jefferson – 82.3 S Genesis Smith – 77.5 LB Troy Dye – 73.1 S Elijah Molden – 71.5 DT Teair Tart – 70.3 Jefferson led the defense with an 83.0 coverage grade and overall was their best defender. The rookie Smith was second in coverage with a 71.4 and second in tackling with an 82.1. Dye played in a rotational role with Del’Shawn Phillips and finished with the third-best tackling grade (79.9). Molden topped the team in tackling with an 84.4. Tart was stout with a 72.8 run defense grade, good for second on the team. Worst DT Nick Barrett – 27.5 CB Donte Jackson – 32.6 DT Justin Eboigbe – 50.4 EDGE Tuli Tuipulotu – 51.3 S Derwin James – 53.9 It was a bad day in coverage for two of the team’s best members of the secondary. Jackson earned a 29.7 coverage grade while allowing four of six passes his way to be completed. James ended with a better overall grade, even in coverage (53.7), but he allowed seven of nine targets to be completed in his area. He also struggled as a tackler, earning a grade of 47.0 in that area. Tuipulotu’s grade was sunk by an uncharacteristic 28.1 tackling grade. He also had eight plays in coverage which was such a frustrating sight. His 42.5 in that area was second worst on the team.

title: Aaron Donald has ‘realistic’ chance to play vs. Giants
summary: There is a “very, very realistic chance” that Aaron Donald could play for the Los Angeles Rams against the New York Giants on Monday Night Football, according to the NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. Given the injury to Myles Garrett that will keep the Rams’ star pass rusher out for at least a month, Donald’s return […]
full_text: There is a “very, very realistic chance” that Aaron Donald could play for the Los Angeles Rams against the New York Giants on Monday Night Football, according to the NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. Given the injury to Myles Garrett that will keep the Rams’ star pass rusher out for at least a month , Donald’s return to the field in Week 2 couldn’t come at a better time. Donald’s return has been THE storyline this offseason, starting with weeks of “Will he?” followed lately by ”When will he?“. With Garrett injured and L.A. looking for a rebound from their ugly Week 1 loss to the 49ers, the “when” can’t come soon enough for the Rams. Donald not expected to be limited Despite not playing in two years, Rapoport expects Donald to push for a full-time workload rather than a strict snap count once he’s on the field. “Part of me wants to say ‘expect Aaron Donald to come in and be a part-time player.’ I know the player too well. And I know human nature too well. We can talk about how he can come in and play 10 to 15 plays a game and sure, that’s a possibility,” Rapoport explained. “But with the game on the line, even in the trenches during the third and fourth quarter, he’s going to want to play.” Rapoport also said that, based on conversations he’s had with “people who know,” Donald is targeting Monday night. He goes on to say that“the goal would be to be out there against the Giants with the entire country watching.” That sounds like Hollywood doesn’t it?

title: Rams vs. Giants: Sean McVay still gives L.A. an advantage
summary: The Los Angeles Rams return home for a Monday Night Football showdown against the New York Giants after disappointing in their season opener. full_text: The Los Angeles Rams return home for a Monday Night Football showdown against the New York Giants after disappointing in their season opener. The Rams were defeated 27-7 by the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia; struggling offensively while allowing Brock Purdy and the 49ers to control the game. Matthew Stafford finished with 155 passing yards, while the Rams managed just 290 total yards. Meanwhile, the New York Giants enter Week 2 with momentum after a 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football . John Harbaugh secured a big divisional win in his first year as Head Coach of the Giants. Jaxson Dart threw three touchdown passes and New York’s rushing attack helped the Giants control possession and dictate the pace. Now, the Rams look to rebound at SoFi Stadium on Monday, September 21 at 8:15 p.m. ET. Here is a look at the primetime matchup. OFFENSE: RAMS Make no mistake, the Rams offense was lackluster in the season opener. However, there were glimpses in which the offense was able to move the ball with the rushing attack. The Cowboys never really tested the Giants defensive front. The Rams are fully capable of kickstarting the offense by committing to their tandem of Kyren Williams and Blake Corum. That will open up the passing game for Matthew Stafford. The Giants offense is not to be taken for granted. Greg Roman has dual threats in Jaxson Dart and Cam Skattebo. There is a similar scheme to the 49ers and the Rams will have to slow that down and force Dart to win the game through the air. DEFENSE: GIANTS On paper, the Rams have the better defense. But execution has been lacking so far and dating back to the end of last season. It’s not just a matter of having the pieces… the pieces must be execute and be used correctly. The Rams will be without Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald’s status for Monday Night remains undetermined. The Giants meanwhile have a strong pass rush featuring Brian Burns, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Arvell Reese, and Abdul Carter. DJ Reader is also a strong presence in the interior for the Giants. The Giants defense is strong and slowed down the Cowboys offense that finished #2 last year. SPECIAL TEAMS: GIANTS John Harbaugh has a special teams pedigree. The Rams meanwhile are still trying to find stability in their special teams. COACHING: RAMS Sean McVay is a more complete coach than John Harbaugh which gives him an edge. But the area to watch here is the assistants. The Rams will want to see a bounce back performance from coaches like Kliff Kingsbury (Assistant Coach), Nate Scheelhaase (OC), and most importantly Chris Shula. Shula in particular is under a microscope. The Giants looked renewed with their new offensive identity and game plan. Dart in particular has grown in Year 2 so credit to the new regime.

title: Are Rams putting their new corners in the best position to succeed?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams made two of the biggest offseason acquisitions in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. McDuffie was brought in via a blockbuster trade. Watson was an out of character free agent investment by LA. But why would the Rams acquire two premium corners if they were going to run a defense designed for […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 22: Los Angeles Rams cornerback Trent McDuffie (22) during the NFL preseason game between New Orleans Saints and the Los Angeles Rams on August 22, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Photo by Jevone Moore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams made two of the biggest offseason acquisitions in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. McDuffie was brought in via a blockbuster trade. Watson was an out of character free agent investment by LA. But why would the Rams acquire two premium corners if they were going to run a defense designed for the players they wanted to replace? That’s exactly what happened in Week 1 in the stunning loss against the San Francisco 49ers. Whether the issue persists is something worth monitoring. Rams vs Chiefs 2025: Coverage Breakdowns Rams zone coverage ranking: 8th at 76.3% Chiefs zone coverage ranking: 24th at 66.3% Rams zone coverage rate vs 49ers: 77.8% Los Angeles ranked in the top 10 in terms of the teams who most often utilized zone coverage according to data from SumerSports. The Chiefs ranked in the bottom 10 of the NFL. These are two distinct approaches to defense, and it was reasonable to expect a shift from LA. Zone coverage can be the great equalizer. You can take heady players who are maybe less physically talented and maximize their production. Zone is more apt for takeaways and allows defenders to keep their eyes on the quarterback. Playing man coverage often requires the horses to do so. Simply put, the Rams did not have them last year. They should now. They shouldn’t continue to play a defense that is designed for the players they were intent on replacing. Counterpoints: Why 49ers were a bad example There are several key reasons why you wouldn’t want to play man coverage against the 49ers: Brock Purdy is athletic enough to gash you Christian McCaffrey is a unique receiving threat The SF offense is designed for YAC Purdy finished with 29 yards on five carries with a long of 18 despite how much zone coverage Los Angeles presented. Asking corners to turn their backs in man coverage proves this was probably a bad matchup. Also, the biggest threat against San Francisco is not that passes are completed—it’s what happens thereafter. The 49ers are built to turn 10-yard catches into explosive gains. Zone coverage is the better method to mitigate this risk than man. But the counterpoints don’t tell the whole story While the 49ers might have been a bad team to deploy a new-look defense against, the single matchup doesn’t completely dismiss the idea that the Rams’ defensive scheme needs to change. McDuffie and Watson are capable of playing sticky man coverage. This would help a talented pass rush, especially after Myles Garrett’s eventual return from injured reserve. The coverage mix is worth keeping an eye on over the coming weeks. We may not get true answers on who the defense wants to be until after they are healthy and back at full force.

title: Sean McVay & Rams W-L record following a 49ers loss
summary: The Los Angeles Rams opened the 2026 season with a disappointing loss to the San Francisco 49ers, leaving Sean McVay and his team with plenty to evaluate heading into Week 2. While the result was not what the Rams wanted, McVay frequently emphasizes one important message following adversity: “controlling their response”. That response will be […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams opened the 2026 season with a disappointing loss to the San Francisco 49ers, leaving Sean McVay and his team with plenty to evaluate heading into Week 2. While the result was not what the Rams wanted, McVay frequently emphasizes one important message following adversity: “ controlling their response ”. That response will be especially important for a Rams team that has high expectations entering the season. McVay and his coaching staff must find ways to correct the mistakes from Week 1 while making sure the loss does not carry over into Monday night’s matchup against the New York Giants. For the players, the challenge is equally simple: learn from the mistakes, move forward and respond with urgency. I was curious to know how Sean McVay was motivated following a loss to his rival, Kyle Shanahan and the San Francisco 49ers. Since both coaches were hired by their respective teams in 2017, here is how McVay has responded after losing to Shanahan. 2017: Week 17 | 34-13 loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 26-13 (playoff) loss to Falcons After choosing to rest their starters in the regular season finale, the Rams could not get their offense moving against Matt Ryan and the Falcons. 2019: Week 6 | 20-7 loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 37-10 win over Falcons The Rams went into Atlanta and dominated. This was the first game that Jalen Ramsey played in horns. 2019: Week 16 | 34-31 loss @ 49ers Next Game: 31-24 win over Cardinals The Rams were knocked out of the playoff race after their Week 16 to the 49ers and there was not much to play for in the regular season finale other than having a winning season. Sean McVay made sure of that. 2020: Week 6 | 24-16 loss @ 49ers Next Game: 24-10 win over Bears The Rams faced Nick Foles and the Bears in primetime. The offense was able to slow down Khalil Mack off the edge in order to get back in the win column. 2020: Week 12 | 23-20 loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 38-28 win over Cardinals Troy Hill had a pick 6 and the Rams scored 21 points in the 4th quarter to clip the birds yet again. 2021: Week 10 | 31-10 loss @ 49ers Next Game: 36-28 loss to Packers After storming out to a 7-1 record, the Rams then lost to the Titans, 49ers, and then Packers. A lot of people thought the Rams were frauds but the 3 game skid led to a 5 game win streak. 2021: Week 18 | 27-24 (OT) loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 34-11 (playoff) win over Cardinals The Rams were pissed for having lost Week 18 to the 49ers. They still secured the NFC West division crown but they became the 4th seed in the NFC. As it turned out they stomped the Cardinals in the Wild Card round. 2022: Week 4 | 24-9 loss @ 49ers Next Game: 22-10 loss to Cowboys Aaron Donald registered two sacks but that was enough to beat Cooper Rush and the Cowboys… 2022: Week 8 | 31-14 loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 16-13 loss to Buccaneers The 2022 was a disaster but none was more unsettling than watching the team hand a game to Tom Brady and the Buccaneers after seemingly having the game secured towards the end of the 4th quarter. 2023: Week 2 | 30-23 loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 19-16 loss to Bengals Apparently Tutu Atwell stepped out bounds… I still will never understand how that call was reversed. 2025: Week 5 | 26-23 (OT) loss vs. 49ers Next Game: 17-3 win over Ravens Puka Nacua was injured midway through the 2nd quarter but the Rams defense held Tyler Huntley and the Ravens offense to just 3 points. After this game, the Rams offense made the switch to using 13 personnel more frequently. In 11 losses to San Francisco, Sean McVay and the Rams are 6-5* in the ensuing games. The 2017 loss to San Francisco was purely out of a decision to rest their starters before the playoffs. At least its more likely than not that the Rams will pick up a win against the New York Giants this week after losing to the 49ers in Week 1 at Melbourne, Australia.

title: Rams Super Bowl chances hinge on 3rd down success
summary: The Los Angeles Rams have played 86 regular-season games from Week 1 of 2021 through Week 1 of 2026. A lot of their success as a offense has been their ability to keep pressure on opposing defenses by moving the chains. Eventually, defenses bust their coverage and the Rams find their way in the end […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams have played 86 regular-season games from Week 1 of 2021 through Week 1 of 2026. A lot of their success as a offense has been their ability to keep pressure on opposing defenses by moving the chains. Eventually, defenses bust their coverage and the Rams find their way in the end zone. Over the last 5 seasons, the Rams season-level third-down rates were: 2021: 44.6% 2022: 39.3% 2023: 41.7% 2024: 36.1% 2025: 37.1% It’s no surprise that the Rams 2021 numbers were so strong as they parlayed that into a Super Bowl championship. The 2022 season saw the team fall drastically because of injuries across the board. The 2023 Rams went from a slow start to strong finish. The 2024 team was remembered for being offensively sluggish. And the 2025 offense, while carried by MVP Matthew Stafford tried to limit its third down frequency by winning on first and second downs. Last year, the Seattle Seahawks were 16th in the league in 3rd down conversion rate with 39.59%. For the sake of this analytical breakdown, I chose 40% as the measurement that the Rams need to be at to find their footing on offense in the 2026 season. 5 YEAR BREAKDOWN… Rams overall record when they convert 40% or more on 3rd down: 30-13 Rams overall record when they convert 39% or less on 3rd down: 19-24 The Rams a significantly different team over the last 5 years when they win 3rd downs at a respectable clip. They are nearly a .700 winning team. On the flip side, when they don’t move the chains as well, they are inconsistent and a sub. 500 team. 2026 Rams when they convert 40% or more on 3rd down: ? 2026 Rams when they convert 39% or less on 3rd down: 0-1 2025 Rams when they convert 40% or more on third down: 7-3 2025 Rams when they convert 39% or less on third down: 5-2 2024 Rams when they convert 40% or more on third down: 6-3 2024 Rams when they convert 39% or less on third down: 4-4 2023 Rams when they convert 40% or more on third down: 5-3 2023 Rams when they convert 39% or less on third down: 5-4 2022 Rams when they convert 40% or more on third down: 3-2 2022 Rams when they convert 39% or less on third down: 2-10 2021 Rams when they convert 40% or more on third down: 9-2 2021 Rams when they convert 39% or less on third down: 3-3 SUPER BOWL SIGNIFICANCE As the Rams move on from their 2026 season opener, a game in which they looked like a sub .500 team because of their sluggish performance on offense, they will need to find consistency winning on “money downs”. In these last 5 NFL seasons, the AFC and NFC representative each year both finished in the top half of the league for third down conversion percentage. 2021 – Los Angeles Rams (44.66 / 6th) , Cincinnati Bengals (40.08% / 15th) 2022 – Philadelphia Eagles (47.58% / 3rd), Kansas City Chiefs (48.90% / 2nd) 2023 – San Francisco 49ers (47.49% / 4th), Kansas City Chiefs (43.32% / 6th) 2024 – Philadelphia Eagles (40.28% / 10th) , Kansas City Chiefs (47.31% / 3rd) 2025 – Seattle Seahawks (39.59% / 16th) , New England Patriots (40.63% / 13th) As it stands right now, albeit a one game sample size, the Rams are 26th in the league (22.22%). If Los Angeles wants to see a Lombardi Trophy return home, they MUST find a way to be successful on third downs week-to-week.

title: Rams Week 2 power rankings round-up: LA drops from top spot
summary: After a very surprising showing in a Week 1 loss to the 49ers, it’s no surprise the Rams have slipped in almost every power ranking. The lone exception was Complex.com’s Matt Burke, who kept at L.A. at the top spot despite the loss and injury to Myles Garrett. Most writers seem to have adopted a […]
full_text: After a very surprising showing in a Week 1 loss to the 49ers , it’s no surprise the Rams have slipped in almost every power ranking. The lone exception was Complex.com’s Matt Burke, who kept at L.A. at the top spot despite the loss and injury to Myles Garrett. Most writers seem to have adopted a wait-and-see attitude before punishing the Rams any further. If they lose to the Giants this week, they will plummet. This sample of eight sites seems to represent the consensus and the average ranking of these eight prognosticators is just over five, which seems about right. Pete Prisco : Dropped from 2 to 5 “So much for the idea they were just going to waltz to the Super Bowl. They have issues on both sides of the ball that were exposed by the 49ers.” Fox Sports Ralph Vacchiano : Dropped from 1 to 5 “The big debate is how far they should plummet because of their opening flop? It could turn out to be a travel-induced anomaly. But if the Rams lose to the Giants on Sunday, you’ll find them in the high teens next week.” NFL.com Nick Shook : Dropped from 1 to 7 “Is it a bit dramatic of me to drop the Rams six spots after a season-opening loss ? You could make that case. But the offseason darlings certainly haven’t done themselves any favors in the last week, appearing unprepared and somewhat fatigued.“ Mike Florio PFT : Dropped from 2 to 11 Mike Florio went the furthest in dropping the Rams, all the way from 2 to 11. Seriously? A bit of an overreaction, perhaps. USA Today Nate Davis : Dropped from 1 to 5 ‘This was likely an anomalous defeat, if a reminder that the Lombardi Trophy is guaranteed to no team.’ SI Conor Orr : Dropped from 1 to 7 “The Rams laid an egg in Australia but the circumstances are such that I’m allowing a pass until we see the team at something closer to optimal.“ Complex Matt Burke : No change, stayed at 1 “The Rams’ team travel director could be on the unemployment line soon as LA’s decision to arrive in Melbourne, Australia just 28 hours before kickoff against the 49ers proved to be costly. New acquisition Myles Garrett is set to miss at least four games as he is undergoing arthroscopic knee surgery. But for now, they are still number one in the rankings.“ NFL Trade Rumors Ethan Woodie : Dropped from 1 to 2 He dropped the Rams one spot due to the Myles Garrett injury. This week’s result against the surprising Giants should move the needle somewhat. The question is which direction.

My Pick: Bills 37-30 Carolina Panthers @ Atlanta Falcons — Sun., 1:00 p.m. ET If the Panthers can bottle up Bijan Robinson, then they should be able to go into Atlanta and secure a Week 2 road win. My Pick: Panthers 29-24 Minnesota Vikings @ Chicago Bears — Sun., 1:00 p.m. ET How Brian Flores gameplans for Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson will be interesting. Baker Mayfield bounce back game? Mayfield earned a huge payday and then turned in a dud in Week 1; fumbling the ball three times. But the combination of Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry is going to be too much for the Saints to handle outside of their dome. My Pick: Ravens 41-20 Cincinnati Bengals @ Houston Texans — Sun., 1:00 p.m. ET The Texans get another elite quarterback early – who came up with their schedule? I have to believe that Demeco Ryans buttons up Burrow who is less mobile/twitchy than Josh Allen. My Pick: Texans 23-17 Jacksonville Jaguars @ Denver Broncos — Sun., 4:05 p.m. ET Trevor Lawrence vs. Bo Nix. Jacksonville will have an extra day to prepare but they will also have to fly across the country. I like Denver at home in afternoon game. Justin Herbert only throwing for 209 yards was shocking to say the least. Could Jim Harbaugh’s seat be getting hot? My Pick: Cowboys 31-21 Seattle Seahawks @ Arizona Cardinals — Sun., 4:25 p.m. ET The Seahawks will roll with Drew Lock as Sam Darnold recovers from his hip injury. title: Brock Bowers, Darien Porter not practicing Wednesday
summary: While the team still has hope, the Las Vegas Raiders’ practice week began Wednesday without starting tight end Brock Bowers and conerback Darien Porter working on the practice field. full_text: (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images While the team still has hope, the Las Vegas Raiders’ practice week began Wednesday without starting tight end Brock Bowers and conerback Darien Porter working on the practice field. Before practice began, Las Vegas coach Klint Kubiak said neither Bowers nor Porter will practice. However, he said he is hopeful they could practice this week before Sunday’s game at the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday. Like he said Monday, Kubiak said both Bowers and Porter are “day-to-day.” Bowers missed a Week 1 victory over the Miami Dolphins because of a knee surgery he had last Tuesday. Porter left the Miami game late in the fourth quarter with a foot injury. Michael Mayer started for Bowers and rookie Zeke Masses played the final 10 plays of the game for Porter. Earlier Wednesday, ESPN reported the Raiders don’t considers Bowers’ injury overly serious and he could play this week, but the team won’t allow him back until he’s completely ready. The reported estimated Bowers will miss a total of three games at maximum, thus he would surely be back for Week 4’s home game against the Chiefs.

(Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images It didn’t take Kwity Paye long to make an impact with the Las Vegas Raiders. In his first game as a Raider, after signing a three-year, $48 million deal in free agency, Paye provided a major pass-rush burst. Paye had two of the Raiders’ five sacks also had six total tackles. He had a team high four quarterback hits. He and superstar Maxx Corsby showed the makings of a dynamic pass-rush tandem. Paye made his huge impact in a fairly limited role. He played in 57 percent of the snaps. So, he made a great impact base don how much he was on the field. Last season, with the Indianapolis Colts, Paye, who turns 28 in November, averaged playing 62 percent of the season. He had just four sacks. In his career, Paye, a first-round draft pick out of Michigan by the Colts in 2021, has averaged playing 64 percent of the snaps and he has 32.5 career sacks. So, he is off to a really strong start to his Raiders’ career.

title: Ashton Jeanty starts 2nd season in a big way
summary: Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2025 draft class fared in a 27-13 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 1 and what to look for Sunday at the Los Angeles Chargers: Ashton Jeanty: The No. 6 overall draft pick played 73 percent of the snaps in Week 1. He averaged […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2025 draft class fared in a 27-13 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 1 and what to look for Sunday at the Los Angeles Chargers: Ashton Jeanty: The No. 6 overall draft pick played 73 percent of the snaps in Week 1. He averaged 77 percent play time as a rookie. He made a big impact. He had 29 touches on 68 offensive plays and accounted for 147 of the Raiders’ 290 scrimmage yards. He is a focal point of the offense. Jack Bech: The second-round pick logged the third most snap totals of the Raiders’ receivers. He played 39 percent of the snaps in Week 1. He played more than seven times last season. Bech had three cathces for 23 yards and a touchdown against Miami. Like all of the Raiders’ receivers, Bech needs to find a way to produce more. Darien Porter: After beating rookies Jermod McCoy and Zeke Masses for the starting job, the third-round pick played every snap in Week 1 until he left with an injured foot. Caleb Rogers: The third-round pick didn’t play on offense after losing a camp battle to Jackson Powers-Johnson at right guard. Rogers did play six plays on special teams. Charles Grant: The offensive lineman, taken in the third round, also only played six snaps on special teams. Dont’e Thornton: The wide receiver, taken in the fourth round, will be on the injured reserve for, at least, three more weeks. Tonka Hemingway: The fourth-round pick played 57 percent of the defensive snaps, the most of any defensive tackle and he played 12 snaps on special teams. He had four tackles (three assisted) against the Dolphins. JJ Pegues: The defensive tackle, taken in the sixth round, was inactive in Week 1, a healthy scratch. He was active in nine of 17 games as a rookie. Cody Lindenberg: The seventh-round pick was also a healthy scratch in Week 1. It was a bit of a surprise. He was active every games and was a core special teamer as a rookie.

title: Las Vegas Raiders slide in some NFL Power Rankings despite win against Miami Dolphins
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders took care of business in Week 1, beating the Miami Dolphins 27-13. However, this was one of the few games the Raiders were expected to win heading into the season, so it’s no surprise that they didn’t climb up most NFL Power Rankings in the Week 2 roundup. That being said, […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders took care of business in Week 1 , beating the Miami Dolphins 27-13 . However, this was one of the few games the Raiders were expected to win heading into the season, so it’s no surprise that they didn’t climb up most NFL Power Rankings in the Week 2 roundup. That being said, a couple of outlets had Las Vegas falling despite the two-possession victory. Sports Illustrated 28. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 27 The Raiders beat the worst team in the NFL in the season opener. The good? We saw a revival from talent that was drafted highly in the 2025 draft and was all but abandoned by the previous regime. The bad news? They are getting a hella pissed off Chargers team coming off the most embarrassing loss of the inaugural weekend. — Conor Orr I’m having a hard time wrapping my head around how the Raiders fell in Orr’s rankings when the only explanation is centered around a game that hasn’t happened yet. Don’t get me wrong, beating the Dolphins isn’t a significant accomplishment. However, how are you saying that the talent the team drafted last year is finally starting to show through while suggesting the coaching staff has improved, and still have the team drop in the rankings? Las Vegas should at least stay the same, in my opinion. For reference, Orr had the Chargers dropping from 10 to 17 after losing to the Cardinals, who leapfrogged the Raiders (30 to 26). Arizona’s ascension is likely the reason for Vegas’ drop, but that’s not clear or stated in the analysis. ESPN 28. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 27 Non-QB newcomer debut: Edge Kwity Paye The Raiders have been searching for a secondary pass rusher to support All-Pro Maxx Crosby. Paye, who signed a three-year deal in free agency, showed Sunday that he could fill that role with two sacks, five pressures and five quarterback hits. Under first-time defensive coordinator Rob Leonard, the Raiders want to be aggressive and make life uncomfortable for opposing quarterbacks. If Paye continues to have performances similar to the one he had in Week 1, the outlook for Las Vegas could be a lot different this season. — Ryan McFadden Another drop for the Raiders! Apparently, the worst thing to happen to the Silver and Black in Week 1 was the Cardinals pulling off the biggest upset of the weekend! I do appreciate McFadden’s analysis, though. Paye did a pretty good job in the complementary role next to Crosby . The free-agent signing didn’t have many quick wins as a pass-rusher, but he did clean up a lot of plays, which is something the Raiders’ defense was missing last year. If that trend continues, I’m going to be pushing for Paye’s nickname to be ‘The Custodian’. NFL.com 29. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 29 The Raiders received the most favorable draw for Klint Kubiak’s head-coaching debut and handled business, overcoming two turnovers to build a two-score lead that was threatened but ultimately held through the final whistle. Most encouraging: Ashton Jeanty finally delivered a game that matched the expectations he brought with him from Boise State. — Nick Shook It’s funny, Shook has the Raiders ranked lower than anyone else here, but I can at least wrap my head around it since he didn’t have them falling. Granted, it’s not like he could have Vegas much lower. But at least he’s consistent, and fair is far. The Raiders didn’t exactly face the 1972 Dolphins on Sunday. And on the note about Jeanty, it’s amazing what can happen when he has a competent offensive line in front of him. Shoutout to Rick Dennison. The Athletic 27. Las Vegas Raiders Last week: 27 What we learned: This season may be different Trepidation is warranted after the Raiders won their opener last season, too, before finishing 3-14. But as our Sam Warren wrote, there are legitimate reasons to think this season could be different under Klint Kubiak. They pulled off the win without tight end Brock Bowers, who could return from injury for Week 2. — Chad Graff, Josh Kendall Warren’s article referenced above dives into how starting 1-0 this year feels different than last season, which ended up being a 3-14 campaign. The improved offensive line was a big reason for that, on top of the improved defense. For the latter, one of the biggest differences I noticed was that the Raiders were constantly pursuing the football, with several defenders around the ball carrier. Las Vegas still had some tackling issues, with Pro Football Focus having them on the hook for 10 misses as a team. However, that wasn’t nearly as impactful with defenders in position to clean up plays and have their teammates’ backs. To me, little things like that are a sign of a culture change, which bodes well for Kubiak and Rob Leonard as leaders. Bleacher Report 24. Las Vegas Raiders Last Week: 26 Fans shouldn’t overreact to a two-touchdown win over a Miami Dolphins team that has one of the NFL’s most underwhelming rosters, especially at home. However, the Las Vegas Raiders looked more like a cohesive team than they did at almost any point last season. It’s too early to declare Klink Kubiak as Las Vegas’ answer at head coach. However, his team was well-prepared for Week 1 and operated like a team that can probably pull off a few upsets in 2026. However, Kirk Cousins (2 INTs) will need to be more careful with the football to keep Las Vegas in the win column and to quiet calls for rookie Fernando Mendoza. — Kristopher Knox Knox kind of picked up where I left off in the section above, noting how the Raiders were more cohesive than last year’s team. That doesn’t say much, seeing as they were so bad in 2025, but it is a step in the right direction and worth celebrating. Also, Knox is on the mark with his analysis of Cousins. Three touchdowns are great, but 5.3 yards per attempt and more interceptions (two) than completions (one) when throwing 10 or more yards past the line of scrimmage isn’t a sustainable winning formula. The 38-year-0ld’s age and injury history are showing when he tries/has to push the ball down the field. He can get the benefit of the doubt without having Bowers out wide, but Cousins’ arm is something to monitor moving forward. Kirk Cousins' passing chart from @NextGenStats Passes 10+ down the field: 1/7, 21 yards, 2 INTs #Raiders pic.twitter.com/ScJOVPMCFl — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) September 14, 2026

title: Kwity Paye makes loud statement in Las Vegas Raiders debut against Miami Dolphins
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders’ defense was pretty dominant in the 27-13 Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins. The Raiders’ pass rush was especially impressive, sacking Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis five times and recording 27 pressures as a team, per Pro Football Focus. Maxx Crosby, Las Vegas’s well-known rusher, was his typical self with 1.5 […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ defense was pretty dominant in the 27-13 Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins . The Raiders’ pass rush was especially impressive, sacking Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis five times and recording 27 pressures as a team, per Pro Football Focus . Maxx Crosby, Las Vegas’s well-known rusher, was his typical self with 1.5 sacks and tying for the defense’s most pressures with eight. However, he wasn’t alone, as Kwity Paye was also impressive. The free-agent signing made his Raiders debut on Sunday and managed to tie for the team lead with six total tackles . Additionally, he led the Silver and Black with two sacks and four quarterback hits while matching Crosby with eight pressures, which is tied for the third-most across the NFL at the position (pre- Monday Night Football ). Here’s the kicker: Paye only had 24 pass-rush snaps, meaning he got pressure on a third of his opportunities. The former Indianapolis Colt didn’t get many opportunities to rack up a large volume of stats against the run with Vegas holding a lead for the majority of the contest. However, he was an efficient run defender, notching a pair of defensive stops on just six snaps against the run, per PFF . With all of this in mind, let’s flip on the tape and breakdown the performance. Well-timed blitz by Rob Leonard -Sends the boundary CB off the edge to influence the handoff vs. triple option -RB runs right into Kwity Paye as the unblocked defender for a TFL -Taron Johnson also gets in the backfield on the nickel blitz #Raiders pic.twitter.com/NpOqb8KxCc — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) September 14, 2026 One reason that Paye was so productive against the Dolphins is that defensive coordinator Rob Leonard called an excellent game. The Dolphins come out in 11 personnel but motion into a 21 personnel formation by motioning the tight end on the line of scrimmage and a wide receiver into the backfield as the H-back in the offset I-formation from the pistol. Miami’s goal is to keep the defense in nickel personnel by leaving three receivers on the field and shifting into a look that they can run a triple option out of. However, Las Vegas has the perfect counter. Whether it was called in the huddle or something the Raiders checked to pre-snap, Leonard has a well-timed blitz to defend the option. The boundary cornerback (Darien Porter) comes off the edge, which influences the quarterback to hand the ball off to the running back and immediately takes away two of the offense’s “options”: the quarterback and pitch man/wide receiver in the backfield. Meanwhile, Paye is supposed to be the defender the quarterback is reading, meaning he’s unblocked. He does a great job of recognizing the play design to avoid getting too far upfield and stays close to the line of scrimmage, squeezing inside on the heel line of the offensive line. That puts him in a perfect position to meet the running back in the backfield for a TFL, with some assistance from nickelback Taron Johnson, who blitzes off the other edge and beats the slot receiver’s block to get penetration. So, this is a scheme-assisted tackle for Paye with a great play call from Leonard. But the edge defender executes his assignment well to be in a perfect spot to make the play. Kwity Paye at 5-tech Nice job getting skinny to split the combo block and escape the G to get a clean-up tackle for a 1-yard gain #Raiders pic.twitter.com/s4zBPe803l — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) September 14, 2026 One way that Paye filled up the stat sheet on Sunday was by making several “clean-up” tackles, like the one above. Something he brings to the defensive line is alignment versatility. The Raiders match this two-tight end or double-wing-esque look (before the motion) from the Dolphins by putting Johnson in the box and getting into an odd front with off-ball linebacker Quay Walker on the edge. As a result, Paye slides inside a bit to play as a 5-technique defensive end rather than a standup outside linebacker or wide defensive end. That also means he’s going to take on a combo block from the left tackle and guard against Miami’s outside zone toss call. In other words, he’s being asked to execute an assignment that edge defenders don’t see much because they’re the end man on the line of scrimmage and won’t have to take on many combo blocks, at least not with two offensive linemen. So, Paye does give up some ground after initial contact. However, he does a good job of attacking the man he’s lined up across from (the left tackle) and then turning his shoulders when he starts to feel pressure from the guard to get skinny and split the offensive linemen. When the tackle works up to the second level, that’s where the versatile defensive lineman comes in, escaping from the guard and making the play for a one-yard gain after Jeremy Chinn misses. #Raiders used Kwity Paye as an interior pass rusher on a lot of 3rd downs vs. MIA Here's one of his best pass rushes, selling the vertical rush and using his quickness to win across the G's face #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/cLVToQFo2B — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) September 14, 2026 Along similar lines, the Raiders used Paye as an interior pass-rusher on a lot of third downs or obvious passing situations. That’s a good way to get him, Maxx Crosby and Malcolm Koonce on the field at the same time, like the play above. Additionally, it helps take advantage of Paye’s lateral movement skills and quickness by giving him matchups against guards. He lines up as a 5-technique again and pushes upfield with his first couple of steps to help sell the vertical rush. That combination gets the left guard to widen, and with the center working in the opposite direction/to Crosby’s side, there’s a big pass-rush lane in the weak-side A-gap. That’s where the five-year veteran’s quickness and lateral movement skills come into play, as he beats the guard across the guard’s face to get pressure. The one tweak that Paye can do here is finishing his pass-rush move with a chop or an arm over rather than a rip. The former would allow him to knock the guard’s inside hand/arm down and get a clean win to have a better chance at finishing with a sack. But regardless, he flushes the quarterback out of the pocket and forces the quarterback to scramble on third and long, leading to a punt. Simulated pressure from Rob Leonard leads to Kwity Paye rushing on the edge, where Paye gets push to collapse the pocket and help set up a Maxx Crosby sack #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/RqWQBPBGGu — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) September 14, 2026 This time, Leonard dials up a simulated pressure out of a double A-gap look, where Koonce and Walker drop into coverage while Paye, Nakobe Dean, Jonah Laulu and Crosby make up the four-man rush. Paye and Koonce are in the same alignments as the previous play; the latter is just in a two-point stance instead of having his hand in the ground this time. So, it’s a similar look for the offensive line. However, when Koonce drops into coverage, Paye works wide to end up rushing on the edge despite starting the rep as a 5-technique. That keeps the offensive line on their toes and gives them something to think about when those two defenders line up next to each other moving forward. Post-snap, Paye gets outside so that he can keep Willis (a running quarterback) in the pocket and rushes with power to be in a position to escape if the quarterback steps up or tries to scramble around the edge. It takes a second since he has to transition from inside to outside and then from upfield to into the quarterback, but Paye gets a nice surge to push through the right tackle’s inside shoulder and collapse the pocket. Then, when Willis tries to step up, he’s in position to slow Willis down and give Crosby enough time to finish with a sack. Here's the play: -3 DL away from Crosby influences C to open left -Dean on LOS keeps RG inside for Crosby 1-on-1 -Walker on a creaper blitz while Dean drops -Nose slants to…

title: Treydan Stukes makes presence felt in Week 1
summary: Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 27-13 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 1 and what to look for Sunday at the Los Angeles Chargers: Fernando Mendoza:The No. 1 overall pick served as Kirk […]
full_text: (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 27-13 win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 1 and what to look for Sunday at the Los Angeles Chargers: Fernando Mendoza: The No. 1 overall pick served as Kirk Cousins backup. he did not play. He was seen taking many notes on the sideline. Treydan Stukes: The Raiders’ second-round pick played all 56 defensive snaps at safety and he played 46 percent of the snaps on special teams. He delivered after earning the starting job over veteran Isaiah Pola-Mao in training camp after a slow start. He had six tackles and he had an interception. What a nice start to his career. Trey Zuhn: The third-round pick didn’t play on offensive, but the versatile offensive lineman did play on six special-teams plays. Jermod McCoy: The fourth-round pick was active, but did not play on defense or on special teams. The Raiders are easing him back from a 2024 knee injury. Mike Washington: The fourth-round pick had 41 rushing yards on seven carries, including a 18-yard run. He played on 13 offensive plays. Expect that number to grow depending on the game plan. Dalton Johnson: The fifth-round pick safety was a healthy scratch. Zeke Masses: The fifth-round pick came in late in the fourth quarter when starter Darien Porter left the game with a foot injury. He played the 10 final snaps of the game. He was tested on his first NFL play and broke up a pass. Malik Benson: The sixth-round pick played seven offensive snaps and two on special teams. title: Strategerie (maybe not a real word)
summary: I am so excited to be a small part of the Fins’ universe. I love reading the Phinsider columns with our great writers and the great comments from our readers(you all are strong!). Keep ‘em coming. Before I start the column proper, I am watching the Chiefs-Broncos butt-whipping, I mean game, and I just saw […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 13: Head Coach Jeff Hafley of the Miami Dolphins stands on the field after an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images I am so excited to be a small part of the Fins’ universe. I love reading the Phinsider columns with our great writers and the great comments from our readers(you all are strong!). Keep ‘em coming. Before I start the column proper, I am watching the Chiefs-Broncos butt-whipping, I mean game, and I just saw Jaylen Waddle drop a perfectly thrown pass from Bo Nix. It had a bit of Grey Poupon on it but it should have been caught. I think we will make out good on that trade. I just read Chris-Early’s column. Wow! That “Wow!” wasn’t just an ordinary “Wow”, it was a “Wow!” with a factorial “!” behind it. In mathematics, a Wow! (factorial) is far superior to an ordinary “Wow.” I get fired up when people put out strong opinions! The Chiefs are pulling out a page from Dennis Erickson’s UM versatile offensive playbook. I went to Auburn, FAU and UCLA but I do root for the Canes. Back in 1992, FSU came into the Orange Bowl to take on the high-flying high-octane passing attack Hurricanes. FSU expected UM to throw the ball a million times but Dennis Erickson saw some weaknesses in FSU’s run defense and ran the ball for 222 yards and ultimately won on the “Wide Right” kick. This change of pace is something that the Dolphins should aspire to but we are not there yet. Does Hafley and company have the “strategerie” to try things like this down the road? I say that because I didn’t see much “strategerie” on Sunday. Say what you want but Coach Hafley seemed like he threw the Dolphins into an underwater maze and left them to their own devices. I didn’t see any obvious coaching changes e.g. all out blitzes, max protect, reverses, counters, sixth offense lineman etc etc etc. I am not gonna harp on that because I saw Andy Reid let Mahomes get killed in two Super Bowls because the Chiefs didn’t have the foresight to have serviceable tackles. I thought Andy Reid would have ran double-tight end or use a sixth blocker (even Mike McDaniel figured that out). Something. Anything to change the momentum of those two Super Bowls. I watched Coach Shula and Tom Olivadotti not figure out to switch defensive fronts and let Tim Tyndale rush for 498 yards (almost) in Shula’s last game ever. Thank God the moronic Bills lost the next week to Pittsburgh! So Hafley was content to not make any noticeable changes or if he did, nothing happened. Mike McDaniel could have done that too. Where is Hafley’s mark as a coach? The fans need to see something positive, something to build on. Even in Shula’s down years, he would pull out one unexpected victory. Repeating myself a bit; I didn’t see anything special from the coaching staff. Speaking of special, there was very little in the special teams. Pathetic is a better word. Is this the coaching upgrade that we were promised? What possible excuse do you use for not being able to stop long kickoff returns? Twice? The camera showed some bewildered coach, acting bewildered. Twice. The bad second coverage was virtually an instant replay of the first bad coverage. I am unsure if he is the special teams’ coach but I already had Keith Armstrong flashbacks. How do we not get special teams right? Special teams (outside of finding a reliable kicker and punter) should be the EASIEST thing to fix. This is how John Harbaugh made his bones. This special team issue is a symptom of something wrong. Maybe I will have to eat some crow? Glad to do it. I am an experienced crow eater!
