full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the Giants get set to take a Los Angeles Rams coming off a tough loss in Australia to open the season. John Harbaugh’s next impact: Staying on Giants’ mistakes to beat Rams | New York Daily News “We understand that how you play this week is not gonna be good enough to win next week,” Harbaugh said Monday afternoon. “How we played [Sunday] night will not win the game next Monday night. It won’t be good enough. So we’ve got to improve.” “We’re putting the ball on the ground entirely too much,” Harbaugh said on Zoom. “It’s gotta change. We’ve gotta make the change on that. Every single ball carrier has got to make sure that it gets better. Sometimes as coaches we gotta drill it, we gotta teach it and we gotta make sure that we do it better. Because the ball was on the ground four times. That’s not even close to being acceptable as an example.” Ricard on the team staying away from distractions Pat Ricard has been impressed with the dedication of his Giants teammates and the organization as a whole: "NYC is right across the river, and guys would rather be in the locker room hanging out two hours after the game" pic.twitter.com/1HZtYXo5i7 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 15, 2026 John Harbaugh effect: Five reasons Giants are different under Super Bowl winning coach | CBSSports.com 5. Harbaugh is rebuilding a broken culture. Coaching turnover and eight losing seasons over the last decade turned a proud franchise into a perennial bottom-dweller in the NFC East. That is a tough hole to climb out of. Reversing the year-in and year-out disappointment requires a strong culture, and Harbaugh is renowned for his ability to create one. It is already taking effect in New York. Harbaugh’s CEO approach, where he also reports directly to team ownership rather than general manager Joe Schoen, seems to be widely accepted in New York. And it might just lead the Giants back to the promised land. 2026 NFL season, Week 1: What We Learned from Sunday’s games | NFL.com What a way to kick off the Harbaugh era. Jaxson Dart was back, so too were Malik Nabers and Cam Skattebo, each of them making contributions to knock off the rival Cowboys in head coach John Harbaugh’s Gotham debut. Facing a franchise that popularized the triplets term, the Giants’ young franchise trio of Dart, Nabers and Skattebo proved to be the offensive catalyst. This was the start Harbaugh and the franchise needed and wanted. Their young guns were firing against a hated adversary. This wasn’t a pretty game. Too many penalties, too many fumbles, some drops. But for Harbaugh and New York, it was a beautiful result for the franchise’s new dawn. Why Malik Nabers’ mom wasn’t at Giants game for WR’s return: ‘He had to do this by himself’ | The Athletic “This game, Malik had to do this by himself,” Tonya told The Athletic on Monday. “He needed to go out there with no pressure from anybody and just perform… It worked out perfectly because if I had been there, I wouldn’t have been able to hide my emotion or my fear. He would have been able to sense that I was nervous or my anxiety was high, and I think I would have made him uneasy. So God’s timing is the best timing. And so this journey he needed to take by himself.” “We knew that it was his moment,” Tonya said. “For him to go out there, for him to decide that, ‘I’m ready,’ it took for him to trust this entire process. Trust the surgeon. Trust the surgery. Trust his workout and his recovery. He had to trust this entire journey for him to step out on that field and know that he was ready to play.” Presence and perspective for Malik Nabers in rousing NY Giants return | The Record Jaxson Dart took the last of three kneel-downs in victory formation, officially closing out Sunday night’s 28-20 triumph over the Dallas Cowboys, and he immediately knew where he was going with the football. Because the quarterback of the New York Giants knew what this meant to Malik Nabers, and Dart knows what Nabers means to him and this franchise, not just in this game, but going forward. Should Giants trade for Joey Porter Jr. with newfound cap space? | New York Post The ink barely dried on safety Jevon Holland’s restructured contract Monday before fan-driven speculation began that the Giants could use their additional $5.8 million in salary-cap savings to trade for Joey Porter Jr. The irony is that the Giants once were “splitting hairs” while trying to place cornerbacks Deonte Banks and Porter on the draft board as late first-round picks in 2023, league sources told The Post. New Giants part-owner details her role with power transfer ‘done’ after Steve Tisch controversy | New York Post Carolyn Tisch Blodgett said the transfer of ownership shares from her uncle Steve Tisch and his siblings Laurie and Jonathan into a trust for their children is “done.” Tisch Blodgett, already the owner of Gotham FC, called the move a “natural next step” for her while speaking onstage at the Front Office Sports Asset Class event in New York as she has been involved with the team for “a number of years in international expansion, in fan development, in the in-game.” “I’m just really trying to get there every day, to be honest, right now,” she said. “I’m not really focused on the future. I just continue to think about how I can contribute to the team every day. And, you know, I think there’s so much work to be done when you think about what it means to bring in a new coach and bring in a new culture, the same can happen on the business side as well. And so I am spending a lot of time thinking about, with a winning product on the field, what does success look like from a business perspective?… What are we doing in flag football? title: Survey: What surprised you in the Giants’ win over Dallas?
summary: Most New York Giants fans picked their team to win against the Dallas Cowboys, but few outside of the Giants’ fandom actually expected the G-Men to come away with the victory. In fact, I suspect that most Giants’ fans hoped for a win, but were prepared for a hard-fought loss. Few were really expecting the […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart runs with the ball against the Dallas Cowboys. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Most New York Giants fans picked their team to win against the Dallas Cowboys, but few outside of the Giants’ fandom actually expected the G-Men to come away with the victory. In fact, I suspect that most Giants’ fans hoped for a win, but were prepared for a hard-fought loss. Few were really expecting the Giants to come out and simply out-play the Cowboys from whistle to whistle. And so that brings us to this week’s question: What surprised you the most in the Giants’ win over the Cowboys? A) Jaxson Dart’s precision as a passer? He was downright surgical in picking apart Christian Parker’s defense, playing on time and in rhythm. Dart was fun as a rookie, but he needed to do a lot of work on playing within the structure of the offense. Against Dallas, Dart had great footwork, was seeing the defense well, marrying his eyes and feet to the tempo of the route concepts, and delivering the ball with great placement. His improved footwork also elevated his arm as he was routinely driving the ball outside the numbers as well as layering it with great touch. B) How well the Nagy-Callahan-Roman offense worked? John Harbaugh’s decision to hire these three men was looked at with derision and confusion from the media at large as well as the Giants’ own fanbase. We had no clue what the offense would look like, or how well it could function. We didn’t know if the three would reinforce each other’s weaknesses or if it would blow up in the Giants’ faces. As it turns out, the play-calling was generally excellent and the Giants used a variety of looks, alignments, and play designs that let them do what they wanted against the Cowboys. C) The run defense holding Dallas to 69 yards rushing. Most fans — and much of the media — were somewhere between “anxious” and “panicking” over the state of the Giants’ run defense after the preseason. It was widely predicted that the Giants would get runover by Dallas’ offense and that they’d be gashed on the ground. Instead, the Giants’ new-look defense held up against the Cowboys’ rushing attack and limited them to just 69 yards on the ground and held Javonte Williams to 3.4 yards per carry. D) Holding CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens to 72 total yards. Like the run defense, many fans and writers were worried (to say the least) about the Giants’ secondary. This was about as tough a test as you could imagine (short of Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins) to start the season for two new starting corners in a new defensive scheme. There were predictions that both would eclipse 100 yards receiving, but instead they fell short combined. The Giants weren’t able to take them out of the game completely, but they contained Lamb and Perkins and prevented Dak Prescott from generating the explosive plays upon which the Dallas offense thrives. Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Giants fans and fans across the country. What was the best surprise from Week 1? Are you feeling confident in the Giants? Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys:

title: Former NY Giants WR Sterling Shepard signs with Jets’ practice squad
summary: Former New York Giants wide receiver Sterling Shepard is returning to The Big Apple and is signing with the New York Jets practice squad, per a report from Mike Garafolo. Shepard joins the Jets as reinforcements with rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. considered “week to week” after suffering an ankle injury. The Giants drafted […]
full_text: Former New York Giants wide receiver Sterling Shepard | Getty Images Former New York Giants wide receiver Sterling Shepard is returning to The Big Apple and is signing with the New York Jets practice squad, per a report from Mike Garafolo . Shepard joins the Jets as reinforcements with rookie wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. considered “week to week” after suffering an ankle injury. The Giants drafted Shepard out of Oklahoma in the second round of the 2016 NFL Draft with the 40th overall pick. He was immediately productive upon being drafted, catching 65 passes for 683 yards and 8 touchdowns as a rookie. He formed a dynamic duo with Odell Beckham Jr. and provided both toughness and reliability for over the middle for Eli Manning in the twilight of his career. Shepard’s best season as a Giant came in Eli’s last full season as a starter, when he started all 16 games, racking up a career-high 872 yards on 66 catches. Unfortunately, Shepard struggled with injury after that year. Over the next several years he would suffer multiple concussions, several hamstring injuries, a ruptured Achilles, and a torn ACL. Shepard joined the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in 2024 and played in 24 games for the Buccaneers between 2024 and 2025. He was briefly with the Houston Texans this summer, but was released in their final cuts.

title: Rams’ QB Matthew Stafford: NY Giants are a ‘dangerous’ team
summary: The New York Giants got the NFL’s attention with their well-deserved 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. Matthew Stafford, quarterback of the Los Angeles Rams — who face the Giants on Monday Night Football in Week 2 — was among those who noticed what the Giants did to the Cowboys. On “Let’s Go”, […]
full_text: Matthew Stafford | Getty Images The New York Giants got the NFL’s attention with their well-deserved 28-20 victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. Matthew Stafford, quarterback of the Los Angeles Rams — who face the Giants on Monday Night Football in Week 2 — was among those who noticed what the Giants did to the Cowboys. On “Let’s Go”, a SiriusXM NFL Radio show he co-hosts with Jim Gray, Stafford called the Giants a “dangerous” team. “I watched the game,” Stafford said of Giants-Cowboys. “My brother-in-law [Chad Hall] is the receiver coach for the Giants, so I’m always pulling for him and pulling for those guys, except for this week when we play them coming up. But I saw a young team with a bunch of talent. “When you look at the defensive side of the ball, a bunch of pass rushers, I thought they did a really nice job in the pass game against the Dallas Cowboys who have as much talent as anybody in the pass game. I think Dak’s played at a high level for a long time now and with CeeDee [Lamb] and Pick [George Pickens] and all those guys, they’re really talented on the outside. So for them to get that win, 28-20, was a big start for their season.” Stafford noted the timing of the game. “Obviously, the young quarterback, Jaxson Dart, I thought played really well, played within himself, made some plays with his feet,” Stafford said. “They’re a dangerous team. I think every team in the NFL, it’s what people out there forget, year in and year out going through training camps and watching preseason, think they can pick who’s gonna win every game. And that’s why we play them. You put the ball down, you go play the games. And I thought the Giants did a heck of a job the other night. I thought it was cool on the weekend of September 11th, 25 years later, for the Giants in New York City to get a win, felt right and felt great to have the NFL have something like that happen and those guys play well.” The Rams, of course, are 0-1 after losing to the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. “It was tough. Obviously had a long journey and didn’t play the way that we wanted to play,” Stafford said. “There were some swing plays in that game where obviously the score was what it was at the end of the game and we thought we had some chances to make it a little bit closer. But didn’t happen. Always difficult to start the season that way, but learned from it, got an extra couple days of rest on the way back and coming into a Monday Night game. So [we’ll] figure out what we can do better, how we can go out there and execute at a higher clip and give ourselves a better chance to win a game.” The Rams are currently 7.5-point favorites, per FanDuel Sportsbook .

title: NY Giants rookies impress against the Cowboys in Week 1
summary: The New York Giants are riding high after a great win over the Dallas Cowboys to open the season on Sunday Night Football. The win over the Cowboys was just about everything the Giants could have asked for. It was a definitive statement win over a division rival that had been relentlessly gassed up over […]
full_text: New York Giants linebacker Arvell Reese before a play against the Dallas Cowboys. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants are riding high after a great win over the Dallas Cowboys to open the season on Sunday Night Football. The win over the Cowboys was just about everything the Giants could have asked for. It was a definitive statement win over a division rival that had been relentlessly gassed up over the previous four months. At the same time, the Giants weren’t perfect and have plenty to work on as they get ready for the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football. Perhaps best of all, the Giants’ young players all stepped up in the win. The Giants are depending heavily on first and second year players to form the core of their team, the Giants’ rookie class certainly looked like they belonged on the field next to their veteran teammates. Let’s take a look at each of the Giants’ rookies who contributed to the win. Arvell Reese The fifth overall pick was on the field for 62 total plays, including 11 penalties, two Cowboys’ kickoffs, and the Giants’ lone punt. Reese was, overall, as advertised. He’s a big, long, and highly athletic linebacker who looked the part surrounded by the Giants’ other big, long, and athletic linebackers. He also showed off his football IQ all game long. Reese is a highly active communicator in the pre-snap phase, and he also appears to process quickly after the ball is snapped. He wastes little time getting to his landmarks, picking up pass catchers in coverage, or coming downhill to play the run. He also clearly understands where his gap responsibilities are, as well as where the defense is trying to funnel the ball. Reese looks smooth and rangy dropping into coverage at the second level, easily getting depth and into his coverage zones. He also did a good job of using his hands to keep blockers from latching on to him and allowing him to navigate traffic in pursuit. We also got to see Reese’s strength and violence as a tackler when the time came to get the ball carrier on the ground. Reese wasn’t quite as flashy as former teammates Sonny Styles and Caleb Downs, but he did finish second to Tremaine Edmunds in total tackles. I’d like to see more splash plays from Reese, and I think we will as the season progresses, but this was an impressive introduction for the linebacker. SiSi Mauigoa is a difference making guard. Watch this raw power on the move once he torques; he tosses Ogbonnia to the deck, allowing Tracy Jr. to cut behind for an extra few yards. pic.twitter.com/3mewi9nYQ4 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 Sisi Mauigoa The big man had a long night, but it was also about as good a debut as you could ask for from the 10th overall pick. Mauigoa was on the field for 78 total snaps, including each of Dominic Zvada’s extra points and eight penalties. I won’t go quite so far as to say that Mauigoa was dominant in his debut, but he was very good in both pass protection and as a run blocker. We knew that Mauigoa is an obviously powerful young man who could distort the line of scrimmage and dig defenders out of gaps in the run game. We also knew that, as a converted tackle, he has great athletic traits for a guard. We got to see both aspects of his game on display against the Cowboys. Mauigoa was easily able to move laterally to mirror interior rushers, get in position to help with center-guard and guard-tackle double teams, and execute both slide protections and outside zone runs. Mauigoa’s power was featured in the downhill run game as well as when he was asked to match up with the likes of Kenny Clark one-on-one. Sisi might not have dominated his opponents, but the right side was rarely a concern for the offense. That’s about as good a thing as you can say for a rookie guard in his first start. #Giants rookie G Francis Mauigoa in his NFL debut: • 36 pass-blocking snaps • 0 pressures allowed • 0 QB hits He's the first rookie since 2018 to record 35+ pass-blocking snaps in Week 1 without allowing a pressure. (via @NextGenStats ) https://t.co/9XK0FvQyFn pic.twitter.com/ecOvTFs5GE — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 14, 2026 Colton Hood Hood didn’t get much work against the Cowboys. The Giants only had their second round pick on the field for 18 plays on Sunday night, the first 11 of which came on special teams. He was a fixture on both the Giants’ kick coverage teams and punt return teams. He did get six snaps on defense, playing when Greg Newsome II or Deonte Banks were off the field. That’s a very small sample size and the Cowboys only targeted Hood twice (one reception). He was generally in good position and was sticky in coverage on his man, including against George Pickens. That said, it’s also appeared as though the game was a bit fast on the reception he gave up. He was too off-balance to make the tackle after the catch on the come-back route, allowing YAC up the sideline. Malachi Fields Fields didn’t get much work as a pass catcher for the Giants. He was targeted four times, catching two passes for a 25 yards, 19 of which came on one catch. Fields was able to get behind the Dallas defense on one of his targets, but Dart overthrew him. It could have been a huge play, but it wasn’t to be. Fields had much more of an impact as a blocker in the run game for the Giants. Greg Roman’s blocking schemes weren’t shy about using condensed sets and using Fields as a blocker on the play side. On some of the plays, they seemed to view him as an extra tight end, and he held up well as such. For instance, the Giants used an uncommon 20-personnel set (two backs, no tight ends) on their second offensive play of the game. It was a curious look that had wide receiver Braxton Berrios line up in the backfield with Devin Singletary while fullback Patrick Ricard line up at tight end next to Andrew Thomas. The Giants asked Fields to release to the second level and pick up linebacker Dee Winters, and he simply took Winters out of the play. ( Fields is the wide receiver on the offensive left wearing red gloves .) The Giants also made use of Fields’ frame as a downfield obstacle, using his routes to help create space for his teammates in various passing concepts. Dominic Zvada Perhaps the best compliment I can give Zvada is that I forgot he was a rookie — as well as long snapper Ben Mann. The special teams operation was as clean as I’ve seen in some time. The Giants didn’t have to ask Zvada to show off his leg strength, but there was never a doubt about his ability to hit extra points. I was particularly impressed by how he handled kickoffs. Zvada was able to consistently drop the ball inside of the Dallas 5-yard line, three times forcing KaVonte Turpin to field the ball from the 1-yard line (2.2-yard line on average). The Giants limited Turpin, one of the NFL’s most dangerous kickoff returners, to 24.4 yards per return and their average starting field position was the 26.4-yard line. Zvada’s accuracy and ability to get distance and hangtime on his kickoffs certainly helped the Giants’ coverage team, while neutralizing Turpin helped create hidden yardage for the defense. Great start for the UDFA rookie.
author: Chris Pflum

title: Tales from the Timeline: NY Giants dominate the Cowboys
summary: The New York Giants opened their 2026 season with a 28-20 upset victory over the Dallas Cowboys. New York’s offense dictated the terms against Dallas’ defense, while Christian Parker’s revamped defensive unit struggled to find answers for Matt Nagy’s scheme. The Giants outgained Dallas by 150 yards and held a commanding 13:20 advantage in time […]
full_text: The New York Giants opened their 2026 season with a 28-20 upset victory over the Dallas Cowboys. New York’s offense dictated the terms against Dallas’ defense, while Christian Parker’s revamped defensive unit struggled to find answers for Matt Nagy’s scheme. The Giants outgained Dallas by 150 yards and held a commanding 13:20 advantage in time of possession. The tape was one of the more enjoyable evaluations I’ve studied. From a philosophical standpoint, little of it was surprising — we knew the Giants wanted to play with heavy personnel and operate more under center. What exceeded my expectations, however, was the degree to which New York successfully established the run, while maintaining efficiency and effectiveness through the air. The Giants consistently created favorable offensive situations, which is one reason why they had four touchdown drives and four drives of 10-plus plays. Dart finished 9 of 11 on third down, and these charts illustrate just how well he performed on Sunday Night Football: Jaxson Dart Final Stats 23/29 (79%) 230 passing yards (7.9 ypa) 10 rushes | 54 rushing yards 3 TDs | 2 sacks | 1 fumble +0.73 EPA/play (98th %ile) 74% success rate (29/39) +10.9% CPOE 8.6 aDOT pic.twitter.com/I39ihnichM — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 Jaxson Dart with the best QB performance in Week 1. • EPA/Play: +0.73 (1st) • WPA/Play: +2.2% (1st) Every 5 plays, Dart added 3.5 expected points and 11% win probability for the Giants. pic.twitter.com/01OTeikQyu — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 It was an elite performance by Dart, who found solutions early in the game, including on this third-and-4 below: Great job by Jaxson Dart to throw away from defensive leverage on the mesh that opened up Isaiah Likely on third-and-four. Dart was DIALED in and poised throughout the game, as the #Giants offensively dictated to Dallas all night. pic.twitter.com/lWb6caT47j — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 I love how Dart threw away from the defender’s position, allowing Isaiah Likely (9) to catch the football and nearly spin away from the tackle and into the end zone. It’s a mesh concept with Odell Beckham Jr. (13) running the MUSH ( man under ) and Likely running the MOSH ( man over ); Devin Singletary (26) was released to the boundary, which created space in the middle of the field. Dallas had several coverage assignments that were blown throughout the game. There was a miscommunication above, as Dallas’ zone defender attempted to push Likely to a defensive player that I’m not convinced was present. Hooker (24) was too patient to close width on Likely, who surrendered the catch, but Singletary’s flare and Beckham’s drag route also removed two defenders from the area. Dart was elite, too, in the two minute drill: Jaxson Dart finished the first half in an excellent fashion after the Holland INT. Dart went 4/4 with this third down conversation, as well as the touchdown to Likely off the blown Dallas' coverage. pic.twitter.com/xIaKXPZAfX — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 Dart made several high-level throws throughout the game, but the story of the offense was still the Giants’ rushing attack. title: NY Giants QB Jaxson Dart was dialed in against the Cowboys
summary: The New York Giants punched the Dallas Cowboys in the mouth en route to a 28-20 Week 1 victory. A smash-mouth, varied rushing attack set the tone for New York, featuring heavy formations and plenty of under-center looks. But the efficient play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart was the catalyst behind the Giants’ rare victory […]
full_text: The New York Giants punched the Dallas Cowboys in the mouth en route to a 28-20 Week 1 victory. A smash-mouth, varied rushing attack set the tone for New York, featuring heavy formations and plenty of under-center looks. But the efficient play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart was the catalyst behind the Giants’ rare victory over Dallas. Dart finished 23 of 29 ( 79% completion rate ) for 230 passing yards and three passing touchdowns, with 54 yards rushingon 11 carries. New York finished 9/11 on third down, and Dart found answers to Christian Parker’s defense, which, in fairness, had several breakdowns in coverage/assingments. Not only did Dart pass the eye-test, but the numbers back his performance up as well: Jaxson Dart with the best QB performance in Week 1. • EPA/Play: +0.73 (1st) • WPA/Play: +2.2% (1st) Every 5 plays, Dart added 3.5 expected points and 11% win probability for the Giants. pic.twitter.com/01OTeikQyu — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) September 14, 2026 Courtesy of Doug Analytics, Dart’s +0.73 EPA/Play ( Expected Points Added ) ranked first, as well as his WPA/Play ( Win Probability Added ). As Doug states, Dart added 3.5 expected points on every five plays the Giants took — an elite performance by the second-year signal caller. Here’s what NFL Next Gen had to say about Dart’s performance, along with his throwing chart: The Giants punted the football one time against Dallas, and they mounted four touchdown drives, as well as four drives of 10-plus plays. Dart wasn’t exactly slinging the ball all over the yard — he didn’t have to — but he led the offense, made the right checks, was in command for much of the game ( he didn’t account for Caleb Downs on the EMPTY blitz ), and made some high-level throws that allowed the Giants to maintain their time-consuming drives. High-level throws via GIPHY The Giants faced this third-and-4 in the red zone. Stalling out and kicking a field goal was the normal outcome in these situations — last time the Giants opened against Dallas, it was a blocked field goal that Andrew Thomas hurt his hamstring on — but I digress. The Giants align in 11 personnel, shot-gun, 3×1 set with a mesh concept over the middle of the field. Dallas ran a cover-four-match play and Isaiah Likely (9) ran the MOSH ( man over ) Odell Beckham Jr.’s (13) MUSH ( man under ). Daron Bland (26) seemed to be in MEG on the backside No. 1 ( Beckham ), and as the veteran receiver ran the MUSH, linebacker Dee Winters (53) pushed the MOSH ( Likely ) toward Bland and safety Malik Hooker (24). Likely sat inside of Hooker, who was late to receive the push, and Dart did a fantastic job putting the football toward Likely’s inside shoulder — away from Hooker. The middle of the field was cleared out by the drag route from Beckham. I appreciate how the mesh concept was Dart’s second read after he saw match principles when viewing his first read toward Malachi Fields (88) and Darnell Mooney (17). The latter was the No. 2 receiver ( innermost ), and he ran to the flat with Fields running a corner off his vertical stem. With the safety over top, Dallas matched three over two, and Dart came off the look and saw the vacated space in the middle of the field and Hooker’s depth. Precise ball placement and a calm read by Dart led to another third-down conversion on the Giants’ first drive. via GIPHY Up 7-0, just outside mid-field, Dart quickly processed the zone coverage and found Malik Nabers for 7 yards on second-and-9. Nabers ran the hook, and Fields ran the wheel as the No. 2 receiver. Dart had to wait for the curl/flat to expand with Cam Skattebo’s (44) flare route. This put the Giants into a third-and-2 that they failed to convert, which led to their only punt of the game. There was plenty of discussion about Dart’s ability to operate quick game concepts efficiently throughout the off-season; sure, this was from the shotgun, and perhaps not perfect, but it did give New York the opportunity to convert on the following play. via GIPHY Jaxson Dart was such a cool customer on 3rd downs. Giants were faced with 3rd&10 here on their second TD drive. A blown pass protection assignment leads to an immediately free A gap pressure. Dart stands tall in the pocket and delivers a seed on the money outside the numbers 👀 pic.twitter.com/Ej4bQjRctC — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) September 14, 2026 Dart extended a drive with this 19yard throw to Likely. Dallas was in Cover-1 and the Giants ran a DAGGER concept to the field. Dart quickly diagnosed man-coverage and attacked the corner route to Likely on the backside. Shavon Revel (28) faced the unfortunate task of guard Likely in space; the tight end manipulated Revel and exploded outside for the first down. Dart was phenomenal under pressure on the play, as the Giants’ offensive line had a rare mishap. Unfortunately, Tyrone Tracy Jr. would fumble plays later. Two-minute drill Dart executed an impressive two-minute drill after Jevon Holland’s interception. Jon Runyan committed a false-start, which put the Giants into this third-and-9: via GIPHY via GIPHY Dart successfully diagnosed the defense during his shotgun drop, prompting him to switch to the backside one (Nabers) and target vulnerabilities in the now-recognized Cover-2 defense. Dart put touch over the top of the flat defender and in front of the bailing-deep- half player. He was mentally and physically dialed in on this play when the lights were brightest in a crucial two-minute drill. He followed this third-and-9 conversion with this far-hash completion to Darnell Mooney (17): via GIPHY Dallas aligned in a Cover-3 strong-side buzz over Likely’s position against a 2×2 set. The deep third defender to the field lost leverage inside to Darnell Mooney’s vertical stem; Mooney exploded toward the sideline when the defender was on the numbers and the curl/flat was enticed to step forward due to the presence of Devin Singletary (26) in the flat. Dart planted and drove the football into Mooney; credit to Mooney for being a professional wide receiver and having soft hands and feet that are spatially aware. Isaiah Likely was 8.8 yards away from the nearest defender when the ball arrived on this touchdown 🫣 DALvsNYG on NBC/Peacock Stream on #NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/rIenIu8EGo — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) September 14, 2026 Dart finished the two-minute drill by finding a wide-open Isaiah Likely in the back of the end zone. The Cowboys had a blown coverage and Dart quickly recognized that two defenders reacted to Mooney’s whip route underneath. The No. 2 receiver on the previous play was Likely, who caught a whip route underneath. Second half via GIPHY via GIPHY The Giants opened the second half with a 12-play, 74-yard drive. On second-and-9, they picked up 16 yards on a catch that was heavily aided by play action. New York had already established the run, and Dallas failed to adjust, allowing the under-center play-action look to pull the linebackers toward the line of scrimmage. That created space for Dart to layer a touch pass over the top to Malik Nabers. And then there was the Devin Singletary sequence: The Singletary sequence wouldn't have happened on previous #Giants teams. However, a blown screen is all too familiar. JMS misses his block, but space was there. Nagy attacked soft leverage w/ Nabers on the next play and then used the attention paid to Nabers to find Singletary… pic.twitter.com/8kjTSBCQb3 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) September 14, 2026 The Giants’ coaching staff, Dart, and the entire Giants team just kept exploiting the vulnerable flats, while Dallas stayed at depth and kept multiple pairs of eyes on Nabers. Dart’s rushing Dart rushed for 54 yards on 11 carries. Dart showed vision that was coupled with timely play calls and designs from the Giants’ coaching staff. Dart on the move!!! 💨 📺: NBC pic.twitter.com/6DwDC4ZUdk — New York Giants (@Giants) September 14, 2026 via GIPHY Final thoughts Dart shined in the bright lights and is now technically 2-0 against…

title: New York Jets: Contextualizing Week 1
summary: It’s been an interesting few days. The Jets won their first game of the season on Sunday, and they did so in dominating fashion. Fast forward a few days and rightfully Jets fans don’t know what to do with themselves. This past Sunday marked only the second time the Jets have won their first game […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - AUGUST 14: Breece Hall #20 of the New York Jets runs during the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on August 14, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (3Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It’s been an interesting few days. The Jets won their first game of the season on Sunday, and they did so in dominating fashion. Fast forward a few days and rightfully Jets fans don’t know what to do with themselves. This past Sunday marked only the second time the Jets have won their first game of the season in the last eight years. And the other time they won Week 1, Jets fans could barely enjoy it. That was the game where Aaron Rodgers tore his Achilles, and the fanbase was left watching in horror as he struggled to stand on the field. So even when the Jets won Week 1, there was an impending sense of dread that the season was already lost. For all intents and purposes, this was the first time in eight years I can confidently say that the Jets won their season opener and it actually felt like a win. And I can’t help but notice that a sizable portion of the Jets fanbase legitimately has no idea how to process this. The other day, on my way to work, I literally heard two Jets fans talking. One of them said, “I forgot what this feels like.” That pretty much sums it up. On one hand, you have a bunch of Jets fans who are overtly optimistic and excited. They are looking at what happened Sunday and thinking, maybe this team is actually good. Maybe this season could be different. On the other hand, you have another sizable portion of the fanbase that seems almost incapable of enjoying it. They’re waiting for the other shoe to drop. They’re prepared for disappointment because, quite frankly, that is what being a Jets fan has taught them to do. Not to get overtly psychological here, but I think there are actually two contrasting things happening. The first is cherophobia. Cherophobia is a psychological term used to describe an irrational fear of feeling happy or hopeful. One of the reasons people experience it is because of past negative experiences or trauma. As Jets fans, we know all about that. When you’ve spent years watching promising seasons fall apart, convincing yourself that things might finally be different only to have the team rip your heart out, eventually you start protecting yourself from the possibility of disappointment. And honestly, I understand it. But then there’s another psychological concept that I think is influencing the other side of the fanbase: the anchoring effect. The anchoring effect is a cognitive bias where people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they receive when making subsequent judgments or estimates. When it comes to estimating the Jets’ chances for the rest of the season, the only regular-season evidence we have right now is overwhelmingly positive. The Jets didn’t just win. They dominated. So naturally, that first piece of evidence becomes the anchor. Fans immediately start reaching for the most positive interpretation of what they just saw. If this is what the Jets look like, then maybe they can do this. Maybe they can do that. Maybe this team is actually capable of making a run. Where does this leave us this week? You have one group of Jets fans whose past experiences are telling them, “Don’t get too happy. You know how this ends.” And you have another group whose immediate experience is telling them, “Why shouldn’t we be excited? Look at what just happened.” Both reactions make sense. The problem, of course, is that neither one of those reactions necessarily tells us what the Jets actually are. It’s been one game. That doesn’t mean we should dismiss what happened Sunday. It also doesn’t mean we should extrapolate the entire season from it. I’m going to do my best to contextualize below what we just saw Sunday. What I think is realistic to get excited about and what isn’t. What Week 1 can tell us about a team and what it normally cannot. Here’s some things we do know: Week 1 Is Not Fundamentally Different Than Any Other Week This is something that I’ve heard a lot over the years. That Week 1 is particularly noisy and should be ignored more than other weeks. However, this isn’t really true when you look at the data. In other words, Week 1 doesn’t contain any less predictive value than using Week 2, Week 3, Week 6, Week 7, etc. The sample is obviously still small, but there isn’t something inherently different about the first game of the season that makes it uniquely unreliable. For starters, I want to preface this by saying that in any situation, looking at a one-week sample can lead to false conclusions. It’s a small sample. Former PFF data scientist Timo Riske outlines this in the thread below, which helps explain why Week 1 has probably developed a reputation for being more “fake” than any other week: With week 1 over, here is one thing I'd like to clarify: Looking at some basic team stats, week 1 is not lying more than other weeks *in retrospective*. When looking at how single week performance correlates to rest-of-season performance, week 1 doesn't stick out at all. — Timo Riske (@Timo_NFL) September 15, 2026 For Jets fans, I think this distinction is important because we are rightfully scared that we are being deceived by what we saw. For starters, most Jets fans remember that last year, the Jets’ offense looked significantly better in Week 1 than it did for much of the rest of the season. So naturally, there is going to be some skepticism that we’re watching the same thing happen again. But just because it happened last year doesn’t mean it is any more likely to happen this year. And that brings me to my second point. The Jets Didn’t Dominate In Flukey Ways If we’re going to look at the things that tend to hold steadier from week to week, I think you have to be at least a little more encouraged by the fact that the Jets dominated in some of the more stable metrics. I frequently cite EPA/Play and Success Rate. EPA/Play is incredibly useful and probably the gold standard in today’s NFL for analyzing offensive and defensive efficiency. However, EPA/Play can be volatile in small samples. One or two plays can have an enormous impact on a team’s EPA/Play in a single game. Over the course of a season, when you have several games in the sample, that volatility begins to stabilize. But in the short term, you can absolutely draw the wrong conclusions from it. Success Rate, for those who don’t know, is a little more measured. In the simplest terms, Success Rate is a metric that measures how consistently a team produces a productive outcome relative to the down and distance. Unlike total yards or yards per play, which can be heavily influenced by one explosive play, Success Rate essentially treats each snap as a binary outcome: Was the play successful or was it not? A play is generally considered successful if it gains: On first down, roughly 40% to 50% of the yards needed. On second down, roughly 60% to 70% of the remaining yards needed. On third or fourth down, 100% of the yards needed to move the chains or score a touchdown. Essentially, we are measuring how often a team stays on schedule rather than allowing one or two massive plays to dictate the numbers. And from a Jets perspective, they ranked really well on both sides of the ball. On first and second downs, the Jets ranked fourth in offensive Success Rate last week, led by a rushing attack that was successful on over 55% of its plays. Defensively, the Jets ranked 12th in Success Rate, led by a rushing defense that ranked sixth. Now, there is obviously no guarantee that any of this lasts. Like I said, it’s one game. But I feel a little more confident knowing that the Jets’ dominance wasn’t simply the result of weird turnovers, one major penalty, or one or two explosive offensive plays caused by a busted coverage. They were consistently successful. Which does make…

full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 21: Omar Cooper Jr. #83 of the New York Jets in action during the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 21, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. title: Eagles vs. Commanders: 14 winners, 5 losers, 5 IDKs
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are 1-0 after beating the Washington Commanders to begin the 2026 season. It was a narrow win, yes, but it was an important one to avoid dropping a division game right off the bat. Time to hand out winners, losers, and I don’t knows. For even more analysis, check out my appearance […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates after a touchdown against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles are 1-0 after beating the Washington Commanders to begin the 2026 season. It was a narrow win, yes, but it was an important one to avoid dropping a division game right off the bat. Time to hand out winners, losers, and I don’t knows. For even more analysis, check out my appearance on the PHLY Eagles postgame show along with the legendary Brandon Graham and Bo Wulf! WINNERS JALEN HURTS My biggest takeaway from this game? Hurts looking good while carrying the offense. The box score: 14/25 (56%), 203 passing yards, 3 TD, 0 INT, 122.2 passer rating … 7 carries, 46 rushing yards*. Hurts converting 3rd-and-18 in the fourth quarter was a massive development. The offense ran 21 plays for just 67 yards and three points on their previous five drives. They needed a spark and he gave them one. The offense as a collective sure didn’t play a stellar game. But Hurts made big plays that were the difference in this win. His first touchdown pass to Dallas Goedert, which came on 3rd-and-goal from the 17-yard line, was thrown into a tight window up the seam. His touchdown pass to Dontayvion Wicks was a nice anticipatory ball. He showed admirable aggression by hitting Wicks deep while the receiver was running a clear out route. His completion to DeVonta Smith deep along the right sideline was a beauty. It’s always easier to feel better about your favorite NFL team’s outlook when the quarterback is playing well. This was an encouraging performance from QB1. *Hurts logged at least 46 rushing yards in just two out of 17 games played last year. Since 1950, three NFL quarterbacks have reached 6-0 in Week 1 games: Roger Staubach Johnny Unitas Jalen Hurts — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 14, 2026 Jalen Hurts had an NFL-high 33% non-target rate in Week 1: 11 non-targets (5 scrambles, 3 throwaways, 3 sacks) on 33 dropbacks. Watching the film, he carried the offense (4 scrambles were nice gains, sacks not his fault) despite major protection issues which nullified the script. pic.twitter.com/bI3XJwAuZb — Deniz Selman (@denizselman33) September 16, 2026 MORO OJOMO With the Commanders in position to tie the game with a two-point conversion, Ojomo sniffed out Washington’s shovel pass to John Bates and sealed the deal by tackling the tight end short of the line of scrimmage. Shame that he doesn’t get officially credited for a TFL on that play since the NFL doesn’t count stats from two-point conversions. Ojomo also missed out on being credited with the sack that he created for Jihaad Campbell. No matter, though, because those numbers will come. Ojomo is very much poised for a big year ahead of being a free agent after this season. ZACK BAUN I’m not convinced that Baun gets proper credit for just how good he is. Locally? Probably. Nationally? Don’t think so. Baun finished fourth in offseason off-ball linebacker rankings based on league polling. He’s top two and I don’t think he’s very far behind Fred Warner at No. 1, if at all. Baun was a monster in this game. He logged a team-high 12 tackles (including one TFL, which came on a 3rd-and-1 to force a Commanders punt) and two pass deflections. The Commanders targeted Baun seven times in coverage. He allowed three catches … for negative two yards . He nearly made an impressive leaping interception along the sideline. The pick didn’t count, no, but it was still a high quality coverage rep to help prevent a reception. After Week 1, Baun leads all NFL defenders in “stops,” which are defined as tackles that constitute a failure for the offense by Pro Football Focus charting. Beast! JALEN CARTER Not the flashiest box score but Carter, who played the second-most snaps of any Week 1 interior defender, did make meaningful contributions to the Eagles’ win. First of all, his blocked extra point was huge. Washington would’ve been in a position to tie the game late with a relatively routine kick instead of a two-point conversion try otherwise. He combined with Baun to stop a Commanders 3rd-and-1 run for no gain to force a punt in the first quarter. Carter forced a fumble on the Commanders’ final drive. The Eagles didn’t manage to recover possession but that was just some bad luck. Had they received a more fortunate bounce, his punch out would’ve been viewed as a massive play. Carter also generated some disruption on the Commanders’ attempt to tie the game with a two-point conversion. I don’t know how much it mattered since Ojomo was in good position to stuff Bates … but Carter did get a piece of the Commanders’ tight end that might’ve slowed him down at least a little bit prior to making the catch for a loss. DALLAS GOEDERT For two years in a row now, the Eagles flirted with moving on from Goedert in the offseason. Thank Goedert they didn’t. The Eagles’ top tight end led the team in receiving with four grabs for 77 yards and two touchdowns. Dallas Goedert has scored 13 touchdowns in his last 15 games. — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 14, 2026 SAQUON BARKLEY Barkley’s 15 carries resulted in 83 yards for a 5.5 average. His longest run of the day was a 42-yarder where he looked pretty explosive. Making his production even impressive was that only FIVE of his yards came before contact. According to my math sources, that means he gained 78 yards after contact. That’s a very flattering stat for Barkley. Speaks to his ability to create much out of nothing. Unfortunately, a much less flattering stat for the Eagles’ blockers. DONTAYVION WICKS If there was any doubt that Wicks is WR2, that should be over. His four targets resulted in 73 yards and a touchdown. His 64-yard reception marked the longest of his career, eclipsing his previous record of just 36 yards. Wicks deserves recognition for his effort on that big play because he was running a clear out route to create space for Goedert underneath. Not all receivers (I think we can think of one) put their best foot forward on that kind on play. Wicks also did a really nice job of tracking the ball in the air … while the Commanders’ defensive backs certainly did not. Wicks’ savvy route-running was on display when he got open for his touchdown reception. He cooked Mike Sainristil (or, as Hogs Haven referred to him , Mike StandRealStill … gottem). We’ll see how Wicks fares moving forward but, early on, the decision to trade for him is looking like a win. The Eagles only had to give up a 2026 fifth-round pick and a 2027 sixth-round pick in the deal with the Green Bay Packers. That’s value. DEVONTA SMITH Smitty’s six targets only resulted in three catches for 57 yards but that over-the-shoulder toe-tapping grab along the rights sideline was pretty sweet. JORDAN DAVIS The Commanders’ running backs gained 101 yards on 27 carries for a 3.7 average. Davis contributed to their lack of success on the ground, logging four “stops,” which was third-most on the Eagles. QUINYON MITCHELL and RIQ WOOLEN Terry was not so scary on Sunday: Terry McLaurin matched up against Quinyon Mitchell (9 snaps) or Riq Woolen (13 snaps): 1 target, 0 catches. — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) September 14, 2026 In total, Mitchell was targeted three times, allowing two receptions for 15 yards. Woolen was targeted five times but allowed just one catch for one yard, which did happen to be a touchdown. Looked like Woolen and Marcus Epps had a miscommunication on that snap. It’s not difficult to feel pretty good about the Eagles’ outside cornerbacks right now. DARIUS COOPER Cooper, a wide receiver, finished sixth on the Eagles in tackles on Sunday. He logged four while playing special teams. That’s an impressive number! Consider that special teams coordinator Michael Clay recently noted…

title: Eagles in the community: Jalen Hurts, Jalyx Hunt make huge impacts
summary: The NFL is filled with players who are deeply committed to the communities in which they play, and the Eagles have a whole lot of guys like that on the roster. After their Week 1 game, QB Jalen Hurts and EDGE Jalyx Hunt both announced some hugely impactful initiatives for some high schoolers in Philly. […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts as he runs with the ball off the field against the Washington Commanders following an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL is filled with players who are deeply committed to the communities in which they play, and the Eagles have a whole lot of guys like that on the roster. After their Week 1 game, QB Jalen Hurts and EDGE Jalyx Hunt both announced some hugely impactful initiatives for some high schoolers in Philly. Jalen Hurts and his foundation announced a $600,000 donation to Northeast High School for a new HVAC system that will bring air conditioning into the often hot and uncomfortable conditions. Already this year, 52 schools without AC have had to close early due to the temperatures — that number is down to 52 from 118 when Hurts first committed to this initiative a few years ago. When speaking to the students about this six-figure donation, Hurts explained that education is so important, and the environment to do that important learning is critical to the work getting done. A comfortable space for students to learn is what every kid deserves. Jalen Hurts stopped by Northeast High School in Philadelphia to address the students after making an incredible donation 🥹 pic.twitter.com/n11ruRQ69h — NBC Sports Philadelphia (@NBCSPhilly) September 15, 2026 The next day, across town, Jalyx Hunt and his foundation announced the creation of three scholarships and an endowment at Little Flower Catholic High School for Girls. The scholarships are named after important women in Hunt’s life, his Mother, his Sister, his Grandmother, and his long-time friend. Two awards will cover two years of tuition, and two will cover four years, and the endowment will sustain the scholarships in the future. “This is longevity,” Hunt said, according to the Inquirer’s Olivia Reiner . “I’ve had a lot of talks with [Little Flower president Kristie] Dugan, and I just know that this is something that helps out a lot. A lot of people at this school require and need some sort of help to pay tuition, and if I can do that, I would love to do that.” Hunt has created a long-term connection with the students and staff at Little Flower HS back in 2024 when the Eagles defender wanted to support underfunded school sports teams. He helped the basketball team two years ago, and now he’s having an even bigger impact to a community he’s deeply committed to.
author: Alexis Chassen

title: Zack Baun is NFC Defensive Player of the Week for the second time in his career
summary: Zack Baun was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his stellar performance in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 1 win over the Washington Commanders, according to an official league announcement. From the release: Baun recorded 12 tackles, two passes defensed and a tackle for loss in Philadelphia’s 24-22 win against Washington. Per Next Gen […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts after a loss against the Washington Commanders during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Zack Baun was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his stellar performance in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 1 win over the Washington Commanders, according to an official league announcement. From the release: Baun recorded 12 tackles, two passes defensed and a tackle for loss in Philadelphia’s 24-22 win against Washington. Per Next Gen Stats, Baun was targeted six times in coverage, allowing three receptions for -2 yards, one of two defenders since the start of last season (Denzel Ward) to allow negative receiving yards on five-or-more targets in a game. This is Baun’s second-career Defensive Player of the Week award (Week 10, 2024). He becomes the third Eagles linebacker to win the award multiple times, joining Seth Joyner (three-time winner) and William Thomas (two). Additionally, Baun’s seven “stops,” which are tackles that constitute a loss for the offense, lead all NFL defenders (not just linebackers) after Week 1. Baun is a beast who deserves more national praise, so, it’s nice to see him recognized in this capacity. I’m just saying, Fred Warner has zero NFC Defensive Player of the Week awards since Baun became a full-time starter and earned two. Baun is the first Eagles player to win NFC Defensive Player of the Week since Cooper DeJean was honored for his Week 16 performance last season.

What does it mean? Are the Eagles about to sign Zach Ertz or make another big move?! Maybe! But maybe not. It’s hardly uncommon for NFL […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 8: Philadelphia Eagles general manager Howie Roseman walks the field prior to the game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on December 8, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles created some cap space in 2026 and 2027 by converting portions of Nolan Smith’s salaries over the next two years into bonuses, according to Spotrac. The #Eagles converted $1.24M of OLB Nolan Smith's salary into signing bonus, creating $992k of cap space. They also converted $12.5M of his 2027 5th-year option salary into an option bonus, opening up $10M of 2027 cap space. — Spotrac (@spotrac) September 16, 2026 Gasp! What does it mean? Are the Eagles about to sign Zach Ertz or make another big move?! Maybe! But maybe not. It’s hardly uncommon for NFL teams — the Eagles included — to create cap space for flexibility purposes … and not necessarily because they immediately make a big move with the newly freed up funds. As a reminder, any cap space that the Eagles free up in the short-term will be rolled over into the future if it goes unused. So, we’ll see if Howie Roseman truly has something up his sleeve or not. Prior to this move, the Eagles were listed at $12,371,633 in 2026 cap space from Over The Cap . For context, that ranked 13th-most in the league. They had $33,104,750 in 2027 cap space, which ranked 14th-most.

title: Eagles-Commanders Film Review: Offense did some good things but must improve
summary: It’s easy to look at the Eagles scoring 24 points, averaging six yards per play, and conclude the offense played well in the first game of the season. Unfortunately, I don’t think it did. The Eagles generated 318 yards, but 180 of them came on four plays. They finished with only 10 first downs, punted […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Saquon Barkley #26 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs against Nick Cross #25 of the Washington Commanders in the second quarter of a game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s easy to look at the Eagles scoring 24 points, averaging six yards per play, and conclude the offense played well in the first game of the season. Unfortunately, I don’t think it did. The Eagles generated 318 yards, but 180 of them came on four plays. They finished with only 10 first downs, punted seven times, and had six possessions without earning a single first down. They also went three-and-out on three consecutive drives in the third quarter. Elite players made enough elite plays to win the game, but they showed little consistency. We saw this at times last season. The Eagles won games despite the offense failing to establish any rhythm, and the result often disguised the performance. That is not sustainable. However, it is Week 1. Sean Mannion is a brand-new offensive coordinator, and the Eagles are still working out what this offense should look like. I’m not panicking after one game. The important thing is whether Mannion recognizes the problems and adapts. Let’s get into the film. We are back, baby! Offense The contrast between the Eagles’ different personnel groupings was significant in this one. They rushed for 118 yards on 14 attempts from 11 personnel, compared with only 18 yards on 11 attempts from 12 personnel. Those figures include Hurts’ rushing production and are heavily influenced by Barkley’s 42-yard run, so they require some context. Still, Washington consistently matched 12 personnel with its base defense, and the Eagles repeatedly ran into condensed, crowded fronts. We saw this exact issue last year. A lot of teams run well out of condensed formations, but I’ve yet to see the Eagles do it well. This counter run was a bad early sign. Dallas Goedert’s positioning makes the pull predictable, there is no real misdirection, and Washington can attack downhill without hesitation. I hoped we would see more misdirection in the run game. The Eagles ran counter only once, and I was surprised that we didn’t see more duo. The run game was overwhelmingly zone-based, which isn’t a shock considering Mannion’s background, but I’m still a little concerned about how it fits our personnel. Individual execution was a problem, but the structure did not provide enough help at times. Running repeatedly from heavy personnel into stacked boxes is making life unnecessarily difficult. We are back! Eagles Week 1 Offense Thread vs. Washington. 1) I started worrying a little early on when I saw this rep of Counter early on. The Eagles seemed to run into stacked boxes from heavy personnel far too often, and it ended as you would have expected. This was the only… pic.twitter.com/JLs7tYeFpN — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 14, 2026 Right, just a heads up. I posted the original thread online before Landon Dickerson acknowledged that he had been playing hurt and was subsequently placed on injured reserve. My immediate reaction to the film was that his movement looked completely wrong. We now know why. I didn’t want to kill him in the review, but I could have posted 30 clips of him looking bad. It was probably the worst offensive line film I’ve watched from an individual. Dickerson played all 55 offensive snaps despite clearly being unable to move properly. He was charged with four pressures, including a sack. I am not blaming Dickerson for that performance. The coaches deserve criticism for letting an obviously compromised player stay on the field for the entire game. I can’t just ignore Dickerson in this review because his play made it really hard to run the offense. But, just be aware I’m not blaming him for this. You can see the physical limitation here. Dickerson cannot adjust his feet or redirect with the defender. This isn’t normal poor technique from a player losing an isolated rep. His body won’t let him execute the assignment. The guy could barely move. The Eagles put both Dickerson and the rest of the offense in a terrible position by asking him to play through it. 2) We saw signs of what was to come early on. I really don't want to spend the whole thread kicking Landon Dickerson, since he's already faced enough criticism, but it really wasn't good. Like, unplayable levels of not good. Just ignore the end result and watch his movement.… pic.twitter.com/ScWunMtILO — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 14, 2026 This was one of the Eagles’ better outside-zone runs, and it highlights the importance of personnel. Johnny Mundt does an excellent job controlling the edge, allowing Barkley to press the run before getting outside. The issue with Mundt is when he’s on the field, the Eagles’ offense can become predictable. They must find a way to get him involved as a receiver at times. The Eagles do not have many receivers who can consistently move defenders from condensed formations. Makai Lemon and DeVonta Smith aren’t big receivers, so a blocking tight end matters. Mundt creates an edge here that the Eagles struggled to establish on several other outside-zone attempts. I’m still concerned about the Eagles leaning too heavily on outside zone. If it is going to become a foundational concept, they must choose their moments more effectively and connect it to the passing game. After showing Washington this look, I expected to see more play-action bootlegs or movement passes building from the same action. Instead, the run and pass games often felt disconnected. Which was a shame, considering everything we have read about Mannion. 3) Hey, a rare nice rep of outside zone! I'm very concerned about the Eagles living in the outside zone world, but if you are going to use it more, you need to pick your moments better. This works because the safety comes downhill from the opposite side, and they are running… pic.twitter.com/kdsuIbsF5h — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 14, 2026 Here is another example of Dickerson’s injury affecting the offense. Once again, forget the outcome and focus on his lower body. His feet are in no position to make contact, and he cannot generate any power or control because his base has collapsed. 4) I promise I won't post a whole thread of Dickerson's failings, but you can't analyze the offense without looking at his performance. You have plays like this that can't even get going. Again, ignore the result; just focus on the movement and technique. Look at the position… pic.twitter.com/FRIT4eRt9z — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 14, 2026 This is the first of the explosive plays that carried the offense. The under center running game struggled, but the Eagles must keep developing it because it enables throws like this. The Eagles use play action and a three-level stretch concept. Based on the design, the ball should go to Goedert, but Hurts likes the matchup downfield and makes an extremely aggressive throw to Dontayvion Wicks. The velocity and placement are outstanding. Hurts’ deep-ball accuracy remains one of the offense’s cheat codes. Wicks deserves enormous credit, too. He runs the clear-out route, but he runs it hard and stays ready for the football. We have seen far too many clear-out routes over the years where a receiver (who might currently be on the Patriots…) slows down or never expects the pass. Wicks stays engaged throughout the whole rep, locates the ball, and finishes the play for a big gain. If you are running a route, you always have to believe the ball might come your way. This is excellent. (should have posted this before the previous play) 5) Hurts' deep ball accuracy remains the offense's cheat code. The velocity and ball placement are just so good. The under center run game didn't work particularly well, but the Eagles need to keep working it into the offense… pic.twitter.com/E2dl28GTnL — Jonny Page…

title: Eagles roster news: Landon Dickerson to IR among 3 moves
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced three roster moves on Tuesday afternoon. Here’s an overview: Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. LANDON DICKERSON Dickerson to IR was previously reported on Monday evening. The Eagles’ three-time Pro Bowl left guard admitted that he “was a complete liability” during the team’s Week 1 win over […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JUNE 10: Philadelphia Eagles guard Landon Dickerson #69 looks on during the Philadelphia Eagles off season minicamp on June 10th, 2026 at the Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced three roster moves on Tuesday afternoon. Here’s an overview: OG Landon Dickerson was placed on injured reserve. WR Britain Covey was signed from the practice squad to the active roster. TE Josiah Deguara was signed to the practice squad. Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. LANDON DICKERSON Dickerson to IR was previously reported on Monday evening. The Eagles’ three-time Pro Bowl left guard admitted that he “was a complete liability” during the team’s Week 1 win over the Washington Commanders. Dickerson also added that he got hurt in training camp and he’s hopeful that the time off will help him get fully healthy. By going on IR, he’s automatically ineligible to play in the Eagles’ next four games. The soonest he can return to the active roster is Week 6. One must wonder if this rest will truly allow Dickerson to get back to form. It seems entirely possible that he’s just physically diminished at this point in his career. That’s a very sad and unfortunate thought … but there’s much to suggest that might be the case: Dickerson has an extensive injury history dating back to his college football days. Dickerson struggled in 2025. Speaking shortly after the conclusion of last season, Dickerson did not sound very optimistic about making a full recovery . Dickerson reportedly gave thought to retiring in the offseason. He’s since denied as much … but he reportedly agreed to a revised deal where he took a pay cut and had a year lopped off his contract. Why would he do that if he felt great about his outlook? Dickerson struggled in training camp this summer and looked to be lumbering around at times. Speaking on SportsRadio 94WIP on Tuesday, Nick Sirianni said the Eagles will be missing Dickerson “ for the foreseeable future .” Dickerson himself talked about the benefit of going on IR in order to “have a good stretch at the back end of the season.” Even putting his health aside, which is impossible to do, there’s question about Dickerson’s fit in the Eagles’ new blocking scheme. To be clear, I hope my skepticism is wrong. It would be such a massive deal if he’s able to return to form. I tend to think that the Eagles didn’t want to outright bench Dickerson, who has earned legendary status for sacrificing his body in order for the team to win Super Bowl LIX. I think he might be done and they’re hoping that the replacement plan will work out well so they don’t have to put him back on the field. It remains to be seen how the Eagles will actually replace him. The expectation is that Drew Kendall will take over at left guard … but we’ll see if that’s the case. BRITAIN COVEY The Eagles temporarily elevated Covey from the practice squad in Week 1 to be their punt returner against the Commanders. To no surprise, he was effective in that capacity. Now he’s back on the roster. This development means that the Eagles are currently carrying seven wide receivers on the roster: DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown, Elijah Moore, and Covey. Smith, Wicks, and Lemon comprise the top three. Cooper saw limited playing time on offense as a fourth receiver in addition to being a major factor on special teams coverage. Brown was active in Week 1 but played zero snaps while Moore was a healthy scratch. JOSIAH DEGUARA The 29-year-old Deguara was originally a third-round pick (No. 94 overall) by the Green Bay Packers in the 2020 NFL Draft. He notably overlapped with current Eagles tight ends coach and run game coordinator Ryan Mahaffey on the Packers from 2021-2023. Making 12 starts in 77 regular season games, Deguara has logged 66 career targets for 53 receptions, 471 receiving yards, and three touchdowns. His most recent NFL stop prior to this was a three-day stint on the New York Giants’ roster back in late August. With the Eagles recently placing Eli Stowers on injured reserve , the team only had three tight ends on the roster (Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, E.J. Jenkins) and none on the practice squad. Now they have a fourth tight end for practice purposes, at the very least. STILL ONE OPEN ROSTER SPOT Dickerson and Stowers going to IR opened up two roster spots. Signing Covey filled one of those openings. The Birds still have one vacancy remaining.

title: NFL Week 1 overreactions and exaggerations
summary: Last season in Week 1 the Raiders beat the Patriots. They then went completely separate ways, the Patriots going 14-3 and to the Super Bowl, the Raiders to 3-14 and the #1 overall pick. Also that week the Vikings beat the Bears, with JJ McCarthy throwing 3 TDs. The Bears went on to win the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 13: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the first quarter against the Carolina Panthers of the game at Bank of America Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last season in Week 1 the Raiders beat the Patriots. They then went completely separate ways, the Patriots going 14-3 and to the Super Bowl, the Raiders to 3-14 and the #1 overall pick. Also that week the Vikings beat the Bears, with JJ McCarthy throwing 3 TDs. The Bears went on to win the NFC North, the Vikings finished with the joint worst record in division and JJ McCarthy fell apart. So Week 1 can be an aberration. But we can still overreact. The New Dream Team The Rams are cooked. No team scored fewer points in Week 1 than Sean McVay’s star studded and jet lagged team. The Falcons were on their third string QB, who had back spasms, and the Dolphins, Browns, and Titans participated in football games; all outscored the Super Bowl favorites. Myles Garrett is out for at least four weeks after doing absolutely nothing in the first week. Maybe Aaron Donald, who hasn’t played in two years, could play soon and turn things around. It’s always good to count on retirees in a football game. Regression is mean Drake Maye threw three interceptions and helped the Patriots blow a 10 point lead to Drew Lock. If you’re keeping track at home, that’s now 11 turnovers in five straight games against teams that made the playoffs last year. Next up: another 2025 playoff team! If the Lions are Super Bowl contenders, then so are the Saints Tyler Shough had 410 yards and 3 TDs and Chris Olave had 182 yards on 10 catches as the Lions and Saints traded punches over five quarters. New Orleans got behind 21-0 but stormed back, on the road, to tie the game 24-24 with just over a minute to play and lost on a failed 2 point conversion. If the Saints are mid, then so are the Lions Detroit gave up 410 yards and 3 TDs to Tyler Shough, and needed a failed two point conversion in OT to defeat New Orleans at home after blowing a 21 point lead. Bears and Panthers, oh my If you’re Chicago or Carolina, you’ve got to feel really good about your offense. The Bears had two 100 yard rushers, a staple of a Ben Johnson offense! Bryce Young had 361 yards and 3 TDs, one of the best games of his career! If you’re Chicago or Carolina, you’ve got to feel pretty horrible about your defense. The Panthers giving up 59 points is of course extremely embarrassing and should result in several changes to the lineup. But the Bears gave up 37 points, despite 3 takeaways. It’s more of the same for the Bears, who last year led the league in turnovers but still had just the 23rd scoring defense. Where were you when… The Chargers, who have the greatest QB of all time in Justin Hebert and football genius Mike McDaniel, scored an unbelievable 14 points against the vaunted Arizona Cardinals. McDaniel’s game plan and Herbert’s jersey are on their way to Canton. Packers offense: 22 points in four quarters. Packers defense: 22 points in the fourth quarter. The Greatest Offense There Is, formerly known as the Dallas Cowboys, had two punts and a turnover on their first four possessions. Cam Skattebo’s quest for 300 carries for 2000 yards (at least 117.7 yards per game at 6.7 yards per carry) began with 18 carries for 81 yards (4.5 yards per carry). Congratulations to Dontayvion Wicks and Makai Lemon, who lead the league in yards per reception and negative yards per reception, respectively!
